There is no Recycle Bin, no undo, and no "are you sure?" prompt by default. Once you run rm , the file is gone. Always double-check your command before pressing Enter. When in doubt, move the file somewhere else with mv rather than deleting it outright. rm hello-backup.txt rm -r old-projects/ rm hello-backup.txt — permanently deletes the file hello-backup.txt . No second chance. rm -r old-projects/ — deletes the folder old-projects and everything inside it recursively. This is the most powerful (and dangerous) form of the command. Triple-check the folder name before pressing Enter. Tip: Add the -i flag to make rm ask "are you sure?" before each deletion: rm -i hello-backup.txt . Type y and Enter to confirm, or n and Enter to skip. Recommended while you are still learning. Editing Files in the Terminal with nano Sometimes you need to create or edit a text file without leaving the terminal — for example when following a guide that says "edit this configuration file". The easiest text editor built into Raspberry Pi OS is called nano . Unlike some other terminal editors, nano tells you what every key does at the bottom of the screen, so you never feel lost. In plain words: nano is a terminal-based text editor. It opens a file inside the terminal window itself, lets you type and edit like a basic notepad, and saves the file when you tell it to — all without using a mouse. Opening and Editing a File with nano nano notes.txt nano notes.txt — opens (or creates, if it does not exist) a file called notes.txt in the nano editor. The terminal screen changes: the file contents appear in the middle, your cursor is at the top, and two rows of keyboard shortcuts appear at the bottom. The caret symbol ( ^ ) in those shortcuts means Ctrl — so ^X means Ctrl + X. Once nano is open, the essential key combinations are: Key What it does Arrow keys Move the cursor around Ctrl + O then Enter Save the file ("Write Out") Ctrl + X Exit nano (it will ask you to save if you made changes) Ctrl + K Cut the current line Ctrl + U Paste the cut line Ctrl + W Search for text (type your search word, then press Enter) Ctrl + G Open the full help page inside nano Tip: The simplest way to save and exit is: press Ctrl + X , then when nano asks "Save modified buffer?", press Y , then press Enter to confirm the filename. Three key presses and you are done. A Quick nano Practice Type nano mynote.txt and press Enter. Nano opens with a blank file. Type a few lines of text — anything you like. Press Ctrl + O to save. Nano shows the filename at the bottom — press Enter to confirm. Press Ctrl + X to exit. You are back at the normal prompt. Type cat mynote.txt to verify the file was saved correctly. sudo — Running Commands as Administrator Some tasks on your Pi — installing software, changing system settings, editing configuration files outside your home folder — require administrator privileges . On Raspberry Pi OS, the way to do this is to put the word sudo in front of your command. In plain words: sudo stands for "superuser do". It temporarily grants your command the power of the root (system administrator) account. Without sudo , the system refuses to touch files that belong to it. With sudo , you become, for just that one command, the most powerful user on the machine. Careful: sudo bypasses all normal safety checks. A sudo command can delete system files, change passwords, or break the operating system if used incorrectly. Only use sudo when a guide or command specifically requires it, and always double-check what you are typing before you press Enter. How sudo Works sudo apt update sudo — run the following command with administrator (root) privileges. apt update — refresh the Pi's list of available software packages from the internet. This command is explained fully in Chapter 7, but it serves as a perfect example: it needs to write to system folders, so it requires sudo . The first time you use sudo in a session, the terminal will ask for your own password (not a separate admin password). Type it and press Enter — the characters will not appear on screen as you type, which is normal. Your password is remembered for a few minutes, so you will not be asked again immediately. Note: On Raspberry Pi OS, the default user (the account you set up on first boot) is automatically granted sudo access. You do not need to do anything special to enable it. Editing a System File with sudo nano A very common pattern in Pi guides is using sudo together with nano to edit a configuration file that belongs to the system: sudo nano /etc/hostname sudo — open the following file with administrator rights, so nano is allowed to save changes to it. nano /etc/hostname — opens the file /etc/hostname , which contains a single line: your Pi's network name. Without sudo , nano would open the file but refuse to save it, because ordinary users are not allowed to change system files. With sudo , you can edit and save it normally. Use the same Ctrl + O / Ctrl + X steps as before. Tip: If you ever see a message like Permission denied when running a command, the fix is usually to put sudo in front of it. But think first: does it make sense for this command to need administrator access? If you are just editing a file in your home folder, Permission denied usually means you typed the wrong path instead. Pipes and grep — Connecting Commands Together One of the most powerful features of the Linux terminal is the ability to chain commands together so that the output of one command flows directly into the next. The symbol that joins them is called the pipe : | (the vertical bar on your keyboard, usually above the backslash key). In plain words: A pipe is a connection between two commands. Whatever the first command would normally print to the screen is instead handed directly to the second command as its input. You can chain as many commands as you like with pipes. grep — Search for Text grep searches for a word or pattern in a file (or in output piped to it) and prints only the matching lines. It is one of the most useful commands in the terminal. grep "raspberry" /etc/os-release grep -i "raspberry" /etc/os-release grep "raspberry" /etc/os-release — search the file /etc/os-release for lines that contain the word "raspberry" (case-sensitive) and print only those lines. grep -i "raspberry" /etc/os-release — the -i flag makes the search case-insensitive, so it matches "raspberry", "Raspberry", "RASPBERRY", etc. Quote your search word if it contains spaces. Using Pipes to Filter Output Now combine ls with grep using a pipe: ls /usr/bin | grep python ls /usr/bin — lists everything in the /usr/bin folder, which contains hundreds of installed programs. On its own, the output would scroll off the screen. | — the pipe: sends that long list to the next command instead of printing it. grep python — filters the list, printing only the lines that contain the word "python". This lets you instantly see which Python-related programs are installed, without scrolling through hundreds of lines. history | grep sudo history — produces your full command history as a list of lines. | — pipes that list to grep. grep sudo — shows only the lines from your history that contained the word "sudo". Useful for finding a complex command you typed earlier. Getting Help at Any Time --help — Quick Reference Almost every command accepts a --help flag that prints a short summary of what it does and which options are available. ls --help ls --help — prints a concise description of the ls command and all its flags, right in the terminal. Scroll up to read it all. Replace ls with any other command name to get help for that command instead. man — The Full Manual In plain words: A man page (short for manual page ) is the built-in documentation for a command. Every standard Linux command has one. They are detailed and sometimes quite technical, but they are always accurate. man ls man ls — opens the full manual page for ls . Navigate it the same way as less : Space to scroll down, B to go back, / to search, Q to quit. Replace ls with any command name to read its manual. Note: Man pages can look intimidating because they are written for experienced users. Scroll past the dense "SYNOPSIS" section at the top and look for the "DESCRIPTION" and "EXAMPLES" sections — those are usually much more readable. Working Smarter: Shortcuts That Save Typing The terminal has several built-in features that make typing much faster. Use these from your very first session — they become automatic very quickly. Tab Auto-completion This is perhaps the single most useful feature in the terminal. When you start typing a command or a filename and press the Tab key, the shell tries to complete it for you automatically. cd Doc Type cd Doc and then press Tab (do not press Enter yet). If there is only one folder starting with "Doc", the shell will complete it to cd Documents instantly. If there are several matches (say Documents and Downloads ), press Tab a second time to see a list of all options. Then type enough extra letters to make it unique and press Tab once more. Tip: Tab-completion works for command names too, not just file and folder names. Type mk and press Tab twice to see all commands that start with "mk". The Up Arrow — Command History The shell remembers every command you have typed in this session (and across sessions). Press the Up arrow key to scroll back through previous commands. Press Down arrow to go forward again. Press Enter to run the selected command, or edit it first if you want to change something. history — See Your Full Command History history history 20 history — prints a numbered list of all the commands you have typed, most recent at the bottom. Each line has a number on the left. history 20 — shows only the last 20 commands. Replace 20 with any number you like. Tip: You can re-run any command from the history list by typing ! followed by its number. For example, if command number 42 was ls -lah Documents , typing !42 and pressing Enter runs it again instantly. Or type !! to repeat the very last command. Ctrl + C — Stop a Running Command Sometimes a command gets stuck, takes too long, or you just change your mind. Ctrl + C sends a "stop" signal to whatever is currently running in the terminal and returns you to the prompt. ping google.com ping google.com — checks whether your Pi can reach google.com over the internet, printing one line per second indefinitely. To stop it, press Ctrl + C . You will see a summary line and then your prompt returns. Ctrl + C is safe to use on any command that has "gone quiet" or seems stuck. Note: Ctrl + C in the terminal is completely different from Ctrl + C in Windows (which copies selected text). In the terminal, copying selected text is usually done with Ctrl + Shift + C , and pasting is Ctrl + Shift + V . Putting it All Together: A Practice Session The best way to learn these commands is to use them. Open a terminal and follow these steps — you cannot break anything here: Open the terminal. Check where you are: type pwd and press Enter. You should see /home/pi (or your username). List what is already in your home folder: type ls and press Enter. Then try ls -lah to see hidden files and file sizes. Create a practice folder: type mkdir terminal-practice and press Enter. Move into it: type cd ter then press Tab to auto-complete, then Enter. Confirm you are inside it: type pwd . You should see /home/pi/terminal-practice . Create a file with echo: type echo My first terminal file > notes.txt and press Enter. Read it back: type cat notes.txt . You should see My first terminal file . Add a second line: type echo A second line >> notes.txt then cat notes.txt again. Open the file in nano: type nano notes.txt . Add a third line, then press Ctrl + O , Enter to save, then Ctrl + X to exit. Search inside the file: type grep "line" notes.txt to see only the lines containing the word "line". Make a copy: type cp notes.txt notes-backup.txt . Then ls to see both files. Rename the backup: type mv notes-backup.txt backup.txt . Then ls again. Delete the backup: type rm backup.txt . Then ls to confirm it is gone. Go back to your home folder: type cd ~ . Clear the screen: press Ctrl + L . If you made it through all of those without an error message, you already know more about the Linux command line than many people who use computers every day. Well done. Quick Reference: Commands at a Glance Command What it does Example pwd Print current folder path pwd ls List files in a folder ls -lah cd Change current folder cd Documents clear Clear the screen clear or Ctrl + L mkdir Create a new folder mkdir projects touch Create an empty file touch notes.txt echo Print text or write to a file echo hi > file.txt cat Print file contents cat notes.txt less Scroll through a long file less bigfile.txt nano Edit a file in the terminal nano notes.txt cp Copy a file or folder cp a.txt b.txt mv Move or rename mv old.txt new.txt rm Delete (no undo!) rm old.txt sudo Run as administrator sudo apt update grep Search for text in output or a file grep "word" file.txt | Pipe output into another command ls | grep python history Show command history history 20 man Open full manual man ls --help Quick command summary ls --help Tab Auto-complete name Type cd Doc + Tab ↑ / ↓ Scroll command history (press arrow key) Ctrl + C Stop running command (press together) Key terms Terminal — a window in which you type commands and read their text output. Shell — the program that runs inside the terminal, reads your commands, and executes them. Raspberry Pi OS uses Bash. Bash — the most common Linux shell; the one you are using on your Pi. Prompt — the line of text the shell prints before your cursor, showing your username, machine name, and current folder. Root ( / ) — the very top of the Linux filesystem tree. Every path starts here. Home folder ( ~ ) — your personal folder, usually /home/pi . The tilde is a shortcut for it. Path — the address of a file or folder. An absolute path starts with / ; a relative path starts from wherever you currently are. Flag / option — a modifier added to a command (e.g. -l , --help ) that changes its behaviour. Argument — the thing a command acts on — usually a file name or folder path. Tab completion — pressing Tab to let the shell finish typing a filename or command for you. man page — the built-in manual for a command, opened with man <commandname> . Redirect ( > , >> ) — sending a command's output into a file instead of the screen. > overwrites; >> appends. Pipe ( | ) — connects two commands so the output of the first becomes the input of the second. grep — a command that searches text for lines matching a word or pattern, printing only the matching lines. nano — a beginner-friendly text editor that runs inside the terminal. Save with Ctrl + O, exit with Ctrl + X. sudo — a prefix that runs a command with full administrator (root) privileges. Use only when required. Ctrl + C — the keyboard shortcut to stop any running command and return to the prompt. Chapter summary The terminal is a text window where you type commands directly; Bash is the shell (the "brain") that runs inside it. The prompt tells you your username, machine name, and current folder; the $ sign means "ready for input". The entire Linux filesystem is one tree starting at / ; your personal files live in /home/pi , written as ~ . Every command follows the pattern: command -options arguments . The essential navigation commands are pwd (where am I?), ls (what is here?), and cd (take me somewhere). You can create files with touch and echo , read them with cat and less , edit them with nano , copy with cp , move/rename with mv , and delete with rm — but remember rm has no undo. Use sudo in front of a command when you need administrator privileges; your own password will be requested and remembered briefly. The pipe character | connects commands together; grep filters output to show only matching lines — together they are incredibly powerful. Tab auto-completion and the Up arrow key save enormous amounts of typing; use them from day one. Get help for any command with --help for a quick summary or man <command> for the full manual. Press Ctrl + C to stop any command that is running or seems stuck.

title: Files, Folders & Permissions
headings: The Filing Cabinet in Your Pi
Copying, Moving, Renaming and Deleting Files
Symbolic Links — Shortcuts on the Command Line
Checking Detailed File Information with stat
sudo, Root, and Why Your Password Is Asked
Putting It All Together — A Practical Workflow
text: Your Raspberry Pi holds everything — programs, settings, photos, scripts — as files organised into folders. In this chapter you will learn to create, view, copy, move and delete files confidently from the terminal, explore the important folders that make up your Pi's filing system, and then unravel one of Linux's most important ideas: the permission system that decides who is allowed to read, change or run each file. By the end you will know exactly what that cryptic drwxr-xr-x string means, and why your Pi sometimes asks "are you sure you're allowed to do that?" The Filing Cabinet in Your Pi Think of your Pi's storage as a giant filing cabinet. At the very top is a single folder called the root of the filesystem, written as a lone forward-slash / . Every other folder and file lives somewhere inside that root, connected in a tree of branches — similar to the folder tree you see in Windows Explorer, just with different names. When you open a terminal you land in your home folder , which is /home/pi (assuming your username is pi , the default on Raspberry Pi OS). In plain words: A filesystem is just the organised layout of all files and folders on your storage card — the same idea as the folders you see in Windows, just with a forward-slash at the top instead of a drive letter like C:\ . You already met the cd (change directory) and ls (list) commands in Chapter 6. This chapter builds on those foundations. Important System Folders Linux uses a standard set of top-level folders that every Raspberry Pi shares. You do not need to memorise all of them, but knowing the main ones prevents confusion when commands refer to them. / (root of everything) /home Your files live here /home/pi /etc System config files /usr Installed programs /var Logs & variable data /tmp Temporary files /boot Bootloader files Folder What lives there Safe to edit? /home/pi Your personal documents, scripts and projects Yes — it is yours /etc System-wide configuration files (network, users, etc.) With sudo only /usr Installed programs and their support files With sudo only /var/log Log files written by the system and services Read freely; write with sudo /tmp Scratch space — cleared on every reboot Yes — wiped on restart /boot/firmware Low-level startup files (config.txt, kernel) Only if you know why The top-level folders (directories) in your Pi's filesystem. Your everyday work happens in /home/pi . The others are system territory — readable but edited only with care. Note: On Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm the boot configuration file lives at /boot/firmware/config.txt (not the older location /boot/config.txt ). If you ever need to tweak the Pi's hardware settings, that is the right file to edit with sudo nano /boot/firmware/config.txt . Editing Text Files with nano The terminal text editor that comes pre-installed on Raspberry Pi OS and is easiest for beginners is called nano . It works entirely inside the terminal window — no mouse needed — and shows its most important keyboard shortcuts along the bottom of the screen at all times. Opening or Creating a File To open an existing file, or to create a new one if it does not exist yet, type nano followed by the filename: nano mynotes.txt Opens mynotes.txt in the nano editor. If the file does not exist yet, nano creates a blank one for you. The file is not actually saved to disk until you explicitly save it. Once inside nano, you can type normally. The cursor moves with your arrow keys. The very bottom of the screen shows a list of shortcuts — the ^ symbol means the Ctrl key. The Essential nano Shortcuts Shortcut What it does Ctrl + O Write Out (save). nano asks you to confirm the filename — just press Enter to accept. Enter (after Ctrl-O) Confirms the filename and writes the file to disk. Ctrl + X Exit nano. If you have unsaved changes, nano asks whether to save them first. Ctrl + K Cut the current line (stores it in a clipboard). Ctrl + U Paste the cut line back. Ctrl + W Search (Where is?). Type a word and press Enter to find it. Ctrl + G Open the help screen with a full list of shortcuts. Ctrl + _ Go to a specific line number (useful when an error message says "line 42"). Tip: The workflow to remember is: type your text → Ctrl-O → Enter → Ctrl-X . That is "save then quit". You will do this hundreds of times. A Quick Practice Run Open a terminal and type nano hello.txt then press Enter . Type a sentence, for example: Hello from my Raspberry Pi! Press Ctrl + O . A prompt appears at the bottom asking "File Name to Write: hello.txt". Press Enter to confirm. You will see "[ Wrote 1 line ]" at the bottom. Press Ctrl + X to exit back to the normal terminal prompt. Type ls and you will see hello.txt is now in your folder. Viewing Files Without Editing Them Sometimes you just want to read a file, not change it. Linux gives you several commands for this, each suited to different situations. cat — Print the Whole File cat hello.txt Prints every line of hello.txt straight to the screen. "cat" is short for "concatenate" — it was originally designed to join files together, but it is most commonly used to quickly view short files. Tip: cat is best for short files. If the file is hundreds of lines long, the text will scroll past faster than you can read it. Use less instead. less — Scroll Through a Long File less /etc/os-release Opens the file /etc/os-release (which contains information about the operating system version) in a scrollable viewer. Use the arrow keys or Page Up / Page Down to scroll. Press Q to quit and return to the terminal. In plain words: less is like a reading mode for the terminal — the file stays still on screen until you choose to scroll or quit. The name is a tongue-in-cheek joke: an older tool was called more , and less can do more than more . head and tail — See the Beginning or End head -n 10 /etc/os-release tail -n 10 /etc/os-release Line 1: Shows only the first 10 lines of the file. The -n 10 part means "10 lines" — you can change the number to whatever you need. Line 2: Shows only the last 10 lines of the file. This is especially useful for log files, where the most recent events appear at the bottom. Tip: If something goes wrong and you want to check the system log, the best command on Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm is journalctl -n 50 — this shows the last 50 log entries from the system journal. (Older guides may say tail /var/log/syslog ; that file only exists if you have installed extra logging software.) Identifying a File's Type On Linux, file extensions like .txt are just a naming convention — the system does not rely on them. If you are ever unsure what kind of file something is, use the file command: file hello.txt file /bin/ls Line 1: Analyses hello.txt and reports something like "ASCII text" — confirming it is a plain text file you can read safely. Line 2: Analyses the ls program and reports it as an "ELF 64-bit LSB executable" — a compiled program, not a text file. You would never try to read this with cat . Creating Empty Files with touch Sometimes you want to create a blank file without opening an editor — for example to mark a placeholder in a folder or to quickly test a command. The touch command does exactly this: touch myfile.txt Creates an empty file called myfile.txt in the current folder. If the file already exists, touch simply updates its "last modified" timestamp without changing its contents. The file is harmless and can be deleted any time. Copying, Moving, Renaming and Deleting Files Copying Files — cp cp hello.txt hello_backup.txt Makes an exact copy of hello.txt and calls the copy hello_backup.txt . Both files now exist side by side. To copy a file into a different folder: cp hello.txt Documents/hello.txt Copies hello.txt into your Documents folder. The original file stays where it is. To copy an entire folder and everything inside it, add the -r flag (which means "recursive" — go into every sub-folder too): cp -r myproject myproject_backup Copies the folder myproject and all its contents into a new folder called myproject_backup . Moving and Renaming — mv The mv command does double duty: it both moves a file to a new location and renames it. Linux treats these as the same action — a rename is simply moving a file to the same folder but with a new name. mv hello.txt greetings.txt Renames hello.txt to greetings.txt . The file itself does not move — only its name changes. mv greetings.txt Documents/greetings.txt Moves greetings.txt into the Documents folder. It disappears from the current folder. Careful: mv does not ask for confirmation. If you move a file to a location where another file with the same name already exists, the existing file is silently overwritten and cannot be recovered. Double-check your target path before pressing Enter. Deleting Files — rm rm hello_backup.txt Permanently deletes hello_backup.txt . There is no Recycle Bin on the Linux command line — once deleted, the file is gone. Careful: The Linux terminal has no undo and no Recycle Bin. Files deleted with rm are gone immediately and permanently. Always double-check the filename before pressing Enter. As a beginner, consider making copies of important files before experimenting. To delete a folder and everything inside it: rm -r myproject_backup Deletes the myproject_backup folder and every file and sub-folder inside it. The -r flag means "recursive" — without it, rm refuses to delete a folder. Careful: Never type rm -rf / or rm -rf * in your home folder. The -f flag means "force" and skips all warnings. Combined with a wide pattern, this can erase your entire system. If you ever see instructions online asking you to run a command like that, stop and ask someone you trust first. Creating Folders — mkdir mkdir myprojects mkdir -p myprojects/python/lesson1 Line 1: Creates a new folder called myprojects inside the current directory. Line 2: Creates the full path myprojects/python/lesson1 in one go, even if none of those folders exist yet. The -p flag means "make parent folders as needed". Finding Files with find As your Pi accumulates files it becomes harder to remember exactly where something is. The find command searches for files and folders matching a pattern. find ~ -name "hello.txt" Searches your entire home folder (the ~ shortcut) for anything named exactly hello.txt . The result is the full path to every matching file, for example /home/pi/hello.txt . find ~ -name "*.txt" Searches your home folder for every file whose name ends with .txt . The quotes around "*.txt" are important — without them the shell might expand the * before find sees it, giving unexpected results. find ~ -name "*.py" -type f Searches for files (not folders) ending in .py (Python scripts). The -type f part means "only match regular files", which stops find from listing folder names that happen to end in .py . Tip: find can be slow if you search the entire system starting from / . Narrow the search by starting from your home folder ( ~ ) or a specific sub-folder whenever possible. Using Wildcards Safely In plain words: A wildcard is a special character that stands in for "anything". The most common one is the asterisk * , which matches any number of any characters in a filename. Wildcards let you work with many files at once without typing each name: ls *.txt cp *.txt Documents/ rm *.log Line 1: Lists every file in the current folder whose name ends with .txt . Line 2: Copies all .txt files into your Documents folder. Line 3: Deletes every file whose name ends with .log . Careful: Always run ls *.log (or whatever pattern you plan to use) before running rm *.log . This way you can see exactly which files match the pattern before you commit to deleting them. Hidden Files — Dotfiles In Linux, any file or folder whose name starts with a dot ( . ) is hidden. These are called dotfiles , and they usually store personal settings and configuration for programs. They are hidden simply to keep your home folder looking tidy — there is nothing secret about them. A plain ls does not show hidden files. To see them: ls -a ls -la Line 1: The -a flag means "all" — lists every file including hidden ones. You will see entries like .bashrc , .profile , and the special entries . (the current folder itself) and .. (the parent folder). Line 2: Combines -l (long listing with details) and -a (all files). This is the most complete picture of a folder's contents. Note: The file .bashrc in your home folder is one of the most important dotfiles — it runs automatically every time you open a new terminal and is where you can add your own shortcuts and settings. You will meet it again in the scripting chapter. Symbolic Links — Shortcuts on the Command Line In plain words: A symbolic link (or symlink ) is exactly like a Windows shortcut — it is a tiny file that points to another file or folder somewhere else. When you open or run the symlink, the system automatically follows it to the real file. You will see symlinks in ls -l output because they show as type l (lowercase L) at the start of the permission string, like this: lrwxrwxrwx 1 pi pi 20 Jun 15 10:30 myscript -> /home/pi/scripts/myscript.sh This is sample output from ls -l , not a command to type. The l at the start shows it is a symlink. The arrow ( -> ) shows where it points: typing ./myscript will actually run /home/pi/scripts/myscript.sh . To create your own symlink: ln -s /home/pi/scripts/myscript.sh ~/myscript Creates a symlink called myscript in your home folder that points to the real file at /home/pi/scripts/myscript.sh . The -s flag means "symbolic" — without it you would create a different (harder to manage) type of link. Understanding Permissions Every file and folder on your Pi has a set of permissions — rules that say who is allowed to read it, change it, or run it as a program. This is how Linux keeps your personal files private and prevents one program from accidentally (or maliciously) damaging another. Users and Groups In plain words: A user is an account on the computer — like your pi account. A group is a named collection of users who share certain permissions, for example a group called audio for everyone allowed to use the sound hardware. Every file has three categories of people its permissions apply to: Owner — the specific user who owns the file (usually whoever created it). Group — a named group of users. The file's group might be pi , audio , video , and so on. Others — everyone else on the system who is not the owner and not in the group. Read, Write and Execute For each of those three categories, there are three possible permissions: Permission Letter For a file For a folder Read r You can view/open the file's contents. You can list what is inside the folder. Write w You can change or delete the file. You can add, rename or delete files inside. Execute x You can run the file as a program or script. You can enter (cd into) the folder. When a permission is absent, a dash - appears in its place. So rw- means "read and write, but not execute". Reading an ls -l Line Run ls -l in any folder and you will see something like this: ls -l Shows a detailed listing of files in the current folder, one file per line, with permissions, owner, size and date. A typical output line looks like this (this is example output, not a command to type): -rw-r--r-- 1 pi pi 1024 Jun 15 10:30 hello.txt This single line describes the file hello.txt . Every part has a specific meaning — the diagram below decodes it field by field. -rw-r--r-- 1 pi pi 1024 Jun 15 10:30 hello.txt - rw- r-- r-- Type + permissions (see detail below) 1 Hard links pi Owner (user) pi Group name 1024 Size (bytes) Jun 15 10:30 Last modified hello.txt Filename - = file | rw- = owner: read+write | r-- = group: read only | r-- = others: read only 10 characters: [type][owner rwx][group rwx][others rwx] Decoding a typical ls -l output line. The first character shows the file type ( - = regular file, d = directory, l = symlink). The next nine characters are three groups of three, showing permissions for the owner, the group, and everyone else. The Permission String in Detail Let us decode -rw-r--r-- character by character: Position Character Meaning 1 - File type: - = ordinary file, d = folder (directory), l = symlink (a shortcut) 2 r Owner can read the file 3 w Owner can write (change) the file 4 - Owner cannot execute the file (dash = permission absent) 5 r Group members can read the file 6 - Group members cannot write 7 - Group members cannot execute 8 r Others (everyone else) can read the file 9 - Others cannot write 10 - Others cannot execute Changing Permissions with chmod In plain words: chmod stands for "change mode" — "mode" is the old Unix word for permissions. It lets you add or remove read, write and execute permissions from a file. The Symbolic (Friendly) Form The easiest way to use chmod is with letters and symbols. The format is: who + action + permission . Letter Stands for u User (the owner) g Group o Others a All three (u + g + o) + Add a permission - Remove a permission = Set exactly these permissions (replacing whatever was there) Here are the most common things you will do: chmod +x myscript.sh chmod -x myscript.sh chmod u+x myscript.sh chmod go-w hello.txt chmod a+r photo.jpg Line 1: Adds the execute permission for everyone — makes myscript.sh runnable as a program. This is the command you will use most often when you write your own scripts. Line 2: Removes the execute permission from everyone. Line 3: Adds execute permission for the owner only (leaving group and others unchanged). Line 4: Removes write permission from the group ( g ) and from others ( o ), so only the owner can change the file. Line 5: Adds read permission for absolutely everyone. The Numeric (Octal) Form You will sometimes see permissions written as three digits, for example 755 or 644 . This is the older "numeric" or "octal" notation. Each digit is a sum of three values: 4 = read, 2 = write, 1 = execute. You add the values for each group: Number Meaning Equivalent 7 4+2+1 = read, write, execute rwx 6 4+2+0 = read and write rw- 5 4+0+1 = read and execute r-x 4 4+0+0 = read only r-- 0 no permissions at all --- So chmod 755 myscript.sh means: owner gets 7 (rwx), group gets 5 (r-x), others get 5 (r-x). The owner can read, write and run it; everyone else can only read and run it. chmod 755 myscript.sh chmod 644 hello.txt Line 1: Sets the classic permissions for an executable script — owner has full control (read, write, execute), everyone else can read and run but not modify. Line 2: Sets the classic permissions for a data file — owner can read and write, everyone else can only read. Tip: As a beginner, stick with the symbolic form ( chmod +x ) — it is much easier to read and remember. The numeric form is handy to recognise when you see it in tutorials online. Checking Detailed File Information with stat ls -l gives you a quick summary, but if you want to see every detail about a file — its exact size in bytes, its precise timestamps, and all its permissions in one place — use the stat command: stat hello.txt Prints a detailed report about hello.txt including: its full size in bytes, the date it was created, last read, and last changed, and its permissions shown both in the rwx form and as a numeric (octal) code. This is especially useful when troubleshooting "why can't I open this file?" problems. Changing Ownership with chown In plain words: chown stands for "change owner". It transfers ownership of a file from one user (or group) to another. sudo chown pi hello.txt sudo chown pi:pi hello.txt Line 1: Makes the user pi the owner of hello.txt . The sudo at the front is needed because changing ownership is a privileged action (explained in the next section). Line 2: Makes pi both the owner and the group of the file. The format is user:group . You will rarely need chown in everyday use. The most common situation is when a file is created by a system command that runs as a different user, and you want to reclaim ownership so you can edit it freely. sudo, Root, and Why Your Password Is Asked You have seen the word sudo appear in several commands. Now it is time to understand exactly what it means. The Root User Every Linux system has a special all-powerful user account called root (also sometimes called the superuser). Root has no restrictions — it can read, write, delete or change any file on the entire system, including system files that keep the Pi running. To protect the system from accidents, you do not normally log in as root. Instead, you log in as your ordinary pi account, which has limited powers. If you try to read or modify a system file as pi , Linux politely refuses with a "Permission denied" message. What sudo Does In plain words: sudo stands for "superuser do". Put it at the start of any command, and that command runs with full root powers — just for that one command. Then your account returns to being a normal user. sudo apt update Runs the apt update command (which refreshes the list of available software updates) with root privileges. Without sudo , this would fail with a "Permission denied" error because updating software requires writing to system folders that ordinary users cannot touch. When you type a command beginning with sudo , the terminal asks for your own password (the password for the pi account, not a root password). After you enter it correctly, sudo remembers for a few minutes, so you will not be asked again for every command in a row. Note: When you type your password at a sudo prompt, nothing appears on the screen — no dots, no asterisks. This is intentional: it prevents someone nearby from seeing how long your password is. Just type it and press Enter. The Difference Between pi and root pi (your normal account) root (superuser) Can read your own files Yes Yes Can read other users' private files No Yes Can install software No (needs sudo) Yes Can edit system files No (needs sudo) Yes Can accidentally break the system Unlikely Very easily Careful: Use sudo only when you genuinely need it — for installing software, editing system configuration files, or working with hardware. Do not get into the habit of putting sudo in front of everything. Running everyday commands as root is risky because a typo can do far more damage than it would as a normal user. Switching to the Root Shell (and Why to Avoid It) It is possible to open a shell that runs entirely as root with sudo -i or sudo su . Your prompt changes from a $ to a # , which is the traditional signal that you are operating as root. Experienced administrators sometimes do this for a batch of system tasks, but as a beginner it is safer to use sudo one command at a time and then return to your safe pi account. Note: The list of users who are allowed to use sudo is controlled by a special configuration file at /etc/sudoers . The default pi user on Raspberry Pi OS is already in that list, which is why sudo works for you out of the box. You should never edit this file with a plain text editor — always use sudo visudo , which checks for mistakes before saving. Making a Script Executable In later chapters you will write your own shell scripts — text files full of commands that run one after another, like a recipe. Before the Pi will actually run a script, you need to mark it as executable. Here is a preview of that process: Create a simple script file: nano greet.sh Opens a new file called greet.sh in nano. The .sh extension is the convention for shell scripts, though Linux does not strictly require it. Type these two lines inside nano: #!/bin/bash echo "Hello from my Pi script!" Line 1: This special first line is called a shebang (or hashbang). It tells the Pi which program should interpret the script — in this case /bin/bash , the standard command shell. It must always be the very first line of the file, with no blank line before it. Line 2: The echo command prints text to the screen. When you run the script, you will see this message. Save with Ctrl + O , then Enter , then exit with Ctrl + X . Check the file's current permissions: ls -l greet.sh Shows the permissions for greet.sh . You will see something like -rw-r--r-- — no execute permission yet, so the Pi will not run it as a program. Grant execute permission: chmod +x greet.sh Adds the execute bit for everyone. Now the Pi knows this file is a runnable program. If you run ls -l greet.sh again you will see -rwxr-xr-x . Run the script: ./greet.sh Runs the script. The ./ at the start means "look in the current folder" — you need this because the Pi does not automatically look in the current folder for programs to run (a safety measure to prevent accidentally running a malicious file placed in the current directory). You should see Hello from my Pi script! printed on screen. Tip: The ./ prefix is something beginners often forget. If you type just greet.sh without the dot-slash, the terminal will say "command not found" even though the file is right there. Always use ./scriptname.sh to run a script in the current folder. Putting It All Together — A Practical Workflow Here is a short walkthrough that ties together everything in this chapter. Imagine you want to create a small project folder, write a note, protect it, and back it up. Create a project folder: mkdir ~/myproject Creates a folder called myproject directly inside your home folder. The ~ is a shortcut that always means "your home folder" — on a default Pi setup that is /home/pi . Move into it and create a notes file: cd ~/myproject nano notes.txt Line 1: Changes into your new myproject folder. Line 2: Opens a new notes file in nano. Type something, save with Ctrl + O and exit with Ctrl + X . Check what you have: ls -la Shows all files including hidden ones, with full permission details. You will see notes.txt listed with permissions like -rw-r--r-- . Make the notes file readable only by you: chmod go-r notes.txt ls -l notes.txt Line 1: Removes the read permission from the group ( g ) and from others ( o ). Now only the owner ( pi ) can read this file. Line 2: Confirms the change — you should now see -rw------- in the permissions column. Back up the whole folder: cp -r ~/myproject ~/myproject_backup Makes a complete copy of your project folder (and everything inside it) with the name myproject_backup in your home folder. Verify the backup exists and check its contents: ls ~/myproject_backup Lists the contents of your backup folder to confirm that notes.txt (and any other files) made it across safely. Key terms Filesystem — the organised layout of all files and folders on your storage card; a single tree rooted at / . Home folder — your personal folder, /home/pi on a default Pi setup; the folder you land in when you open a terminal. nano — a simple, beginner-friendly text editor that runs inside the terminal; keyboard shortcuts are shown along the bottom of the screen. cat — a command that prints the entire contents of a file to the screen. less — a command that opens a file in a scrollable viewer; press Q to quit. head / tail — commands that show only the first or last few lines of a file. file — a command that identifies what type of data a file contains, regardless of its extension. touch — a command that creates an empty file, or updates the timestamp of an existing file without changing its contents. cp — the copy command; use -r to copy entire folders. mv — the move/rename command; there is no undo. rm — the delete command; files deleted with rm are gone permanently with no Recycle Bin. mkdir — creates a new folder; use -p to create several nested folders at once. find — searches for files and folders matching a name pattern, starting from a folder you specify. Wildcard (*) — a special character meaning "any number of any characters", used to match multiple filenames at once (e.g. *.txt ). Dotfile — a file or folder whose name starts with a dot, making it hidden from ordinary ls listings; usually stores program settings. Symbolic link (symlink) — a file that acts as a shortcut pointing to another file or folder elsewhere; shown as type l in ls -l output. Permission — a rule controlling who can read ( r ), write ( w ), or execute ( x ) a file. Owner — the specific user account that owns a file (usually whoever created it). Group — a named collection of user accounts that share a set of permissions on files assigned to that group. chmod — the command to change a file's permissions; symbolic form ( chmod +x ) is easiest, numeric form (e.g. chmod 755 ) is also common. chown — the command to change which user and group owns a file. stat — a command that shows full details about a file including exact timestamps, size and permissions. root — the all-powerful system administrator account on Linux; it has no permission restrictions and can do anything on the system. sudo — a prefix that runs a single command with root (superuser) privileges, then immediately returns to your normal user account. Shebang — the special first line of a script ( #!/bin/bash ) that tells the system which interpreter should run the file. Executable — a file that has been given the execute ( x ) permission, meaning the system is allowed to run it as a program. Chapter summary Your Pi's files are arranged in a single tree starting at / ; your personal files live in /home/pi , and system files live in /etc , /usr , /var and other protected folders. nano is the beginner's terminal text editor: open with nano filename , save with Ctrl + O then Enter , and exit with Ctrl + X . Use cat for short files, less for long ones (press Q to quit), and head / tail to see just the start or end; use file to find out what type of data a file contains. touch creates an empty file; mkdir creates a folder; use mkdir -p to create a chain of nested folders in one step. cp copies, mv moves or renames, and rm permanently deletes — there is no undo or Recycle Bin for rm . Use find ~ -name "*.txt" to search your home folder for files matching a pattern. Wildcards like *.txt match multiple files; always preview with ls before using a wildcard with rm . Hidden files (dotfiles) start with a dot and are only shown when you add -a to ls ; symlinks (type l ) act as shortcuts to another file. Every file has three permission groups — owner, group, others — and three permission types: read ( r ), write ( w ), execute ( x ); ls -l shows the full 10-character string. chmod +x file makes a file executable; chmod go-r file removes read access from group and others; chmod 755 is the classic permission for a shared script. root is the all-powerful system account; sudo lets you run one command with root powers without switching accounts permanently — use it only when necessary. Mark a script executable with chmod +x and run it with ./scriptname.sh — the ./ prefix is required.

title: Installing & Updating Software
headings: How Software Gets Onto the Pi
The Terminal: Where You Type Commands
The APT Command — Your Swiss Army Knife
A Quick Reference: APT Commands at a Glance
The Graphical Alternative: Add / Remove Software
Keeping the Pi's Firmware Up to Date
When the App You Want Is Not in APT
text: Your Raspberry Pi comes with a lot of software already installed, but sooner or later you will want to add something new — a media player, a game, a useful tool. This chapter shows you exactly how to do that safely and confidently, explains what is happening behind the scenes, and builds the habit of keeping everything up to date so your Pi stays secure and running smoothly. How Software Gets Onto the Pi On Windows you usually visit a website, download a .exe file, and run it. On Raspberry Pi OS things work differently — and, once you get used to it, much more conveniently. Almost every program you will ever want is available from a central, trusted collection managed by the operating system itself. You do not need to hunt around the web. In plain words: A package is a ready-to-install bundle containing a program (or a library the program needs), plus instructions telling the system where to put all its files. Think of it like a flat-pack furniture box: everything is inside, and the assembly instructions are included. In plain words: A repository (often shortened to "repo") is an enormous, carefully organised online library of packages — a bit like an official app store, except it is run by the people who make your operating system, not a private company. Raspberry Pi OS uses the Debian repositories plus a few Raspberry Pi-specific ones. Every package in there has been tested and is known to work safely together. In plain words: A package manager is the program that talks to the repository for you. You tell it what you want; it fetches the right package (and any other packages that program depends on), checks that nothing is broken, and installs everything in the right order. The package manager on Raspberry Pi OS is called APT (Advanced Package Tool). Debian / Raspberry Pi Repositories (online) apt downloads APT Package Manager Your Raspberry Pi (installed!) Thousands of free, checked packages Figure 8-1 — APT fetches packages from the online repositories and installs them on your Pi. The Terminal: Where You Type Commands Most software-management tasks are done by typing short commands in the Terminal — a text window where you talk directly to the operating system. Open it by clicking the black screen icon in the taskbar at the top of the desktop. Do not be put off by the plain look; each command is short, and this chapter explains every one. In plain words: The Terminal (also called the command line or shell) is like a chat window with your Pi. You type an instruction, press Enter, and the Pi carries it out and replies. It feels different from clicking around a graphical interface, but for managing software it is faster and more reliable. The APT Command — Your Swiss Army Knife Every APT command that changes something on the system starts with sudo . In plain words: sudo stands for "superuser do". It temporarily grants you administrator-level power for just the one command that follows. The system will ask for your password the first time you use it in a session. Without sudo , APT cannot write files to protected system folders — which is exactly what installing software requires. Note: When you type your password after sudo , the cursor does not move and no dots or asterisks appear. This is normal — the password is being recorded silently for security. Type it and press Enter. Step 1 — Refresh the catalogue: sudo apt update Before you install or upgrade anything, always tell APT to check the repositories for the latest list of available packages. This does not install anything; it only updates APT's local "catalogue" so it knows what versions are currently available. sudo apt update sudo — run the following command as administrator. apt update — contact every repository listed in your configuration, download the current package lists, and store them locally. You will see lines scrolling by as APT contacts each server. This usually completes in under a minute. You should run sudo apt update every time before installing or upgrading, and ideally at least once a week. Step 2 — Install available upgrades: sudo apt full-upgrade After refreshing the catalogue, you can apply any newer versions of packages that are already installed. sudo apt full-upgrade apt full-upgrade — compares what is installed against the freshly downloaded catalogue. If newer versions exist, it downloads and installs them. Unlike the simpler apt upgrade , full-upgrade is also allowed to remove old packages that are blocking an update — which is sometimes necessary on Raspberry Pi OS. You will be shown a summary and asked to confirm with Y then Enter before anything is changed. Tip: You can chain both commands into one line so you never forget to update first: sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade sudo apt update — refreshes the package catalogue. && — means "run the next command only if the previous one succeeded without errors". sudo apt full-upgrade — installs all available updates. The two commands run one after the other automatically, so you only need to confirm once at the end. Note: A full upgrade can take several minutes if many packages need updating — especially the first time after a fresh install. Leave the Terminal open and let it finish. Installing a new package: sudo apt install sudo apt install <package-name> Replace <package-name> with the actual name of the package you want. APT will look it up in the catalogue, list everything it needs to download (including any dependencies — other packages the program relies on), and ask you to confirm. Press Y then Enter to proceed. You can install several packages at once by listing their names separated by spaces: sudo apt install vlc fastfetch Installs both vlc (the VLC media player) and fastfetch (a tool that displays a summary of your system) in a single operation. APT fetches both together and asks for one confirmation. Removing a package: sudo apt remove and sudo apt purge There are two levels of removal: Command What it removes Configuration files? sudo apt remove <name> The program itself Left behind — useful if you reinstall later sudo apt purge <name> The program and all its configuration files Deleted — a completely clean slate Use remove if you think you might want the program back one day. Use purge for a truly clean removal — for example, if you had configured a server wrongly and want to start fresh. sudo apt remove fastfetch Removes the fastfetch program but keeps any settings files it created, so your configuration is preserved if you reinstall it later. sudo apt purge fastfetch Removes fastfetch and deletes its configuration files completely. Use this when you want a clean slate and are sure you will not reinstall the package. Searching for a package: apt search If you are not sure of the exact package name, you can search the catalogue. This command does not need sudo because it only reads information — it does not change anything. apt search chess Searches all package names and descriptions for the word "chess" and lists every match. You can then pick the exact name you want and use apt install with it. Tip: The list can be very long. Pipe it through less so you can scroll one page at a time: apt search chess | less — press the spacebar to move forward a page and q to quit back to the prompt. Learning about a package before installing: apt show apt show vlc Displays detailed information about the vlc package: its version number, download size, a plain description, what other packages it depends on, and who maintains it. Useful for checking you have the right package before committing to an install. No sudo needed — this only reads information. Checking the installed version of a package: dpkg -l Once a package is installed, you can check exactly which version is on your system: dpkg -l vlc dpkg is the lower-level tool that APT sits on top of. You will sometimes see it mentioned in error messages, so it is good to know its name. -l vlc — list the status and installed version of the vlc package. A line beginning with ii means the package is correctly installed. This command needs no sudo . Cleaning up afterwards: sudo apt autoremove and sudo apt clean Over time, APT can accumulate packages that were only installed to support something else (called dependencies ) but are no longer needed after you removed the main program. It also keeps downloaded package files in a cache folder even after installation. sudo apt autoremove Automatically finds and removes packages that were installed as dependencies but are no longer needed by any remaining program. APT will show you exactly what it plans to delete and ask for confirmation before removing anything. Safe to run regularly. sudo apt clean Deletes the downloaded .deb package files from the local cache (stored in /var/cache/apt/archives/ ). The packages are already installed, so the cached files are just consuming space on your microSD card. This command reclaims that space. It does not remove any installed programs. Tip: Run this full sequence once a month to keep your Pi tidy and up to date: sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade && sudo apt autoremove && sudo apt clean sudo apt update — refresh the package catalogue. sudo apt full-upgrade — install all available updates. sudo apt autoremove — remove dependency packages no longer needed. sudo apt clean — delete cached installer files to free up disk space. Each step only runs if the previous one completed successfully (thanks to && ). You will be asked to confirm upgrades and autoremove before they proceed. A Quick Reference: APT Commands at a Glance Command What it does Needs sudo? sudo apt update Refresh the list of available packages Yes sudo apt full-upgrade Install all available updates Yes sudo apt install <name> Install a new package Yes sudo apt remove <name> Remove a package (keep config files) Yes sudo apt purge <name> Remove a package and all its config files Yes apt search <word> Search for packages matching a keyword No apt show <name> Show details about a package No dpkg -l <name> Show the installed version of a package No sudo apt autoremove Remove unneeded dependency packages Yes sudo apt clean Delete cached downloaded package files Yes Three Concrete Examples Reading about commands is one thing — seeing them applied to real programs makes everything click. Here are three installs you can try right now. Example 1 — Fastfetch (a system information display) Fastfetch prints a colourful summary of your Pi's hardware and software — processor model, RAM, operating system version, uptime, and more. It is a satisfying first install because the result appears immediately. sudo apt update sudo apt install fastfetch fastfetch Line 1: Refresh the package catalogue so APT knows the latest version is available. Line 2: Download and install fastfetch. APT will list the package and ask you to confirm with Y then Enter. Line 3: Run fastfetch. No sudo is needed to run a program — only to install it. You should see a Raspberry Pi logo made of coloured characters on the left, and columns of information on the right. Any time you open a new Terminal session you can type fastfetch to see that summary instantly. Example 2 — Ninvaders (a text-based Space Invaders game) The repository contains several classic text games. ninvaders is a Space Invaders clone that runs entirely in the Terminal window — no extra graphics needed. sudo apt install ninvaders ninvaders Line 1: Installs the ninvaders package. If you have already run sudo apt update in this session, you do not need to run it again before every install. Line 2: Launches the game. Use the left and right arrow keys to move your ship and the spacebar to fire. Press q to quit. Example 3 — VLC Media Player VLC is one of the most popular media players in the world. It plays almost any video or audio format, including streamed internet content. sudo apt install vlc Installs VLC and all the supporting libraries (called codecs — small programs that decode different audio and video formats) that it needs. This may take a couple of minutes because there are quite a few dependencies. After installation, VLC appears in the Sound & Video section of the application menu (click the raspberry icon at the top-left of the desktop). Note: The Raspberry Pi 5 has no headphone socket. Audio from VLC comes out through your HDMI-connected monitor or TV's built-in speakers. If your monitor has no speakers, you can connect a USB audio adapter or USB speaker instead. The Graphical Alternative: Add / Remove Software If you prefer not to use the Terminal for installing software, Raspberry Pi OS includes a graphical application called Add / Remove Software . You can find it in the application menu under Preferences . Click the raspberry icon at the top-left of the desktop to open the application menu. Go to Preferences and click Add / Remove Software . Use the search box at the top to type the name or description of what you want. Click the checkbox next to a result to select it, then click Apply . Enter your password when prompted and wait for the installation to finish. Note: The graphical tool is a front-end for APT — it does exactly the same thing under the hood. Many people prefer it when starting out. Either method is perfectly fine and results in the same installed software. Keeping the Pi's Firmware Up to Date As well as software packages, the Raspberry Pi has a piece of low-level software called the bootloader (sometimes called firmware). This tiny program is stored in a special chip on the board and is what runs the instant you press the power button — even before the operating system loads. The Raspberry Pi Foundation occasionally releases bootloader updates to improve stability, add features, or fix bugs. In plain words: EEPROM stands for Electrically Erasable Programmable Read-Only Memory. It is a small chip on the Pi 5 board that stores the bootloader permanently, even when the power is off. Think of it as the Pi's ignition system — it fires up first and hands control over to the operating system. First, check whether a newer bootloader version is available: sudo apt update sudo apt install rpi-eeprom sudo rpi-eeprom-update Line 1: Refresh the package catalogue. Line 2: Make sure the EEPROM update tool is installed. On a fresh Bookworm installation it is usually already present; APT will simply confirm it is at the latest version. Line 3: Check whether a newer bootloader is available. If everything is current, the output will include BOOTLOADER: up to date and you are done. If an update is available, the output will tell you. If an update is available, apply it with: sudo rpi-eeprom-update -a sudo reboot sudo rpi-eeprom-update -a — schedules the bootloader update to be applied on the next reboot. The -a flag means "apply". Nothing is changed until the Pi actually reboots. sudo reboot — restarts the Pi. During the reboot you may briefly see a green screen or a progress display as the new bootloader is written to the EEPROM chip. This is completely normal. Tip: Check the bootloader every few months. You do not need to do it every week — bootloader updates are infrequent. Careful: Do not press the power button or cut the power while the Pi is rebooting after an EEPROM update. Wait until the desktop (or login prompt) appears before touching anything. Interrupting a bootloader write is extremely rare to cause permanent damage, but it is best avoided. When the App You Want Is Not in APT The Debian / Raspberry Pi repositories are very large — there are over 60,000 packages. But occasionally the program you want is not there, or only an outdated version is available. In that situation you have a few options. Option 1 — Flatpak In plain words: Flatpak is a newer packaging system — think of it as a second, parallel app store. Each Flatpak package bundles everything the program needs inside itself, so it works independently of what APT has installed. The main Flatpak hub is called Flathub , and it hosts thousands of applications. To set up Flatpak on Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm: sudo apt install flatpak sudo flatpak remote-add --if-not-exists flathub https://dl.flathub.org/repo/flathub.flatpakrepo sudo reboot Line 1: Install the Flatpak system itself via APT. Line 2: Register Flathub (the main Flatpak app library) as a trusted source. The --if-not-exists flag prevents an error if you have already done this step before. Line 3: Reboot the Pi so the Flatpak integration is picked up correctly by the desktop environment. After rebooting, you can install a Flatpak app like this (using the GIMP image editor as an example): flatpak install flathub org.gimp.GIMP flatpak install flathub — download from the Flathub source. org.gimp.GIMP — the Flatpak application ID for GIMP. Flatpak uses reverse-domain IDs (like org.gimp.GIMP ) instead of short names to avoid conflicts between publishers. You can find an app's exact ID by searching on flathub.org . To run a Flatpak app from the Terminal: flatpak run org.gimp.GIMP flatpak run — launch the specified Flatpak application. Flatpak apps also appear in the application menu after installation, so you can just click their icon there instead. Note: Flatpak packages are larger than APT packages because they bundle their own dependencies. On a 64 GB or larger microSD card this is not usually a problem, but be aware that a single Flatpak app can take several hundred megabytes. Option 2 — AppImage In plain words: An AppImage is a single portable file that contains an entire application. You download the file, mark it as runnable, and double-click it — no installation needed, and no administrator password required. You can delete it simply by dragging it to the bin. To use an AppImage: Download the .AppImage file from the developer's official website and save it to your Downloads folder. Open a Terminal and move into your Downloads folder: cd ~/Downloads cd — "change directory", i.e. move to a different folder. ~/Downloads — the ~ symbol is a shortcut for your home folder ( /home/pi by default). So this moves you into /home/pi/Downloads . Make the file executable (runnable) and launch it: chmod +x MyApp.AppImage ./MyApp.AppImage chmod +x — changes the file's permissions to mark it as executable. You only need to do this once per file. Replace MyApp.AppImage with the actual filename you downloaded. ./MyApp.AppImage — runs the application. The ./ at the start means "look for this file in the current folder" (not somewhere else on the system). Careful: AppImages and software downloaded directly from websites bypass the safety checks that APT and Flatpak provide. Only download AppImages from the official website of the software you want. If you are not sure whether a source is trustworthy, do not run the file until you have verified it. Option 3 — A Project's Own Install Script Some projects — particularly developer tools — provide their own installation script, usually a command beginning with curl or wget that you paste into the Terminal. These are common and generally safe when they come from a well-known project's official documentation, but they run with administrator privileges. Always copy the command from the official project page rather than from a random forum post or social-media message. Python Software in Particular Python deserves a special mention. Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm marks the system Python as externally managed , which means running plain pip install directly will show an error. This is intentional — it protects the operating system's own tools from accidental breakage. In plain words: pip is Python's own package manager — it installs Python libraries (add-on collections of code written in Python). On Bookworm, running pip install directly into the system-wide Python is blocked, because the OS itself relies on certain Python packages being at specific versions. Instead, choose one of these safe approaches: Approach Best for How Thonny's package manager Beginners; installing libraries for use in Thonny In Thonny: Tools > Manage packages APT python3-* packages Popular libraries available system-wide sudo apt install python3-numpy (for example) Virtual environment Projects that need specific library versions python3 -m venv myenv then source myenv/bin/activate Using APT for Python libraries sudo apt install python3-numpy python3-matplotlib Installs the NumPy maths library and the Matplotlib plotting library via APT. These are available system-wide to all Python scripts, without needing pip or a virtual environment. Many popular libraries have an apt package named python3-<libraryname> . Using a virtual environment A virtual environment is an isolated copy of Python that belongs to one project. You install packages into it freely with pip, and it never touches the system Python. python3 -m venv myenv source myenv/bin/activate pip install requests deactivate python3 -m venv myenv — create a new virtual environment in a folder called myenv . You only do this once per project. source myenv/bin/activate — switch into the virtual environment. Your Terminal prompt will change to show (myenv) at the start, confirming it is active. Any pip install now goes into myenv , not the system Python. pip install requests — as an example, installs the popular requests HTTP library into the virtual environment only. deactivate — leave the virtual environment and return to normal. The libraries you installed stay inside myenv for next time. Tip: To re-enter the virtual environment in a future session, just run source myenv/bin/activate again from the same folder. You do not need to recreate it. Note: If you are just starting out with Python, use Thonny . It manages its own private environment behind the scenes, so you can install libraries through its menu (Tools > Manage packages) without any of the above complexity. Come back to virtual environments when you are more comfortable. Enabling System Features with raspi-config Some software — particularly programs that talk to physical hardware like sensors, displays, or cameras — requires certain features of the Pi to be switched on before they will work. The tool for this is raspi-config . In plain words: raspi-config is a configuration menu that you open in the Terminal. It lets you turn on or off built-in features of the Pi — for example, the camera, SSH remote access, SPI and I2C communication buses for electronics, and more. Think of it as the Pi's "System Settings" for things that cannot easily be changed from the graphical desktop. sudo raspi-config Opens the raspi-config text menu. Use the arrow keys to highlight an option and Enter to select it. Navigate to Interface Options to enable features like the camera, SSH, SPI, or I2C. Navigate to System Options to change the hostname or password. Press Tab to reach the Finish button, then reboot if prompted. Note: You will rarely need raspi-config as a beginner. It becomes important when you start connecting physical components to the GPIO pins (covered in a later chapter), or when you want to access the Pi remotely from another computer. Building the Update Habit Keeping your Pi's software up to date is one of the most important things you can do for security and stability. Updates fix bugs, patch security holes, and sometimes add new features. Think of it like antivirus updates on Windows — routine maintenance that protects you without requiring you to understand all the details. A simple, sensible routine: Once a week (or any time before you do important work), open a Terminal and run: sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade Once a month, add the clean-up steps: sudo apt autoremove && sudo apt clean Every few months, check the bootloader: sudo rpi-eeprom-update Tip: The taskbar sometimes shows a small software-update icon (a circle with an arrow). Clicking it runs the equivalent of apt update and offers to apply upgrades without you typing anything — useful on days when you do not want to open the Terminal. Careful: If an upgrade summary shows it will remove a package you deliberately installed and care about, read the list carefully before typing Y to confirm. This is rare, but it is worth a quick check. If you are unsure, type N to cancel and search online for why that package is being removed. Weekly sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade Security & stability Monthly + sudo apt autoremove && sudo apt clean Free up disk space Every few months + sudo rpi-eeprom-update (apply if update found) Bootloader firmware Figure 8-2 — A simple maintenance schedule: weekly updates, monthly clean-up, occasional firmware check. Key terms Package — a bundle containing a program (or library) and instructions for installing it on your system. Repository (repo) — a large, trusted online library of packages, maintained by the OS team. APT — the package manager built into Raspberry Pi OS; the tool that installs, updates, and removes packages. sudo — a command prefix that grants temporary administrator privileges for a single command. Dependency — a package that another package requires in order to work; APT installs these automatically. apt update — refreshes APT's local catalogue of available packages (does not install anything). apt full-upgrade — installs all available updates for packages already on your system. apt autoremove — removes dependency packages no longer needed by any installed program. apt clean — deletes cached downloaded package files from /var/cache/apt/archives/ to free disk space. dpkg — the lower-level tool APT sits on top of; use dpkg -l <name> to check an installed package's version. EEPROM / bootloader — the low-level firmware in a tiny chip on the Pi 5 board; it runs before the OS and can be updated with rpi-eeprom-update . Flatpak / Flathub — an alternative packaging system (Flatpak) and its main app library (Flathub); apps bundle their own dependencies. AppImage — a portable single-file application that needs no installation; download, mark executable, and run. pip — Python's own package manager; on Bookworm, use it only inside a virtual environment or via Thonny, not directly into the system Python. Virtual environment — an isolated Python workspace created with python3 -m venv , letting you use pip freely without affecting the system Python. raspi-config — a Terminal menu tool for enabling Pi hardware features such as SSH, SPI, I2C, and the camera interface. Chapter summary Raspberry Pi OS uses APT to install software from trusted online repositories — no need to download files from random websites. Always run sudo apt update before installing or upgrading to ensure APT has the latest package information. sudo apt full-upgrade installs all pending updates; run it weekly to keep the system secure and stable. sudo apt install <name> installs a package; sudo apt remove uninstalls it (or purge for a completely clean removal including config files). Use apt search to find packages by keyword, apt show to read details before installing, and dpkg -l to check what is already installed. sudo apt autoremove and sudo apt clean keep your microSD card tidy by removing unneeded files monthly. The graphical Add / Remove Software tool does the same job as APT commands but with a point-and-click interface — equally valid for beginners. The Pi 5's bootloader firmware can be updated with sudo rpi-eeprom-update -a followed by a reboot; check it every few months. Software not in APT can come from Flatpak (Flathub), AppImage files, or a project's own install script — always use the official source. For Python libraries, use Thonny's built-in package manager, an APT python3-* package, or a virtual environment — never plain pip install into the system Python on Bookworm. Use sudo raspi-config to enable hardware interfaces (camera, SSH, SPI, I2C) that some software requires before it will work.

title: Getting Connected: Network & Remote Control
headings: Step Zero: Change Your Password First
How Your Home Network Fits Together
Remote Access Option A: SSH — Command Line
Remote Access Option B: Full Remote Desktop with VNC
Remote Access Option C: Raspberry Pi Connect — Access from Anywhere
Copying Files Between Windows and the Pi
Setting Up SSH Key Authentication (Optional, but Recommended)
Keeping Your Pi Secure on the Network
Changing or Checking Your Pi's Hostname
text: Your Raspberry Pi 5 becomes far more powerful the moment it can talk to the rest of your home network — and even more so when you can control it from your Windows PC without ever touching a keyboard or mouse connected to the Pi. This chapter walks you through networking basics in plain words, shows you how to find your Pi on your home network, and then takes you step by step through four ways to reach your Pi remotely: a command-line connection, a full remote desktop, a cloud-based browser link, and file copying. Careful: Before you enable any form of remote access, change the default password on your Raspberry Pi. Anyone on your home network — or, with some tools, anyone on the internet — could log in using the factory default. We cover this right at the start. Step Zero: Change Your Password First If you set up your Pi using the Raspberry Pi Imager (covered in Chapter 3), you will have created a username and password during that process. If you did not, or if you are not sure, do the following before anything else in this chapter. Open a Terminal on your Pi (the black screen icon on the taskbar, or go to Applications > Accessories > Terminal ). Type the command below and press Enter : passwd This runs the passwd command, which lets you change the password for the account you are currently logged in to. It will ask for your current password first, then your new password twice. Nothing appears on screen as you type — that is completely normal. Choose a password that is at least 12 characters long and that you will remember. A short phrase with a number works well — for example BlueSky!Clouds7 . Tip: Write the new password down and keep it somewhere safe. If you forget it and cannot log in, recovering access is possible but inconvenient (it requires booting from the microSD card on another computer to reset it). Networking for Total Beginners Before we connect anything, let us understand what is actually happening when two devices talk to each other. What a home network is In plain words: A network is simply a group of devices that can send information to each other. Your home network is the collection of phones, laptops, smart TVs, and other gadgets all connected through your internet router. At the centre of your home network sits a router — the box your internet provider gave you, or one you bought yourself. The router acts like a post office: every device on your network has its own address, and the router makes sure messages get to the right place. In plain words: An IP address is the unique number that identifies a device on a network — just like a street address identifies a house. A typical home IP address looks like 192.168.1.42 . The numbers before the last dot ( 192.168.1 ) identify your local network; the last number ( 42 ) identifies the specific device. In plain words: A hostname is a human-friendly name for a device, so you do not have to remember its number. Your Raspberry Pi's default hostname is raspberrypi . You can change it in settings. How the Pi gets its address automatically (DHCP) In plain words: DHCP stands for Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol. It sounds complicated, but it just means "the router automatically hands out IP addresses to every device that connects." You do not need to do anything — when your Pi connects to your network, the router gives it a free address automatically, usually within a few seconds. The downside of DHCP is that the router might give your Pi a different number the next time it restarts. This matters for remote access because you need to know the address to connect. We will look at how to deal with this later in this chapter. Wired Ethernet vs Wi-Fi Your Pi 5 has two ways to join your home network: Method Speed Reliability Setup needed Best for Wired Ethernet Up to 1,000 Mbps (Gigabit) Excellent — no interference Plug in a cable. Done.
