The dot before append means "call this action on this particular list". colours.remove("green") — removes the first occurrence of green from the list. If the item is not in the list, Python will raise a ValueError . Dictionaries — storing information with labels A dictionary is like a list, but instead of numbered positions you access each item by a meaningful key . Think of a real dictionary: you look up a word (the key) to find its meaning (the value). In plain words: A dictionary in Python stores pairs of information: a key and a value. You look up a value by its key, just like looking up a word in a printed dictionary. Dictionaries use curly braces {} . person = { "name": "Alice", "age": 30, "city": "London" } print(person["name"]) print(person["age"]) person["age"] = 31 print(person["age"]) person["country"] = "UK" print(person) person = {"name": "Alice", ...} — creates a dictionary with three entries. Each entry is a key-value pair separated by a colon. Keys are usually strings (in quotes); values can be any type. person["name"] — retrieves the value stored under the key "name" , which is Alice . You use square brackets with the key name, not a number. person["age"] = 31 — updates the value of an existing key. The old value (30) is replaced with 31. person["country"] = "UK" — adds a brand-new key-value pair to the dictionary. Dictionaries grow automatically as you add keys. print(person) — prints the entire dictionary, showing all keys and their current values. Functions — packaging instructions you will reuse A function is a named block of code that you write once and can call (run) as many times as you like, anywhere in your program. You define one with the keyword def . def greet(person_name): print(f"Hello, {person_name}!") print("Great to have you here.") greet("Alice") greet("Bob") greet("everyone") def greet(person_name): — defines a new function called greet . Inside the brackets is a parameter — a temporary variable that will hold whatever value you pass in when you call the function. The colon and indentation work the same way as with if . The two indented print lines — the body of the function. They only run when the function is called, not when Python first reads the definition. greet("Alice") — calls the function and passes Alice as the value of person_name . The body runs with person_name equal to Alice . The function is called three times with different names, without repeating the code three times — this is the core benefit of functions. Functions can also send a result back using return : def add(x, y): result = x + y return result total = add(7, 3) print(f"7 plus 3 equals {total}") def add(x, y): — defines a function that accepts two values, named x and y . result = x + y — calculates the sum and stores it temporarily. return result — sends the calculated value back to wherever the function was called from. Once Python hits return , the function stops and hands the value back. total = add(7, 3) — calls the function with 7 and 3; the returned value (10) is stored in total . Comments — notes inside your code A comment is a line (or part of a line) that Python completely ignores. It is there for you — to explain what the code is doing, leave reminders, or temporarily disable a line. # This whole line is a comment -- Python skips it entirely. age = 30 # The user's age in years # TODO: add a check that age is a positive number print(age) # — any text after a hash symbol on a line is a comment. Python ignores everything from the # to the end of that line. You can put a comment on its own line, or at the end of a line of code. # TODO: ... — a common convention. Writing TODO in a comment is a reminder to yourself of something you still need to add or fix. Comments are extremely valuable — even experienced programmers write them constantly. Get into the habit of explaining why you wrote something, not just what it does. Handling errors gracefully — try / except Sometimes your program will encounter a situation it cannot handle — for example, the user types "hello" when you expected a number. Without protection, Python crashes with an error message. The try / except block lets your program catch the problem and respond politely instead. In plain words: try / except is Python's way of saying "try this; if something goes wrong, do this instead". It stops a crash from reaching the user. try: raw = input("Enter a number: ") number = int(raw) print(f"Double your number is {number * 2}") except ValueError: print("That doesn't look like a number. Please try again.") try: — starts the protected block. Python attempts every line inside this block. number = int(raw) — converts the input to a whole number. If the user typed something that is not a number, this line would normally crash the program. except ValueError: — if a ValueError occurs anywhere inside the try block (which is what int() raises when given non-numeric text), Python jumps here instead of crashing. print("That doesn't look like a number...") — the friendly message shown to the user instead of a scary error. The program continues normally after this. Tip: You do not need to wrap every line in a try / except . Use it wherever you take input from the user or read from a file — those are the places where unexpected things are most likely to happen. Putting it all together — a number-guessing game Now let us build a complete, working program that uses everything you have just learned. The game picks a secret number between 1 and 20, then keeps asking the player to guess it, giving hints ("too high" or "too low") until the player gets it right. It also handles the case where the user types something that is not a number, without crashing. In Thonny, open a new file ( File → New ), type the code below exactly as written, then save it as guess_game.py ( File → Save As… ) and press the green Run button. import random # Pick a secret number between 1 and 20 secret = random.randint(1, 20) attempts = 0 print("Welcome to the Number Guessing Game!") print("I have picked a number between 1 and 20.") print("Can you guess it?\n") def check_guess(guess, secret): if guess < secret: return "Too low! Try higher." elif guess > secret: return "Too high! Try lower." else: return "correct" # Keep looping until the player guesses correctly guessed = False while not guessed: raw = input("Your guess: ") try: guess = int(raw) except ValueError: print("Please enter a whole number.") continue attempts = attempts + 1 hint = check_guess(guess, secret) if hint == "correct": print(f"\nYou got it! The number was {secret}.") print(f"It took you {attempts} attempt(s). Well done!") guessed = True else: print(hint) print("\nThanks for playing!") import random — loads Python's built-in random module, which contains tools for generating random numbers. The import keyword loads a module (a collection of ready-made functions) so you can use them. secret = random.randint(1, 20) — picks a random whole number between 1 and 20 (both 1 and 20 are possible) and stores it in secret . This is different every time the program runs. attempts = 0 — a counter that starts at zero and increases each time the player makes a valid guess. print("...\n") — the \n inside a string prints a blank line, making the output easier to read. \n is called a newline character — it is an invisible instruction to move down one line. def check_guess(guess, secret): — defines a function that compares the player's guess to the secret number and returns a hint string, or the word "correct" if the guess is right. guessed = False — a boolean variable (its value is either True or False ) that tracks whether the player has won yet. while not guessed: — keeps looping for as long as guessed is still False . As soon as guessed becomes True , the loop stops after the current pass. try: guess = int(raw) — safely converts the typed text to a number. If the user typed something like "abc", the except ValueError catches it instead of crashing. continue — inside a loop, continue skips the rest of the current pass and goes straight back to the top of the loop (the while condition check). This restarts the loop without incrementing the attempts counter for an invalid entry. attempts = attempts + 1 — increments the attempt counter. We only reach this line if the input was a valid number. hint = check_guess(guess, secret) — calls our function and stores the returned hint string. if hint == "correct": — if the function returned the exact string "correct" , the player has won. Note the double equals sign for comparison. guessed = True — sets the flag so the while loop will stop after this pass. else: print(hint) — if the guess was wrong, display the "too low" or "too high" message and loop around again. print("\nThanks for playing!") — runs once the loop has ended, after the player has guessed correctly. Tip: Once the game works, try changing 20 to 100 in the randint call to make it harder. Try adding a maximum number of guesses — if the player reaches 7 wrong guesses, print "Game over!" and reveal the secret number. Experimenting like this is the fastest way to learn. Errors are normal — do not panic Every programmer, beginner and expert alike, sees error messages constantly. An error message is Python's way of telling you exactly where it got confused. It is helpful, not an accusation. The three most common error types you will see: Error type What it means Common cause SyntaxError Python could not understand the line at all — it is not valid Python Missing colon after if , def , or for ; unmatched brackets; wrong quote marks NameError You used a variable or function name that Python does not know about Typo in the name, or using a variable before creating it TypeError You tried to do something with the wrong type of value Adding a number and a string without converting one of them first, e.g. "score: " + 5 ValueError The right type, but an impossible value Calling int("hello") — the string is the right type but cannot be converted to a number IndexError You tried to access a list position that does not exist A list has 3 items but you asked for mylist[5] Always read the last line of the error message first — it tells you the error type and a short description. The lines above it show the traceback — the chain of code that led to the crash, with the exact line number. In Thonny the offending line is also highlighted in red. Note: If the error message seems baffling, copy the exact error text and search for it online — you will almost always find a clear explanation on a site called Stack Overflow, or in the Raspberry Pi forums at forums.raspberrypi.com. Saving and re-running scripts In Thonny, save your file with Ctrl + S . Choose a meaningful name ending in .py and save it somewhere easy to find, such as a folder called python_projects inside your home directory. To re-run a saved file from the terminal, navigate to its folder first and then run it: cd ~/python_projects python3 guess_game.py cd ~/python_projects — changes the current directory to your python_projects folder. The tilde ( ~ ) is shorthand for your home directory (for example /home/pi on a standard Raspberry Pi OS install). If the folder does not exist yet, create it first with mkdir ~/python_projects . python3 guess_game.py — runs the file. The terminal prints the output exactly as it would in Thonny's Shell panel. Tip: Press the Up arrow key in the terminal to recall your previous commands. This saves a lot of retyping when you are testing and re-running a program repeatedly. Adding extra Python libraries — the Bookworm-correct way Python's real power comes from its huge collection of libraries (also called packages or modules ) — ready-made bundles of code that do specific jobs, from drawing charts to talking to web APIs to controlling the Pi's GPIO pins. In plain words: A library is a collection of functions someone else has already written and packaged up so you can use them with a single import statement. You do not need to understand how they work internally — you just use them. On Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm the system Python is externally managed . This means the operating system itself uses and maintains Python, and it protects itself by preventing you from installing packages into it with the plain pip install command. If you try, you will see a message like: error: externally-managed-environment This is not a bug — it is a deliberate safety measure introduced in Debian 12 (Bookworm) to stop accidental changes to the system Python from breaking the operating system itself. It means "stop — you need to use one of the safe methods below instead". You have two safe, recommended approaches. Approach 1 — install via apt (for common libraries) For the most popular Python libraries, Raspberry Pi OS provides pre-packaged versions through its built-in package manager apt . This is the simplest method and is fully supported by the system. sudo apt update sudo apt install python3-requests sudo apt install python3-numpy sudo apt install python3-matplotlib sudo apt update — refreshes the list of available packages from the internet so you get the latest versions. Always run this first before installing anything. sudo apt install python3-requests — installs the requests library (used for fetching web pages and data from the internet) in a way that is fully compatible with the system Python. The naming pattern is always python3- followed by the library name. python3-numpy — installs NumPy, a library for numerical calculations and arrays, widely used in science and data analysis. python3-matplotlib — installs Matplotlib, which draws charts and graphs. To find out whether a library is available through apt , search for it: apt-cache search python3- | grep requests apt-cache search python3- — lists all Python 3 packages known to apt . The list can be very long. | grep requests — the vertical bar (pipe) sends that list through the grep filter, which only shows lines containing the word requests . Replace requests with whatever library you are looking for. Approach 2 — use a virtual environment (for everything else) If the library you need is not in apt , or you need a newer version than apt provides, use a virtual environment . This is a self-contained, isolated copy of Python that lives in a folder of your choosing. You can install anything into it with pip without touching the system Python at all. In plain words: A virtual environment is like a separate room for your project's Python setup. Anything you install inside that room stays in that room and cannot affect the rest of the system. You can have as many rooms as you like — one per project. Here is the full process, step by step: Create the virtual environment. Choose a folder name — we will use myenv . In a terminal: python3 -m venv myenv python3 -m venv myenv — tells Python 3 to run its built-in venv module ( -m venv ) and create a virtual environment in a new folder called myenv . You only need to do this once per project. The folder contains its own Python interpreter and its own library storage area. Activate the virtual environment. source myenv/bin/activate source myenv/bin/activate — "activates" the virtual environment. Your terminal prompt changes to show (myenv) at the front, reminding you that you are inside the virtual environment. From this point on, python3 and pip refer to the virtual environment's own copies, not the system ones. Your prompt now looks something like (myenv) pi@raspberrypi:~ $ . That (myenv) prefix confirms the virtual environment is active. Install any library you like with pip. pip install requests pip install requests — installs the requests library into the virtual environment only. No sudo is needed and the system Python is not affected. Replace requests with any library name from the Python Package Index (PyPI), which hosts over half a million Python libraries. Run your Python script as normal. python3 my_script.py While the virtual environment is active, python3 automatically uses the environment's Python and can see all the libraries you installed with pip inside it. Deactivate when you are finished. deactivate deactivate — returns your terminal to normal. The (myenv) prefix disappears. The virtual environment still exists in its folder — you just are not inside it any more. Next time you need it, run source myenv/bin/activate again to re-enter it. Note: You need to activate the virtual environment again each time you open a new terminal window. If you try to run a script that needs a library and get a ModuleNotFoundError , the most likely cause is that you forgot to activate the environment first — just run source myenv/bin/activate and try again. System Python (externally managed) OS tools, Thonny, apt pkgs python3-requests (apt) python3-numpy (apt) protected wall Virtual Environment (myenv/) source myenv/bin/activate pip install anything -- safe here! pip install flask pip install pillow The two safe installation zones. The system Python is protected by Bookworm; a virtual environment is your personal sandbox where pip can install freely without risk to the system. Which approach should I use? Situation Best approach Common library (requests, numpy, matplotlib, RPi.GPIO, pygame…) sudo apt install python3-<name> Library not available via apt, or you need the very latest version Create a virtual environment and use pip install inside it Trying someone else's project that has a requirements.txt file Create a virtual environment, activate it, then run pip install -r requirements.txt . A requirements.txt file is a plain text list of all the libraries a project needs — pip reads it and installs them all at once. Quick one-off test in Thonny, library available via apt sudo apt install python3-<name> — Thonny uses the system Python by default Tip: If you use a virtual environment and want Thonny to use it too, open Thonny, go to Tools → Options → Interpreter , click Browse… and navigate to myenv/bin/python3 inside your project folder. Thonny will then use that environment's Python and see all its installed packages. Keep experimenting The best way to learn programming is to break things on purpose and fix them. Change a number, rename a variable, delete a colon and see what error you get. Every mistake teaches you something a textbook cannot. Python is patient — it will never be upset by your experiments, and the worst that can happen is an error message that points you straight to the problem. Save a new copy of your guessing game and try adding: A maximum number of guesses (end the game after 7 attempts, printing "Game over!" and revealing the secret number). A score that starts at 100 and goes down by 10 for each wrong guess. A "play again?" question at the end using input() , wrapping the whole game in an outer while loop. A list that keeps track of all the numbers the player has already guessed, warning them if they guess the same number twice. In the next chapter you will use Python to talk directly to the Pi's GPIO pins — controlling real-world electronics from code you write yourself. Key terms Program — an ordered list of precise instructions written in a language the computer can follow. Python — a popular, beginner-friendly programming language pre-installed on Raspberry Pi OS. Thonny — the beginner-friendly Python editor included with Raspberry Pi OS. REPL — the interactive Python shell, launched by typing python3 alone in a terminal; lets you run one line at a time and see results instantly. print() — a built-in Python function that displays text or values on screen. Variable — a named container that stores a value in your program; the stored value can change at any time. String — a piece of text in Python, written inside quote marks. Integer — a whole number (no decimal point), such as 7 or −3. Float — a decimal number in Python, such as 3.14. Boolean — a value that is either True or False ; used to track yes/no states in a program. f-string — a string prefixed with f that lets you embed variable values directly inside curly braces {} . input() — a built-in function that displays a prompt and waits for the user to type something; always returns a string. if / elif / else — keywords used to make decisions: run different code depending on whether conditions are true or false. Indentation — the spaces or tabs at the start of a line that tell Python which lines belong inside an if , for , while , or def block. Loop — a block of code that repeats. A for loop repeats a fixed number of times; a while loop repeats until a condition becomes false. List — a single variable holding multiple values in order, written with square brackets [] . Dictionary — a variable holding key-value pairs, written with curly braces {} ; you look up values by their key rather than by position. Function — a named, reusable block of code defined with def ; can accept inputs (parameters) and return a result. Comment — a note in code starting with # that Python ignores; written for human readers. try / except — a block that catches errors gracefully so the program can respond politely instead of crashing. Library (module / package) — a bundle of ready-made Python functions you can load with import . pip — the Python package installer, used to download and install libraries from the PyPI repository on the internet. apt — the Raspberry Pi OS package manager; use sudo apt install python3-<name> for system-safe Python library installs. Virtual environment (venv) — a self-contained, isolated Python installation in a folder, created with python3 -m venv , where pip can install freely without affecting the system. Externally managed — the Bookworm protection that prevents pip from installing packages into the system Python directly, guarding against accidental damage to the OS. Chapter summary A program is a precise, ordered list of instructions; Python reads them from top to bottom. Thonny is the easiest way to write and run Python on the Pi; the terminal command python3 filename.py also works once a file is saved. The Python REPL (launched by typing python3 alone) lets you test single lines instantly without creating a file. print() displays output; input() collects text typed by the user (always returned as a string). Variables store values; strings hold text (in quotes), integers hold whole numbers, floats hold decimals, and booleans hold True or False . F-strings (e.g. f"Hello, {name}!" ) are the cleanest way to build sentences that include variable values. if / elif / else lets your code make decisions based on conditions; use == (two equals signs) to compare, not = . for loops repeat a fixed number of times; while loops repeat until a condition becomes false. Lists store multiple values in a single variable; dictionaries store key-value pairs for labelled data. Functions defined with def let you name and reuse blocks of code. try / except catches errors gracefully so bad user input does not crash your program. Comments (lines starting with # ) explain your code to future readers, including yourself. On Bookworm, install common Python libraries safely with sudo apt install python3-<name> ; for anything else, use a virtual environment ( python3 -m venv myenv ) and then pip install inside it. Errors are normal and helpful — read the last line of the error message and the line number it points to; then fix and try again. The best way to learn is to tinker: change the code, break it deliberately, fix it, and build on it.

title: Physical Computing: The GPIO Pins
headings: Going Further: Sensors, the Camera, and HATs
text: The Raspberry Pi has a secret superpower hidden along its top edge: a row of 40 metal pins that can talk directly to the real world — switching lights on and off, reading button presses, measuring temperature, detecting motion, and far more. In this chapter you will learn what those pins do, understand just enough electricity to use them safely, and build your first two real electronic projects from scratch. What Is the GPIO Header? Along the top edge of your Pi 5 board you will see two parallel rows of tiny metal pins — 20 in each row, 40 in total. This connector is called the GPIO header . In plain words: GPIO stands for General-Purpose Input/Output . "General-purpose" means each pin can be used for many different jobs. "Input" means the Pi can sense something connected to it (a button, a sensor). "Output" means the Pi can control something (an LED, a buzzer, a motor driver). Not every pin does the same thing. The 40 pins are divided into three groups: Power pins — supply electricity to your components. There are two 5 V pins and two 3.3 V pins. Ground (GND) pins — the return path for electricity. Think of these as the negative terminal of a battery. There are eight GND pins spread around the header for convenience. GPIO pins — the programmable ones. Your Python code can set each of these HIGH (3.3 V) or LOW (0 V), or read whether something connected to them is HIGH or LOW. Careful: The GPIO pins on the Raspberry Pi 5 operate at 3.3 V logic . If you connect anything that pushes 5 V into a GPIO input pin, you will permanently damage the Pi 5 — there is no fuse to protect it. Always use 3.3 V-compatible components on GPIO pins, or use a level-shifter circuit when you must interface with 5 V devices. Also, never let two pins touch each other (a "short circuit") — this can instantly destroy the board. Handle the header gently and double-check your wiring before powering up. The 40-Pin Pinout The diagram below shows every pin. The two columns of numbers are the physical pin numbers (the position on the header, 1–40). The labels beside them show what each pin does. Pin 1 is nearest the corner of the board marked with a tiny triangle on most Pi boards. Raspberry Pi 5 — 40-Pin GPIO Header Odd pins (1,3,5…) on the left column · Even pins (2,4,6…) on the right column Left label Pin Pin Right label 3.3 V power 5 V power Ground (GND) GPIO (programmable) Special function GPIO 3.3 V 1 2 5 V GPIO 2 (SDA1) 3 4 5 V GPIO 3 (SCL1) 5 6 GND GPIO 4 7 8 GPIO 14 (TXD) GND 9 10 GPIO 15 (RXD) GPIO 17 ★ 11 12 GPIO 18 (PWM0) GPIO 27 ✦ 13 14 GND GPIO 22 15 16 GPIO 23 3.3 V 17 18 GPIO 24 GPIO 10 (MOSI) 19 20 GND GPIO 9 (MISO) 21 22 GPIO 25 GPIO 11 (SCLK) 23 24 GPIO 8 (CE0) GND 25 26 GPIO 7 (CE1) GPIO 0 (ID_SD) 27 28 GPIO 1 (ID_SC) GPIO 5 29 30 GND GPIO 6 31 32 GPIO 12 (PWM0) GPIO 13 (PWM1) 33 34 GND GPIO 19 (MISO) 35 36 GPIO 16 GPIO 26 37 38 GPIO 20 (MOSI) GND 39 40 GPIO 21 (SCLK) ★ GPIO 17 = Project 1 (LED) · ✦ GPIO 27 = Project 2 (Button) ▶ PIN 1 The 40-pin GPIO header. Physical pin 1 (top-left, marked ▶) is closest to the board corner. ★ = GPIO 17 used in Project 1 (LED). ✦ = GPIO 27 used in Project 2 (button). Tip: A handy trick to identify pin 1 on your actual board: look at the corner of the header nearest the microSD card slot — pin 1 is on that end, in the left-hand row when the board is oriented with the GPIO header at the top. Pin 1 also usually has a slightly squared-off pad on the underside of the board. A Quick Tour of the Pin Types Pin type Voltage What it's for Example physical pins 3.3 V power 3.3 V Supply power to 3.3 V components 1, 17 5 V power 5 V Supply power to 5 V components (never feed this into a GPIO input) 2, 4 Ground (GND) 0 V Complete the circuit — the return path for current 6, 9, 14, 20, 25, 30, 34, 39 GPIO (general) 0–3.3 V Programmable: set HIGH/LOW or read HIGH/LOW 11 (GPIO 17), 13 (GPIO 27), etc. GPIO (special function) 0–3.3 V Same as above, but also supports a hardware protocol (SPI, I²C, UART, PWM) 8 (GPIO 14/TXD), 19 (GPIO 10/MOSI), etc. Note: GPIO pin numbers can be confusing because there are two numbering systems. The physical pin number is the position on the header (1–40). The GPIO number (also called the BCM number) is the internal label used in software. In this chapter, and in the gpiozero library, we always use GPIO (BCM) numbers in code — so LED(17) means GPIO 17, which is physical pin 11. Electricity for Absolute Beginners You do not need an engineering degree to use GPIO safely, but understanding three basic ideas — voltage, current, and resistance — will stop you damaging things. The Water Analogy Imagine electricity flowing through a wire just like water flowing through a pipe. Voltage (measured in Volts, V) is the pressure pushing the water through the pipe. A higher voltage pushes harder. Your Pi's GPIO pins provide 3.3 V "pressure". Current (measured in Amperes, A, or milliamps, mA) is how much water is actually flowing per second. Too much current through a small wire (or a GPIO pin) will overheat it. Resistance (measured in Ohms, Ω) is how narrow the pipe is — it slows the flow down. Adding resistance reduces the current. These three are tied together by Ohm's Law : Current = Voltage ÷ Resistance . If you know two of the values, you can always work out the third. You will use this to calculate safe resistor values. In plain words: An LED (Light-Emitting Diode) is a tiny lamp that only lets electricity flow in one direction. It lights up when current flows through it from its longer leg (the positive side, called the anode ) to its shorter leg (the negative side, called the cathode ). Fitting one in backwards means no light — but also no damage. Why Every LED Needs a Resistor An LED has almost no resistance of its own. If you connect it directly to 3.3 V and GND without anything to slow the current down, too much electricity flows through it, and it burns out immediately — sometimes taking the GPIO pin with it. A series resistor is placed in the same wire as the LED to limit the current to a safe level. "Series" just means in a chain, one after the other. A typical red, yellow, or green LED needs about 10–20 mA (milliamps) of current and "uses up" about 2 V of the supply. Here is how to work out the resistor value: Start with the supply voltage: 3.3 V Subtract the LED's forward voltage (roughly 2 V for a standard red LED): 3.3 − 2 = 1.3 V left for the resistor. Choose a target current — 10 mA (= 0.01 A) is safe and bright enough. Divide: 1.3 V ÷ 0.01 A = 130 Ω . Round up to the nearest standard resistor value. The closest common value above 130 Ω is 270 Ω or the even safer 330 Ω . Either works perfectly. A 330 Ω resistor is the standard beginner choice. Tip: When in doubt, use a 330 Ω resistor for any standard LED connected to a 3.3 V GPIO pin. The LED will be slightly less bright than its theoretical maximum, but it will last for years. Reading Resistor Colour Bands Resistors are colour-coded. A 330 Ω resistor has four colour bands: Orange – Orange – Brown – Gold . You can also just check the label on its plastic bag if it came in a starter kit — this is the quickest approach. How to read a 330 Ω resistor Orange 3 Orange 3 Brown ×10 Gold ±5% = 330 Ω 3 × 3 × 10 A 330 Ω resistor has bands Orange – Orange – Brown – Gold. The first two bands give the digits (3, 3), the third is the multiplier (×10), and the gold band means ±5% tolerance. What Is a Breadboard? In plain words: A breadboard is a plastic board full of tiny holes. Inside, metal strips connect certain holes together so you can plug in components and wire them up without any soldering. You simply push wires and component legs into the holes, and the metal inside makes the electrical connection. A standard half-size breadboard is divided like this: Two long rows along the top and bottom edges, labelled + and − , running the full length. These are called power rails — all holes in the same rail are connected together. A large central area with numbered rows (usually 1–30). Each row is split into two halves (a–e on the left, f–j on the right) by a gap down the middle. Every hole in the same half-row (e.g., 1a, 1b, 1c, 1d, 1e) is connected together, but the left half and right half are NOT connected to each other across the gap. So if you push an LED's leg into hole 10e and a wire into hole 10c, they are connected. But a wire in 10f is not connected to 10e — it is on the other side of the gap. How a breadboard is connected inside + power rail (all holes connected along the full length) − power rail ── Centre gap: left and right sides NOT connected ── Rows a–e: each row is connected left↔right within this half Rows f–j: separate from the a–e half + power rail − power rail Inside the breadboard, holes along each coloured rail are connected all the way along. Within the central area, holes in the same numbered half-row share a connection — but the left and right halves are separated by the centre gap. Project 1 — Blink an LED This is the "Hello, World!" of physical computing: making an LED flash on and off under the Pi's control. It proves that your software can talk to the real world. What You Need A Raspberry Pi 5 (already set up and running Raspberry Pi OS) 1 × LED (any colour — red is traditional) 1 × 330 Ω resistor (orange-orange-brown-gold bands) 2 × jumper wires (short wires with push-on connectors — female-to-male: the female end fits a GPIO pin, the male end fits a breadboard hole) 1 × mini breadboard Careful: Power off your Pi before wiring anything. Shut down from the desktop (click the Raspberry Pi menu > Shutdown), wait for all the green lights to go out, then remove the power lead. Wiring with the power on is the most common way to accidentally damage a GPIO pin. Only plug the power back in once you are confident your wiring is correct. Wiring Diagram Project 1 — LED Blink Wiring Diagram GPIO Header Pin 11 (GPIO 17) Pin 6 (GND) 330 Ω LED +long −short Breadboard Purple wire: GPIO 17 (pin 11) → 330 Ω resistor → LED long leg (+) Dark wire: LED short leg (−) → GND (pin 6) Current flows: GPIO 17 → Resistor → LED → GND Wiring for Project 1. The purple path carries current from GPIO 17 through the 330 Ω resistor into the LED's long leg (anode). The dark path returns from the LED's short leg (cathode) to a GND pin. The breadboard holds everything in place. Step-by-Step Wiring Instructions Careful: Your Pi must be fully shut down and unplugged from power for all wiring steps. Do not plug it back in until step 8. Prepare your breadboard. Place the mini breadboard on a flat surface in front of you with the numbered rows visible. You will use rows 5 and 6 in this project — but any two adjacent rows work fine. Insert the LED. Push the LED's two legs into the breadboard so that the long leg (anode, positive) goes into hole 6e and the short leg (cathode, negative) goes into hole 6f . Because the centre gap separates e from f, each leg is in its own separate electrical group — perfect. Insert the resistor. Push one leg of the 330 Ω resistor into hole 6b (the same row as the LED's long leg, so they are connected by the breadboard's internal strip). Push the other resistor leg into hole 4b (a different row, which gives you a free connection point for the GPIO wire). Connect the GPIO wire. Take a female-to-male jumper wire. Push the female end (the socket) firmly onto physical pin 11 on the Pi's GPIO header — that is GPIO 17, left column, sixth pin from the top. Push the male end (the pin) into hole 4a — the same row as the free leg of the resistor. Connect the GND wire. Take a second female-to-male jumper wire. Push the female end onto physical pin 6 on the GPIO header — that is a GND pin, right column, third from the top. Push the male end into hole 6g — the same row as the LED's short leg on the right-hand side of the breadboard. Trace the full circuit. Follow the path: GPIO 17 (pin 11) → jumper wire → hole 4a → resistor → hole 6b → LED long leg (6e) → LED short leg (6f) → hole 6g → jumper wire → GND (pin 6). Every step should be connected, with no wires touching each other except where intended. Check the LED orientation. The long leg must connect toward the GPIO side (via the resistor). The short leg must connect toward GND. Getting this backwards simply means the LED will not light — it will not damage anything. If the LED does not come on, try pulling it out and turning it around. Only now, plug in your Pi's power lead and let it boot to the desktop. Writing the Python Program The Pi's recommended Python library for GPIO is called gpiozero . It comes pre-installed on Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm and uses the lgpio backend on the Pi 5 — so there is nothing to download. In plain words: A library is a collection of ready-written code that you can use in your own programs. Instead of writing dozens of lines to control a GPIO pin from scratch, you import gpiozero and use its simple commands like LED(17) . Open Thonny (click the Raspberry Pi menu → Programming → Thonny Python IDE). You will see a blank editor area at the top. Type the following program exactly as shown: from gpiozero import LED from signal import pause led = LED(17) led.blink() pause() Line 1 — from gpiozero import LED : The gpiozero library contains ready-made objects for common components. This line pulls in the LED object so we can use it. Think of it as fetching the right tool from a toolbox. Line 2 — from signal import pause : Brings in a helper called pause() that keeps the program running and waiting. Without it, the program would finish and close in an instant before the LED had a chance to blink. Line 4 — led = LED(17) : Creates a software object representing the LED connected to GPIO pin 17. The number 17 is the GPIO (BCM) number, which corresponds to physical pin 11 on the header. Line 5 — led.blink() : Tells the LED to start blinking — on for one second, off for one second, repeating forever. You can customise the speed (see the Tip below). Line 6 — pause() : Keeps the program alive indefinitely so the blinking continues. The program will stay here until you stop it. Tip: You can control the blink speed by passing arguments to blink() . For example, led.blink(on_time=0.2, off_time=0.8) makes the LED flash quickly (on for 0.2 seconds, off for 0.8 seconds). Try different values and experiment! Running the Program In Thonny, click File → Save and save the file as blink.py in your home folder. Click the green Run button (the triangle ▶) at the top of Thonny, or press F5 . Watch your LED — it should start blinking on and off once per second. If it does not, check your wiring: most likely the LED is backwards (swap it around), or a jumper wire is not pushed in firmly. To stop the program, click the red Stop button in Thonny (the square ◼). The LED will go off and stay off. Note: If Thonny shows a pin-factory error such as No module named 'lgpio' , the lgpio backend may need to be installed. Open a terminal and run sudo apt install python3-lgpio , then close and reopen Thonny. If you see a permissions error, make sure your user account is in the gpio group (see the section "Checking GPIO Access" later in this chapter). Congratulations — you have just written a program that controls a physical object in the real world. That is the essence of physical computing. Project 2 — Read a Push Button In Project 1, your Pi was the boss — it sent signals out. In Project 2 you flip it around: you will tell the Pi to listen for a signal coming in from a push button you press with your finger. Press the button, the LED comes on. Release it, the LED goes off. What You Need Everything from Project 1 (LED + 330 Ω resistor + breadboard still wired up) 1 × push button (a small tactile switch — four legs, fits a breadboard) 1 × additional female-to-male jumper wire Careful: Shut down and unplug your Pi before adding the button wiring. How a Push Button Works A small tactile push button has four legs, but electrically it only has two connections: one pair of legs on one side, and one pair on the opposite side. When you press the button, the two sides connect. When you release it, they disconnect again. To use a button with gpiozero, you connect one side to a GPIO pin and the other side to the 3.3 V power pin. The gpiozero Button object automatically switches on an internal pull-down resistor inside the Pi. This invisible resistor gently pulls the GPIO pin to LOW (0 V) whenever the button is open. When you press the button, 3.3 V flows into the pin and it reads HIGH. You do not need any external resistor for the button — gpiozero handles it all. In plain words: A pull-down resistor is a resistor connected between a GPIO pin and GND. It ensures the pin reads a definite LOW (0 V) when nothing else is driving it. Without it, the pin would "float" — picking up electrical noise and randomly reading HIGH or LOW. The Pi 5 has these built in, and gpiozero enables them automatically when you create a Button object. Wiring the Button Push the button across the centre gap of the breadboard (its legs straddle the gap) in a new area of rows, away from the LED circuit — for example rows 12–13. Project 2 — Button Wiring (adds to Project 1 setup) GPIO Header Pin 13 (GPIO 27) Pin 1 (3.3 V) Breadboard (rows 12–13) Button GPIO 27 side 3.3 V side Purple: GPIO 27 Orange: 3.3 V How it works: Button released: GPIO 27 is pulled LOW by internal pull-down → LED off Button pressed: 3.3 V drives GPIO 27 HIGH → LED on Only 2 wires needed — no external resistor required Project 2 button wiring. One side of the button connects to GPIO 27 (pin 13, purple wire); the other side to 3.3 V (pin 1, orange wire). No GND wire is needed for the button — gpiozero's built-in pull-down handles that automatically. Push the button across the breadboard centre gap — legs straddling the gap in rows 12–13 (or any spare rows). This keeps the two sides of the button electrically separate until it is pressed. Connect the GPIO 27 wire. Take a female-to-male jumper wire. Push the female end onto physical pin 13 on the GPIO header — that is GPIO 27, left column, seventh pin from the top. Push the male end into the breadboard hole on the left side of the button (e.g., row 12, hole b). Connect the 3.3 V wire. Take another female-to-male jumper wire. Push the female end onto physical pin 1 on the GPIO header — that is the 3.3 V pin, top-left corner of the header. Push the male end into the breadboard hole on the right side of the button (e.g., row 12, hole f — the other side of the centre gap). That is all for the button. You do not need a GND wire for the button itself — gpiozero enables a built-in pull-down resistor inside the Pi chip, which holds the GPIO 27 pin at LOW when the button is not pressed. The LED circuit from Project 1 stays exactly as it is. Double-check, then reconnect power and let the Pi boot up. Note: The left and right sides of a tactile button are defined by looking at it from above. Two legs on one side are always connected together; the other two legs on the opposite side are always connected together. When you press the button, the left pair connects to the right pair. If your button is in a 4-hole square arrangement, left and right are the pairs that face each other across the longer axis. The Button Program Open a new file in Thonny (File → New) and type the following: from gpiozero import LED, Button from signal import pause led = LED(17) button = Button(27) button.when_pressed = led.on button.when_released = led.off pause() Line 1 — from gpiozero import LED, Button : This time we import two objects from gpiozero: the same LED from Project 1, and a new one called Button . Line 2 — from signal import pause : Same as before — keeps the program alive so it can keep listening for button events. Line 4 — led = LED(17) : Represents our LED on GPIO 17, exactly as before. Line 5 — button = Button(27) : Represents the push button connected to GPIO 27. By default, gpiozero enables the built-in pull-down resistor, keeping the pin at LOW until the button is pressed — no extra wiring needed. Line 7 — button.when_pressed = led.on : Tells Python: "Whenever the button is pressed, run led.on() " — which switches the LED on. Notice there are no parentheses after led.on ; you are handing the action to the button to call later, not calling it right now. Line 8 — button.when_released = led.off : Tells Python: "Whenever the button is released, run led.off() " — switching the LED off again. Line 10 — pause() : Keeps the script running indefinitely so it can respond to button events. Without this, the program would end immediately. Save this as button_led.py and run it with the green button in Thonny. Now press your physical button — the LED should light up while you hold the button, and go off when you release it. Tip: You can make the button do anything you like. Instead of controlling an LED, you could make it print a message. Here is how to define your own action for the button: def button_was_pressed(): print("Button was pressed!") button.when_pressed = button_was_pressed Lines 1–2 — def button_was_pressed(): and print(...) : Define a new function called button_was_pressed . The indented print line below it is what happens when the function is called — it displays a message in the Thonny console. Line 4 — button.when_pressed = button_was_pressed : Hands this new function to the button object, so gpiozero calls it every time the button is pressed. Again, no parentheses — you are pointing at the function, not calling it yet. Checking GPIO Access in Bookworm Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm manages GPIO permissions through user groups. Your user account is automatically added to the gpio group during first-time setup, so GPIO programs should work without any changes. If you ever get a "permission denied" error when running GPIO code, open a terminal and check which groups your account belongs to: groups groups : Prints all the user groups your account belongs to. Look for gpio in the output. If it is missing, run the command shown below to add yourself, then log out and back in for the change to take effect. If gpio is not listed, run this to add your account: sudo usermod -aG gpio $USER sudo : Runs the command with administrator ("superuser") privileges — required for changing group memberships. usermod -aG gpio : Modifies a user account ( usermod ) by appending ( -a ) them to an additional group ( -G gpio ). The gpio group is the one that grants access to GPIO pins. $USER : A built-in variable that automatically expands to your current username, so you do not need to type it yourself. Note: After running the command above, you must log out and log back in (or reboot the Pi) before the change takes effect. Group memberships are only read when you first log in. Going Further: Sensors, the Camera, and HATs Once you are comfortable with an LED and a button, a whole universe of electronics opens up. Here are the most popular next steps for Pi beginners. Sensors Sensors let your Pi sense the world around it. They all connect to the GPIO header (or sometimes via USB). Sensor What it detects Connection Python library PIR motion sensor (HC-SR501) Movement (up to ~7 m) Power, GND, 1 GPIO signal pin MotionSensor in gpiozero DHT11 / DHT22 Temperature and humidity Power, GND, 1 GPIO data pin adafruit-circuitpython-dht HC-SR04 ultrasonic Distance to an object (like sonar) Power, GND, 2 GPIO pins (trigger + echo) DistanceSensor in gpiozero DS18B20 temperature probe Precise temperature (waterproof version available) 1-Wire protocol, 1 GPIO pin + 4.7 kΩ resistor Built into the OS kernel Note: Many sensors come with their own Python libraries. On Bookworm, install them with sudo apt install python3-<library-name> where possible — this uses the system's tested packages and does not conflict with anything. Alternatively, install inside a virtual environment with pip install <library-name> . Do not run plain pip install directly into the system Python on Bookworm — it will be blocked with an "externally managed environment" error, and bypassing it can break your system. See Chapter 11 for virtual environment guidance. PIR Motion Sensor Example A PIR (Passive Infrared) sensor detects heat from people and animals moving nearby — it is what triggers security lights. Wire it so its VCC pin goes to a 5 V power pin (most HC-SR501 PIRs need 5 V for their internal electronics), its GND pin to any GND pin, and its OUT signal pin to GPIO 4. Then: from gpiozero import MotionSensor from signal import pause pir = MotionSensor(4) pir.when_motion = lambda: print("Motion detected!") pir.when_no_motion = lambda: print("All quiet.") pause() Line 1 — from gpiozero import MotionSensor : Imports the ready-made gpiozero object for PIR sensors. Line 4 — pir = MotionSensor(4) : Creates a MotionSensor object listening on GPIO 4 (physical pin 7). gpiozero reads the signal from the sensor and handles all the pin logic internally. Line 6 — pir.when_motion = lambda: print("Motion detected!") : lambda is a quick way to write a tiny, one-line function without giving it a name. This says: when motion is detected, print a message to the console. You could replace this with any action — flashing an LED, sending an email, starting a video recording. Line 7 — pir.when_no_motion = lambda: print("All quiet.") : The same pattern for when motion stops being detected. Line 9 — pause() : Keeps the script running indefinitely, waiting and listening for motion events. The Raspberry Pi Camera Module The Pi 5 has two dedicated camera connectors (labelled CAM0 and CAM1 ) — slim ribbon-cable sockets on the board. An official Raspberry Pi Camera Module v2 or v3 plugs in with a flat ribbon cable. Once connected, you can take photos and record video in Python using the picamera2 library, which is pre-installed on Bookworm. Note: On the Pi 5 with Bookworm, the camera works automatically as soon as the ribbon cable is connected — there is no enable toggle needed in settings. The picamera2 library uses the modern libcamera stack. You can test that the camera is detected by opening a terminal and running rpicam-hello : a preview window should appear for a few seconds. from picamera2 import Picamera2 cam = Picamera2() cam.start() cam.capture_file("photo.jpg") cam.stop() Line 1 — from picamera2 import Picamera2 : Imports the Picamera2 library that comes with Bookworm for controlling the camera hardware. Line 3 — cam = Picamera2() : Creates a camera control object. If no camera is detected, an error will appear here. Line 4 — cam.start() : Powers up the camera sensor and starts the image pipeline. There may be a brief warm-up pause. Line 5 — cam.capture_file("photo.jpg") : Takes a single photograph and saves it as photo.jpg in the current folder (usually your home folder when run from Thonny). Line 6 — cam.stop() : Powers the camera down neatly after the photo is taken. Tip: The Camera Module v3 has a motorised autofocus lens — it focuses automatically. The v2 has a fixed-focus lens. Both work with the same picamera2 code. Find the saved photo.jpg in the Files app (in your home folder) to view it. HATs — Hardware Attached on Top In plain words: A HAT (Hardware Attached on Top) is an add-on board that plugs directly onto the full 40-pin GPIO header, sitting on top of the Pi like a hat on a head. HATs follow a standard design that allows the Pi to automatically identify what is connected. Popular HATs for beginners include: Sense HAT — contains an 8×8 LED matrix display, temperature, humidity, pressure and compass sensors, and a joystick, all in one board. A fantastic all-in-one learning tool — and the same board used on the International Space Station. Explorer HAT / Motor HAT — controls DC motors and stepper motors, great for robots. Pimoroni Unicorn HAT — a grid of colourful LEDs for light shows and animations. NVMe Base HAT — adds an M.2 NVMe SSD via the Pi 5's PCIe connector (this one goes underneath the Pi, not on the GPIO header). Each HAT comes with its own Python library and installation instructions. Most install with a single sudo apt install command or a one-line installer script from the manufacturer's website. Note: The Pi 5 uses a new version of the HAT standard called HAT+ . Most older HATs designed for the Pi 4 still fit physically, but always check the manufacturer's compatibility notes for the Pi 5 before buying. GPIO Safety Checklist Before every session with the GPIO header, run through this quick checklist: Power off before wiring. Shut down the Pi fully (menu → Shutdown), wait for the green activity light to go out, then unplug the power lead. Only connect or change wiring with no power. Never feed 5 V into a GPIO input pin. The Pi 5 GPIO is 3.3 V logic only — 5 V will destroy the pin instantly and permanently. Never short two pins together. Letting two metal pins touch via a stray wire or misplaced component can instantly damage the Pi. Always check your wiring carefully before powering on. Always use a current-limiting resistor with LEDs. A bare LED with no resistor will burn out in seconds — and may take the GPIO pin with it. GPIO pins supply only a small current. Each GPIO pin can safely supply up to about 8–16 mA, and the total for all pins combined is limited. Do not try to power a motor, relay, or high-current buzzer directly from a GPIO pin — use a driver board or transistor circuit instead. Handle with care and avoid static. Avoid putting your fingers on the Pi's circuit board components while the power is on. Before handling the bare board, touch a grounded metal object (such as a radiator) to discharge any static electricity from your body. Key terms GPIO - General-Purpose Input/Output; the 40 programmable pins on the Pi that can communicate with electronic components. Header - The double row of 40 metal pins along the top edge of the Pi board. BCM number - The GPIO pin numbering system used in software (e.g., GPIO 17), as opposed to the physical position on the header (e.g., physical pin 11). Voltage (V) - Electrical "pressure", measured in Volts. The Pi's GPIO pins output 3.3 V. Current (A / mA) - The flow of electricity, measured in Amperes or milliamps. Each GPIO pin can safely supply around 8–16 mA. Resistance (Ω) - Opposition to current flow, measured in Ohms. A series resistor protects components from receiving too much current. Ohm's Law - The rule that Current = Voltage ÷ Resistance, used to calculate safe resistor values for LEDs and other components. LED - Light-Emitting Diode; a small efficient lamp that lights up when current flows through it in the correct direction. Anode - The positive leg of an LED (the longer one); current enters here. Cathode - The negative leg of an LED (the shorter one); current exits here toward GND. Series resistor - A resistor placed in-line with an LED to limit current to a safe level. 330 Ω is the standard beginner choice for a 3.3 V GPIO. Breadboard - A reusable plastic prototyping board with internal metal strips connecting rows of holes, allowing components to be connected without soldering. Pull-down resistor - A resistor connected between a GPIO input pin and GND that keeps the pin reading LOW when nothing else is driving it. The Pi 5 has these built in; gpiozero enables them automatically for buttons. gpiozero - A beginner-friendly Python library pre-installed on Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm that makes controlling GPIO components very simple. On Pi 5 it uses the lgpio backend. lgpio - The low-level GPIO library used as the backend by gpiozero on the Raspberry Pi 5 / Bookworm. Pre-installed; install with sudo apt install python3-lgpio if ever missing. PIR sensor - Passive Infrared sensor; detects movement by sensing changes in infrared (heat) radiation from warm bodies. picamera2 - The Python library pre-installed on Bookworm for controlling the Raspberry Pi Camera Module using the libcamera stack. HAT - Hardware Attached on Top; an add-on board that plugs onto the 40-pin GPIO header and follows a standard that lets the Pi identify it automatically. Chapter summary The 40-pin GPIO header is the Pi's gateway to the physical world, providing 3.3 V and 5 V power pins, ground pins, and up to 26 programmable GPIO pins. GPIO pins operate at 3.3 V logic only — feeding 5 V into them will permanently damage the Pi 5. Always power off and unplug the Pi completely before connecting or changing any wiring. An LED always needs a series resistor (330 Ω is the safe standard for a 3.3 V GPIO) to prevent it burning out. A breadboard lets you prototype circuits quickly without soldering, using internal metal strip connections — left and right halves of each row are separated by a centre gap. Software uses the BCM (GPIO) number, not the physical pin position; LED(17) controls GPIO 17 = physical pin 11. The gpiozero library on Bookworm uses the lgpio backend on Pi 5; LED(17) and Button(27) work out of the box with no extra configuration. Project 1 demonstrated output: blinking an LED by driving GPIO 17 HIGH and LOW in a repeating pattern with led.blink() . Project 2 demonstrated input: reading a push button on GPIO 27 and using gpiozero's built-in pull-down resistor so that button.when_pressed and button.when_released trigger actions automatically. The correct button circuit with gpiozero is: one button leg to GPIO pin, other leg to 3.3 V — just two wires, no external resistor required. Sensors (PIR, DHT22, ultrasonic), the Camera Module (use picamera2 on Bookworm), and HAT add-on boards are natural next steps that all build on the same GPIO foundation.

title: A Media Centre for Your TV
headings: A Word on Media You Can Play
Full Worked Path: Jellyfin on Raspberry Pi OS
4K and HEVC: What the Pi 5 Can Handle
Alternative: Installing Kodi on Raspberry Pi OS
text: Your Raspberry Pi 5 is powerful enough to be a proper home media centre — one that plays films in crystal-clear 4K, streams your music collection to every room, and lets you control everything from your phone or TV remote. This chapter walks you through your options, gives you a clear recommendation, and then takes you step by step through a full working setup that any beginner can complete. What Are Your Options? There are four main approaches to turning your Pi into a media box. They suit different situations, so read through them before picking one. Option What it is Best for Cost Kodi A media-player app you install on top of Raspberry Pi OS. Your Pi still runs a normal desktop. People who want a general-purpose Pi that also plays media stored locally on a USB drive. Free LibreELEC A tiny, stripped-down operating system that is just Kodi — nothing else. Very fast to boot and very simple. A Pi that will only ever be a media box plugged into the TV. Free Jellyfin A media server that runs on your Pi and streams your film/music library to phones, tablets, smart TVs, and browsers around the house. People with a large collection of films or music who want to watch on multiple devices. Free & open source Plex Similar to Jellyfin but partly commercial. The free tier works well; some features (such as offline downloads and live TV) need a paid "Plex Pass". People who want a polished interface and do not mind optional paid features. Free (core); paid optional In plain words: A media server is software that sits on one computer (your Pi) and "serves" — sends — your films and music to other devices over your home Wi-Fi or network, just like a tiny Netflix running in your own house. Which Should You Choose? Here is a plain-English recommendation: Use LibreELEC if you want a dedicated box that boots straight to a TV-friendly media player, with big remote-friendly menus. You flash it to your microSD card exactly like Raspberry Pi OS (using Raspberry Pi Imager), and the Pi becomes a media box. You lose the desktop, but everything is simpler. Visit libreelec.tv for the download. Use Jellyfin if you want to keep Raspberry Pi OS (so your Pi stays useful for everything else) and you have a library of films, TV episodes, or music you want to watch on any screen in the house. This chapter follows this path end to end. Use Kodi on Raspberry Pi OS if you want a local media player without a server — just install it with one command and point it at your USB drive. Quick instructions are at the end of this chapter if you prefer this lighter option. Note: LibreELEC replaces Raspberry Pi OS entirely on the microSD card. If you flash LibreELEC, you will need a second microSD card if you ever want to go back to your normal Pi desktop. Keep that in mind before flashing. A Word on Media You Can Play Careful: Only use Jellyfin, Kodi, or any media software with films, music, and TV shows that you own or have the legal right to play. Downloading copyrighted content without paying for it is illegal in most countries, including the UK and EU. This guide assumes you have your own DVD/Blu-ray rips, home videos, or legally downloaded files. Full Worked Path: Jellyfin on Raspberry Pi OS We will install Jellyfin on your Pi, point it at a USB drive full of films, and then watch from your phone or TV. This takes about 20–30 minutes, most of which is waiting for downloads. What You Will Need Your Pi 5 running Raspberry Pi OS (Bookworm, 64-bit) and connected to your home network. A USB drive (or USB hard drive) containing your media files — films, TV shows, music. A phone, tablet, or smart TV on the same Wi-Fi network as your Pi. An internet connection for the Pi to download Jellyfin. Step 1 — Plug In Your USB Drive and Check It Is Recognised Plug your USB drive into one of the blue USB 3.0 ports on the Pi (the blue-coloured connectors are USB 3.0 — faster than the black USB 2.0 ports, which matters for large video files). Open a Terminal on your Pi (click the black screen icon on the taskbar, or press Ctrl + Alt + T ). Now check which devices are connected: lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,MOUNTPOINT,LABEL,FSTYPE lsblk lists every storage device connected to your Pi. The flags after -o choose which columns to display: the device name, its size, where it is mounted (accessible), its human-readable label, and its filesystem type. Look for a line like sda1 with a size matching your USB drive. The MOUNTPOINT column shows the path you use to reach its files — for example /media/pi/MOVIES . The FSTYPE column tells you whether the drive is formatted as vfat (FAT32), exfat , ntfs , or ext4 — make a note of this, as you will need it later. Tip: If the MOUNTPOINT column is empty for your drive, Raspberry Pi OS has not yet mounted it automatically. Usually it does so within a few seconds of plugging in. Wait a moment and run the command again. You can also open the File Manager (the folder icon on the taskbar) — this often triggers the automatic mount. Make a note of the mountpoint path and the filesystem type. We will use both in later steps. For the rest of this chapter, examples use the path /media/pi/MOVIES — substitute your actual path wherever you see that. Step 2 — Install Support for Windows-Formatted Drives (if needed) Most USB drives bought in Europe come formatted as exFAT or NTFS — the formats Windows uses. Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm can read these, but only if the right support packages are installed. Check your filesystem type from Step 1 and install the right one: If your drive is exFAT (most common for drives under 2 TB bought recently): sudo apt install exfatprogs -y Installs exfatprogs , the modern tool that lets Raspberry Pi OS read and write exFAT drives. Without this, an exFAT drive may fail to mount or Jellyfin may report errors. The -y flag confirms installation automatically. If your drive is NTFS (common for older drives or ones formatted by Windows 10/11): sudo apt install ntfs-3g -y Installs ntfs-3g , the driver that allows full read and write access to NTFS drives on Linux. Without this, NTFS drives mount in read-only mode or may not mount at all. -y confirms the installation. Note: If your drive is already formatted as ext4 (Linux's own format) or vfat (FAT32), no extra package is needed — both are supported out of the box. Step 3 — Update Your Pi Before installing anything new, bring your Pi up to date: sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y sudo apt update refreshes the list of available software packages from the internet. && means "only run the next command if the first one succeeded without errors". sudo apt upgrade -y then installs all available updates; the -y flag answers "yes" automatically so you do not have to confirm each update. This can take a few minutes. Step 4 — Install Jellyfin from Its Official Repository In plain words: A repository (often shortened to "repo") is an online library of software packages. Adding Jellyfin's official repository means your Pi knows where to find the Jellyfin software and how to verify it is genuine. Future updates then happen automatically alongside your normal system updates — you do not have to re-download or re-install Jellyfin manually. First, make sure the curl download tool is installed: sudo apt install curl -y Installs curl , a small tool for downloading files from the internet. It is often already present on Raspberry Pi OS, but this command ensures it is there before the next step relies on it. Now run the official Jellyfin installer script: curl -fsSL https://repo.jellyfin.org/install-debuntu.sh | sudo bash This single command does the entire Jellyfin setup for you. Breaking it down: curl -fsSL downloads a file from the internet silently and stops cleanly if there is an error. The URL points to the official Jellyfin installer script on repo.jellyfin.org . The | (pipe) symbol passes the downloaded script directly to sudo bash , which runs it with administrator permission. The script automatically detects that your Pi 5 is a 64-bit ARM device (arm64), adds Jellyfin's repository to your Pi, imports a security key so your Pi can verify the software is genuine, and then installs Jellyfin. A lot of text will scroll past — that is normal. Wait for the prompt to return before moving on. Note: Running a script downloaded from the internet with sudo is worth doing thoughtfully. Here we are using the official URL published by the Jellyfin project itself ( repo.jellyfin.org ). If you prefer to review what the script does before running it, you can open that URL in a browser and read it first — it is a plain text file. Step 5 — Start Jellyfin and Make It Start Automatically at Boot sudo systemctl enable --now jellyfin systemctl is the tool that manages background services on Raspberry Pi OS. enable registers Jellyfin to start automatically every time the Pi boots up. --now also starts it immediately right now, without needing a reboot. jellyfin is the name of the service. After this command, Jellyfin is running in the background. Confirm that Jellyfin is running: sudo systemctl status jellyfin Shows the current status of the Jellyfin background service. Look for the words active (running) in green near the top. If you see that, everything is working correctly. Press q to exit the status view and return to the normal command prompt. Tip: If Jellyfin shows as "failed" rather than "active (running)", try rebooting the Pi ( sudo reboot ) and checking the status again. If it still fails, run sudo journalctl -u jellyfin -n 50 to see the last 50 lines of error messages — copy them into a web search to find a solution. Step 6 — Find Your Pi's IP Address To reach Jellyfin from other devices on your home network, you need to know your Pi's address. Run: hostname -I Prints all network addresses assigned to your Pi. You will see one or two numbers such as 192.168.1.42 . The first number shown is your Pi's address on your home network (its Wi-Fi or Ethernet address). Write it down — you will type it into a browser on other devices shortly. In plain words: An IP address is your Pi's "house number" on the home network. Any device on the same Wi-Fi (phone, laptop, tablet, smart TV) can reach your Pi by typing this number into a web browser, just like typing a web address. Your Home Network (Wi-Fi Router) Raspberry Pi 5 Jellyfin server 192.168.1.42:8096 USB Drive Films / Music files USB 3.0 streams streams streams Smart TV Jellyfin app or browser Phone / Tablet Jellyfin app Laptop / Desktop Any web browser TV in another room Jellyfin app streams Jellyfin running on your Pi reads films from a USB drive and streams them simultaneously to any device on your home network — TVs, phones, laptops, and tablets. Step 7 — Open the Jellyfin Setup Wizard On your Pi (or on any device on the same network), open a web browser and type the following address into the address bar: http://192.168.1.42:8096 Replace 192.168.1.42 with your Pi's actual IP address that you noted in Step 6. The :8096 part is the port number — think of it as a door number within the Pi's address. Jellyfin listens on port 8096 by default. Because Raspberry Pi OS does not have a firewall enabled by default, this port is immediately reachable from any device on your home network. In plain words: A port number is a number added after an IP address (like :8096 ) that tells your computer which specific service to connect to. Just as a building can have many flats, one computer can run many services — each listens on its own port number. You should see the Jellyfin welcome screen. Follow the on-screen wizard: Choose your display language and click Next . Create an admin username and password. Write these down somewhere safe — you will need them to log in and manage Jellyfin. Do not use a password you use anywhere else. On the Set up your media libraries screen, click Add Media Library . Choose a Content type from the drop-down: for films choose Movies ; for TV series choose Shows ; for music choose Music . Click the + button next to Folders and type (or browse to) the path to your USB drive — for example /media/pi/MOVIES . Make sure the path matches exactly what you saw in Step 1. Click OK , then Next . Jellyfin will scan the folder and download artwork, descriptions, and ratings for your films automatically. This may take several minutes for a large library — be patient. Complete the rest of the wizard and click Finish . You will be taken to the Jellyfin home screen. Tip: Jellyfin works best when your film files are named clearly — for example Inception (2010).mkv or The Grand Budapest Hotel (2014).mp4 . Including the year in brackets helps Jellyfin identify the correct film and download the right artwork. For TV shows, use a folder structure like Breaking Bad/Season 1/Breaking Bad S01E01.mkv . If Jellyfin cannot match a file, rename it and trigger a library rescan from the Dashboard. Step 8 — Watch Something You can now watch from almost any device on your home network. Watching from a web browser (any device) Open a browser on your phone, laptop, or tablet and go to http://192.168.1.42:8096 . Log in with the username and password you created. Click any film and press play. No app is needed — the web browser is enough. Watching from a phone or tablet (Jellyfin app) Search for Jellyfin in the App Store (iPhone/iPad) or Google Play Store (Android). Install the free official Jellyfin app, tap Add Server , and enter http://192.168.1.42:8096 . Log in and your library appears. The app also lets you control playback on a TV and download films for offline viewing. Watching on a Smart TV Many smart TVs (Samsung, LG, Android TV, Amazon Fire TV, Chromecast with Google TV) have a Jellyfin app in their app store. Search for "Jellyfin" and install it, then enter your server address and login details. If your TV does not have a Jellyfin app, you can usually cast to it from the phone app, or use the TV's built-in web browser to access the Jellyfin web interface. Step 9 — Keep Your USB Drive Always Mounted By default, Raspberry Pi OS only mounts your USB drive after someone logs in at the desktop. If the Pi reboots overnight, Jellyfin may lose access to your files. To make the drive mount automatically at boot every time (even without anyone logged in), you need to add an entry to a file called /etc/fstab . In plain words: /etc/fstab is a configuration file that tells Raspberry Pi OS exactly which drives to connect and where to put them every time it starts up. Think of it as a shopping list the Pi reads at boot time — "attach this drive, put it here". First, find the unique ID of your USB drive. This ID is called a UUID — a long string of letters and numbers that never changes even if you plug the drive into a different USB port: sudo blkid blkid ("block ID") lists every storage device and shows its UUID and filesystem type. Find the line for your USB drive — match it by the label or size you noted earlier. Copy the UUID="..." value carefully. For FAT32/exFAT drives it looks something like A1B2-C3D4 ; for NTFS or ext4 drives it is a longer string like a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7890-abcd-ef1234567890 . In plain words: A UUID (Universally Unique Identifier) is a permanent serial number assigned to a storage drive when it is formatted. It never changes, so the Pi can identify your drive even if you plug it into a different USB socket. Now create a permanent folder where the drive will always appear: sudo mkdir -p /mnt/media Creates the folder /mnt/media . The -p flag means "also create any missing parent folders and do not complain if the folder already exists". This folder is the permanent location — the mount point — where your USB drive's files will be accessible after we set up automatic mounting. Next, give Jellyfin permission to read the drive's contents. Jellyfin runs as a background service under its own system user called jellyfin . The jellyfin user needs to be able to read the files on your USB drive. The easiest way is to add the jellyfin user to the same group that owns the mount point: sudo usermod -aG pi jellyfin usermod modifies a user account. -aG pi means "append (add without removing existing) the user to the group named pi ". jellyfin is the user being modified. Adding the jellyfin service account to the pi group lets it read files owned by pi , which includes the default automatic mounts under /media/pi/ . This change takes effect after Jellyfin is restarted in a moment. Now open the fstab file to add your drive's entry: sudo nano /etc/fstab Opens the file /etc/fstab in the nano text editor with administrator permission. This is the file that controls automatic drive mounting. Be careful here — a mistake can prevent the Pi from booting. (If that happens, boot into recovery mode and edit the file to remove the incorrect line.) Use the arrow keys to move to the very bottom of the file. Add one new line. Use the correct filesystem type for your drive: For a FAT32 drive ( FSTYPE was vfat ): UUID=YOUR-UUID-HERE /mnt/media vfat defaults,uid=1000,gid=1000,umask=002,nofail,x-systemd.automount 0 0 Each part of this line explained: UUID=YOUR-UUID-HERE identifies the exact drive by its unique ID (paste the UUID you copied). /mnt/media is where to make the drive's contents available. vfat is the filesystem type (FAT32). defaults uses standard mount settings. uid=1000,gid=1000 makes files on the drive appear to be owned by the default pi user (user ID 1000 on Raspberry Pi OS). umask=002 makes files readable and writable by the owner and group, readable by everyone else. nofail means the Pi still boots normally even if the drive is absent. x-systemd.automount tells the system to wait until the drive is genuinely ready before mounting it (more reliable for USB drives that take a moment to spin up). The two 0 s at the end disable filesystem checking at boot, which is recommended for USB drives. For an exFAT drive ( FSTYPE was exfat ): UUID=YOUR-UUID-HERE /mnt/media exfat defaults,uid=1000,gid=1000,umask=002,nofail,x-systemd.automount 0 0 Identical to the FAT32 line above except exfat replaces vfat as the filesystem type. This requires the exfatprogs package installed in Step 2. For an NTFS drive ( FSTYPE was ntfs ): UUID=YOUR-UUID-HERE /mnt/media ntfs-3g defaults,uid=1000,gid=1000,umask=002,nofail,x-systemd.automount 0 0 Identical to the other lines except ntfs-3g is the filesystem type. This uses the ntfs-3g driver installed in Step 2 to provide full read and write access. Note the filesystem type here is ntfs-3g (with a hyphen), not just ntfs . For a Linux ext4 drive ( FSTYPE was ext4 ): UUID=YOUR-UUID-HERE /mnt/media ext4 defaults,nofail,x-systemd.automount 0 2 For ext4 Linux-formatted drives, no uid/gid/umask options are needed — Linux permissions on the drive itself control access. The last digit is 2 instead of 0 , which allows the filesystem integrity check to run at boot (recommended for ext4). You may still need to adjust permissions on the drive's folders so the jellyfin user can read them (see the Tip below). Save and exit nano: press Ctrl + O , then Enter to confirm the filename, then Ctrl + X to exit. Test the new fstab entry without rebooting: sudo mount -a Tells the Pi to mount everything listed in /etc/fstab right now. If you see no error output, the line is correct and your drive is now accessible at /mnt/media . If you see an error message, open /etc/fstab again with sudo nano /etc/fstab , check the line carefully (UUID matches? filesystem type correct?), fix it, save, and run sudo mount -a again. Restart Jellyfin so it picks up the group change and the new mount: sudo systemctl restart jellyfin Stops and restarts the Jellyfin service. This is needed so Jellyfin (running as the jellyfin user) picks up the group membership change made with usermod earlier, and also reconnects to the newly mounted drive path. Now go back into the Jellyfin web interface at http://192.168.1.42:8096 , log in, go to the menu icon (top-left) and choose Dashboard → Libraries . Edit your library and update the folder path to /mnt/media (or the subfolder within it where your films live). Jellyfin will re-scan and the library will work reliably after every reboot. Tip: If Jellyfin still reports it cannot access the folder after all the above steps, check the folder permissions by running ls -la /mnt/media in the terminal. If the folder shows as owned by root with no group or other read access, run sudo chmod -R a+rX /mnt/media to make it readable by all users including the Jellyfin service. 4K and HEVC: What the Pi 5 Can Handle In plain words: HEVC (also called H.265) is a modern video compression format used for most 4K films — it makes huge 4K video files a manageable size. Direct play means a client device plays the file in its original format with no conversion needed. Transcoding means the server converts the video from one format to another on the fly so a device can play it — this requires much more processing power. The Pi 5's VideoCore VII graphics chip can hardware-decode HEVC (H.265) and H.264 video — the two most common formats for 4K and 1080p films. This means it can handle 4K direct play to a TV connected via HDMI with ease, barely breaking a sweat. If a client device (such as an older phone or a browser on a Windows PC) cannot play HEVC natively, Jellyfin will transcode the video on the fly. The Pi 5 can handle a single 1080p software transcode comfortably. Transcoding a 4K stream in real time is much heavier work and may cause stuttering; if this happens, lower the quality setting in the Jellyfin player. Tip: For the best experience, prefer client devices that support HEVC natively — most modern smartphones and smart TVs do. When HEVC is supported, Jellyfin uses direct play and the Pi barely works at all, leaving plenty of spare power for other tasks. Enabling Hardware Transcoding in Jellyfin If transcoding is necessary, you can enable hardware-accelerated transcoding to use the Pi 5's GPU rather than the main processor. This is optional but worthwhile if you regularly transcode: In the Jellyfin web interface, log in as admin and click the menu icon, then choose Dashboard . Under Server , click Playback . Find the Hardware acceleration dropdown and select Video4Linux2 (V4L2) . This is the correct option for the Raspberry Pi 5's VideoCore VII GPU. Scroll down and click Save . Note: Hardware transcoding on the Pi 5 via V4L2 works best with H.264 and HEVC content. For very unusual codecs (such as older AVI or WMV files), the Pi may fall back to software transcoding automatically.
