Controlling Playback HDMI-CEC: Use Your TV Remote In plain words: HDMI-CEC (Consumer Electronics Control) is a hidden signalling channel built into the HDMI standard. It lets devices on your TV's HDMI ports talk to each other — for example, it lets your TV remote control your Pi, or lets the Pi automatically switch your TV on and select its input when the Pi starts playing something. The Pi 5 supports HDMI-CEC, and Raspberry Pi OS enables it by default. If you are using Kodi (or another media player app) directly on the Pi with its HDMI output connected to your TV: Your TV remote's arrow keys and OK button will navigate the on-screen menus. The volume buttons on your TV remote will adjust the audio level. Starting a media player can automatically wake the TV and switch it to the Pi's HDMI input. CEC must also be enabled on your TV. Look in your TV's settings — brands use their own names for the same feature: TV Brand Their name for HDMI-CEC Where to find it Samsung Anynet+ Settings → General → External Device Manager → Anynet+ LG SimpLink Settings → General → SIMPLINK (HDMI-CEC) Sony Bravia Sync Settings → Watching TV → External inputs → Bravia Sync Philips EasyLink Setup → TV settings → EasyLink Panasonic VIERA Link Setup → VIERA Link settings Note: HDMI-CEC control works automatically for Kodi and LibreELEC once it is enabled on the TV. For Jellyfin (where you watch on a separate phone, tablet, or smart TV), your TV remote already controls that device natively — no extra setup is needed. Phone Remote Apps If you are using Kodi on your Pi, install the free Kodi Remote app (search for it in the App Store or Google Play Store) to control playback from your phone over Wi-Fi — pause, skip, browse your library, and adjust volume, all from the sofa. For Jellyfin, the Jellyfin mobile app doubles as a remote control — tap the cast icon in the app to control playback on a TV or another device on your network. Alternative: Installing Kodi on Raspberry Pi OS If you would rather just have a local media player on your Pi without setting up a server, Kodi is a single command away. Kodi is the right choice if your films are on a USB drive plugged directly into the Pi and you only ever watch on the TV that the Pi is connected to. sudo apt update sudo apt install kodi -y The first line refreshes the list of available software packages from the internet, so the Pi knows about the latest version of Kodi. The second line installs Kodi from Raspberry Pi OS's built-in software repository. The -y flag answers "yes" to the confirmation prompt automatically. After this completes (it may take a few minutes to download), you will find Kodi in the application menu under Sound & Video , or you can launch it by typing kodi in the terminal and pressing Enter . Once Kodi opens, use the Videos → Files → Add videos... option from the home screen to point it at your USB drive. Kodi will scan the folder, download artwork, and build a library automatically — very similar to Jellyfin's setup wizard, but entirely local on the Pi. Tip: If you want Kodi to launch automatically when the Pi boots (so it behaves like a dedicated set-top box), you can create a small autostart file. In the terminal, run: mkdir -p /home/pi/.config/autostart and then create a file at /home/pi/.config/autostart/kodi.desktop containing: [Desktop Entry] Type=Application Name=Kodi Exec=kodi This makes Kodi launch automatically when your Pi desktop starts up. For most beginners, though, simply launching Kodi from the application menu when you want to watch something is perfectly fine. Careful: The autostart method above places a plain text file in your home folder. It is completely safe and easy to undo — simply delete the file ( rm /home/pi/.config/autostart/kodi.desktop ) and Kodi will stop auto-launching. It does not modify any system files. Troubleshooting Common Problems Problem Likely cause What to do Cannot reach Jellyfin from another device The other device is on a different network, or you have the wrong IP address Make sure both devices are connected to the same Wi-Fi network (not one on 2.4 GHz and one on 5 GHz if your router keeps them separate). Re-run hostname -I on the Pi to confirm the current IP. Try accessing http://localhost:8096 in a browser on the Pi itself first — if that works, Jellyfin is fine and the issue is network connectivity. Jellyfin cannot see my USB drive files The drive is not mounted, or Jellyfin does not have permission to read it Run lsblk to confirm the drive is mounted. Check the library path in Jellyfin's Dashboard → Libraries matches the actual mount point exactly (paths are case-sensitive). Check permissions with ls -la /mnt/media and ensure the jellyfin user can read the folder. Video stutters or buffers Transcoding is happening and the Pi is under heavy load, or your Wi-Fi is slow In the Jellyfin player, lower the quality setting to Auto or 1080p . Connect the Pi to your router by Ethernet cable for maximum throughput. Enable hardware transcoding (V4L2) in Jellyfin's Dashboard → Playback settings. Prefer client devices that support HEVC natively so Jellyfin can use direct play. No sound over HDMI The wrong audio output is selected (the Pi 5 has no 3.5 mm headphone jack — audio goes via HDMI or USB only) Right-click the speaker icon in the Pi taskbar and select the HDMI audio device. In Kodi, go to Settings → System → Audio and select the HDMI output device from the list. TV remote does not control Kodi HDMI-CEC is disabled on the TV Find your TV brand's name for HDMI-CEC in the table above and enable it in your TV's settings. Then restart the Pi (or restart Kodi) for the Pi to detect the CEC connection. Jellyfin library shows no artwork or wrong films Jellyfin could not match the files because the filenames do not include the film title and year Rename your files to include the film title and year in brackets — e.g. Dune (2021).mkv — then go to Dashboard → Libraries, select your library, and click Scan All Libraries to trigger a fresh scan. Pi's IP address has changed (Jellyfin address stopped working) Your router assigned a different IP to the Pi after a reboot Re-run hostname -I to find the new address. To prevent this in future, log into your router's admin page and set a "DHCP reservation" for the Pi's MAC address so it always gets the same IP. See your router's manual for how to do this. drive not mounting at boot despite fstab entry The UUID is wrong or the filesystem type is incorrect in fstab Run sudo blkid and compare the UUID with what is in /etc/fstab . Open fstab with sudo nano /etc/fstab , correct the UUID or filesystem type, save, then run sudo mount -a to test. Keeping Jellyfin Updated Because you installed Jellyfin via its official repository, updating it is the same as updating everything else on your Pi: sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y This is the same update command you use for all software on your Pi. Because Jellyfin was added as a proper repository, this single command will also fetch and install any new version of Jellyfin automatically. Running this once a month is a good habit — you get bug fixes, security patches, and new features in one go. Tip: After a Jellyfin update, the service restarts automatically. Check it is still running with sudo systemctl status jellyfin if you want to confirm. Key terms Kodi — a free, open-source media player application you install on top of Raspberry Pi OS; plays films, music, and TV shows stored on a local drive. LibreELEC — a tiny operating system built entirely around Kodi; it replaces Raspberry Pi OS and is ideal for a dedicated media box. Jellyfin — a free, open-source media server that runs on your Pi and streams your personal library to phones, tablets, TVs, and browsers over your home network. Media server — software that stores your media on one computer (the Pi) and sends it to other devices over the network, like a private Netflix in your home. Repository (repo) — an online library of trusted software packages that your Pi downloads and installs software from. IP address — a unique number (like 192.168.1.42 ) that identifies a device on a network; your Pi's "house number" on your home Wi-Fi. Port number — a number appended to an IP address (like :8096 ) that identifies a specific service on a device; like a flat number within a building. HEVC / H.265 — a modern video compression format used for most 4K content; the Pi 5 can decode it in hardware, making 4K playback smooth. Direct play — when a client device plays a video file in its original format without the server having to convert it; the most efficient and highest-quality mode. Transcoding — when the server converts a video from one format to another on the fly so a device can play it; more demanding on the Pi's processor. HDMI-CEC — a built-in feature of the HDMI standard that lets devices on HDMI ports talk to each other; allows a TV remote to control the Pi. UUID — a permanent unique identification code assigned to a storage drive; used in /etc/fstab to reliably identify a drive regardless of which USB port it is plugged into. /etc/fstab — a system configuration file that tells Raspberry Pi OS which drives to connect and where to put them every time it starts up. Mount / mount point — "mounting" a drive means making its contents accessible at a folder path on the system; the folder it appears at is called the mount point. exFAT — a filesystem format commonly used on larger USB drives sold ready-to-use; readable on Windows, macOS, and (with exfatprogs ) Linux. NTFS — the filesystem format Windows uses on internal hard drives; readable on Linux with the ntfs-3g driver. V4L2 — Video4Linux2; the interface that lets Jellyfin use the Pi 5's GPU for hardware-accelerated video transcoding, reducing the load on the main processor. Chapter summary The Pi 5 makes an excellent media centre — choose LibreELEC for a dedicated box, Jellyfin for streaming to multiple devices around the house, or Kodi on Raspberry Pi OS for a straightforward local player. Jellyfin is installed from its official repository using a single installer command and streams films, TV, and music to any browser, phone app, or smart TV app on your home network. Windows-formatted USB drives (exFAT or NTFS) need the exfatprogs or ntfs-3g package installed on Bookworm before they mount reliably. Adding a correctly formatted line to /etc/fstab with the drive's UUID and the nofail,x-systemd.automount options ensures the USB media drive mounts automatically at every boot, so Jellyfin always has access to your files. The Jellyfin service account ( jellyfin ) needs to be in the pi group, or the mount point needs to be world-readable, before Jellyfin can access files on the USB drive. The Pi 5 decodes 4K HEVC video in hardware (VideoCore VII), making high-quality direct playback smooth and efficient without any special configuration. Hardware-accelerated transcoding can be enabled in Jellyfin's Dashboard → Playback by selecting V4L2 , which offloads conversion work to the GPU. HDMI-CEC lets your existing TV remote control Kodi on the Pi; enable it in your TV's settings (Anynet+, SimpLink, Bravia Sync, EasyLink, or VIERA Link depending on your brand). Update Jellyfin with sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y — the same command used for all software on your Pi. Only use media software with content you legally own or have the right to play.

title: Retro Gaming
headings: What Is Retro Gaming on the Pi?
The Legal Picture — Please Read First
Step 2 — Flash Batocera to Your Spare Card
Performance — What to Expect on the Pi 5
Audio — No Headphone Socket on the Pi 5
Useful Tips for the Best Experience
text: Your Raspberry Pi 5 is a surprisingly powerful little games machine — capable of running arcade classics, 16-bit console favourites, and even early 3D games without breaking a sweat. In this chapter you will choose a retro-gaming platform, get it running, connect a controller, add your games, and start playing — all without needing any technical background. What Is Retro Gaming on the Pi? Before the modern era of online gaming and downloads, people played games on dedicated consoles (Nintendo, Sega, Sony) or in arcades. Those original machines are now decades old, but a technique called emulation lets your Pi pretend to be one of those old machines in software. In plain words: An emulator is a program that mimics an old games console so that game files designed for that console can run on your Pi. A ROM is the digital copy of a game cartridge or disc — the file that the emulator loads and plays. Two layers of software work together to make this happen: EmulationStation — the graphical front-end (the menu you see on screen, organised by console, with artwork for each game). RetroArch / libretro — the engine underneath that actually runs the emulators. You rarely interact with it directly; it just works. In plain words: Think of EmulationStation as the TV remote control — it lets you browse and pick games — while RetroArch is the television itself, doing the actual work of playing them. Choosing Your Platform Three popular choices exist, each with a different philosophy: Platform What it is Best for Pi 5 support Batocera A complete, standalone operating system dedicated to gaming. You flash it to a separate card; it replaces Pi OS entirely on that card. Beginners who want a plug-and-play games console experience with the least fuss. Excellent. First-class Pi 5 image available; automatic controller detection. RetroPie A package that adds emulation on top of your existing Raspberry Pi OS. You keep everything you already set up. People who want Pi OS for other things and gaming on the same card. Good. Community-supported; some manual steps needed on Pi 5 with Bookworm. Lakka Another standalone OS, based on LibreELEC. Very lightweight. Exposes RetroArch directly. Experienced users who want to tune every emulator setting manually. Good, but less polished on Pi 5 than Batocera at the time of writing. Tip: This guide recommends Batocera for beginners. It installs quickly, detects your controller automatically, looks beautiful on a TV, and needs almost no configuration. The guide covers Batocera in full first, then RetroPie as an advanced alternative at the end. Use a second microSD card (16 GB or larger) so your main Pi OS card is completely untouched. The Legal Picture — Please Read First Careful: Emulators themselves are legal. However, ROM files may be protected by copyright . Downloading ROMs for games you do not own is illegal in most countries, including the UK and across the EU, regardless of how old the game is. You may legally use ROMs of games you personally own (for example, by dumping your own cartridges with a purpose-built device). There are also legitimate freeware and homebrew sources — games specifically released for free by their creators. Searching for "freeware ROMs" or "homebrew games [console name]" will find legal downloads. This guide does not name or link to piracy sites. Playing legally protects you and supports the people who made those games. What You Will Need A spare microSD card — 16 GB minimum, 32 GB or larger recommended (more space means more games). The USB card reader that came with your kit. Your Windows 11 PC to flash the image. A USB or Bluetooth game controller. Almost any USB gamepad works out of the box; Xbox One/Series and PlayStation 4/5 controllers are recognised automatically. A USB keyboard can be used temporarily if you have no controller yet. Your Pi connected to a monitor or TV via the micro-HDMI cable. An internet connection (for downloading cover art and updates later). Two microSD cards diagram Two microSD cards shown side by side — the left card labelled "Main card: Raspberry Pi OS" and the right labelled "Spare card: Batocera". An arrow between them shows they are swapped in and out of the Pi. Main card Raspberry Pi OS (your desktop, projects) Label it! ⇄ swap Spare card Batocera (games console OS) Label it! Pi's microSD slot Keep your two microSD cards clearly labelled. Swap them in the Pi's microSD slot to switch between Raspberry Pi OS and Batocera. The two systems never interfere with each other. Step 1 — Download Batocera On your Windows PC, open a web browser and search for Batocera Linux . The first result should be the official website at batocera.linux . Click through to that site. Click Download , then choose Raspberry Pi 5 from the list of devices. Download the compressed image file. It will have a name like batocera-bcm2712-rpi5-v40.img.gz . The exact version number will be higher by the time you read this — that is fine, always download the latest. Make a note of where the file saved (usually your Downloads folder). Note: The file ends in .img.gz , meaning it is a compressed disk image. Raspberry Pi Imager (which you used in Chapter 4) handles this format directly — you do not need to unzip it first. Step 2 — Flash Batocera to Your Spare Card This process is almost identical to what you did in Chapter 4 when you first installed Raspberry Pi OS. If you need a reminder of the steps, flip back there now. Insert your spare microSD card into the USB card reader, then plug the reader into your Windows PC. Open Raspberry Pi Imager (the blue raspberry icon on your desktop or in your Start menu). Click Choose OS . Scroll to the bottom of the list and select Use custom . Browse to your Downloads folder and select the Batocera .img.gz file. Click Choose Storage and select your spare card. Double-check you are picking the correct one — everything on the chosen card will be erased. Click Next . When Imager asks if you want to apply OS customisation, click No — Batocera has its own first-boot setup and does not use Imager's customisation. Confirm the write and wait for it to finish (typically five to ten minutes depending on your card speed). Once Imager says it is complete, eject the card safely from Windows: right-click the drive letter in File Explorer and choose Eject before removing it physically. Careful: Make absolutely sure you select the spare card, not the card holding your main Raspberry Pi OS. Both cards may appear as drives in Imager. Label your cards with a sticky note or a piece of masking tape so you always know which is which — this takes ten seconds and could save you from accidentally wiping your work. Step 3 — Boot into Batocera Make sure the Pi is powered off. Remove the power cable. Take out your main Raspberry Pi OS card from the Pi's microSD slot (on the underside of the board). Insert the Batocera card into the Pi's microSD slot. Plug in your HDMI cable and your USB game controller (or a keyboard if you have no controller yet). Plug in the power cable. The Pi will start. The first boot takes longer than usual — Batocera expands itself to fill the entire card. You will see text scrolling on screen, then a progress bar. This is completely normal; wait for it to finish (around two to three minutes). After that first-boot process, the system restarts once more automatically. You will arrive at the EmulationStation main menu — a colourful screen showing a list of game systems along the left. EmulationStation layout diagram Diagram showing the main areas of the EmulationStation interface: a left-hand system list, a centre game list, and a right-hand game info panel. EmulationStation — Main Screen SYSTEMS ▶ NES SNES Mega Drive Game Boy PlayStation Arcade (MAME) GAME LIST ▶ My Homebrew Game Another Game And Another GAME INFO [Cover Art] Publisher: Year: Players: A = Select B = Back Start = Menu Hotkey+Start = Quit game The three main panels of EmulationStation: the system list on the left, the game list in the centre, and game information and cover art on the right. Common button shortcuts are shown in the bar at the bottom. Step 4 — Configure Your Controller If you plugged in a USB controller before booting, Batocera almost certainly detected it automatically. Bluetooth controllers need to be paired first. USB Controller If EmulationStation shows a controller configuration screen on first boot, follow the on-screen prompts to map your buttons. The screen will ask you to press each button in turn (A, B, X, Y, triggers, and so on). Hold any button for a moment to skip a button your controller does not have. If no mapping screen appeared, your controller was recognised automatically and is already working — press a button to confirm. Bluetooth Controller From the EmulationStation main menu, press Start (or Enter on a keyboard) to open the Main Menu . Choose Controller & Bluetooth Settings . Select Pair a Bluetooth Device Automatically . Put your controller into pairing mode: PS4 controller: hold the Share button and the PS button together until the light bar flashes rapidly. PS5 DualSense: hold the Create button and the PS button together until the light flashes. Xbox One/Series controller: hold the small Pair button on top of the controller until the Xbox logo flashes rapidly. 8BitDo and other gamepads: check the manual — there is usually a dedicated pairing button or a Home + another button combination. Your controller should appear in the list on screen. Select it and wait for the "Paired" confirmation. Press B (or Backspace on a keyboard) to go back to the main menu. Your controller is now ready. Tip: Xbox One and Series controllers connected via USB cable require no setup at all in Batocera — they are recognised the moment you plug them in. Step 5 — Connect to Your Network You need a network connection to copy games to Batocera over Wi-Fi (covered in the next section). You can also use an Ethernet cable plugged into the Pi's Ethernet port and skip this step entirely — wired is always more reliable. Press Start to open the Main Menu. Choose Network Settings . Turn Enable Wi-Fi on. Select Wi-Fi SSID , find your home network name in the list, and select it. Enter your Wi-Fi password using the on-screen keyboard, then confirm. After a few seconds, an IP address (a number like 192.168.1.50 ) will appear next to the network name, confirming you are connected. Make a note of this number — you may need it later. In plain words: An IP address is your Pi's unique address on your home network — like a house number on a street. Other devices on the same network use it to find your Pi. Step 6 — Copy Games onto Batocera Batocera creates a shared folder on your network automatically — this is called a Samba share . You can drag game files into it from your Windows PC exactly like copying files to a USB stick. In plain words: A Samba share is a way for a Linux computer (like your Pi) to make a folder appear in Windows Explorer over your home network, so you can copy files into it as if it were just another folder on your PC. Method A — Copy over the Network (Samba) On your Windows PC, open File Explorer (the folder icon in the taskbar). Click in the address bar at the top, type \\BATOCERA and press Enter . Windows will connect to the Pi and show its shared folders. Open the share folder, then open the roms folder inside it. Inside roms , you will find a sub-folder for each system — for example nes , snes , megadrive , psx (PlayStation), mame (arcade), and many more. Copy your legal ROM files into the correct console sub-folder. For example, a NES ROM (a file ending in .nes ) goes into the nes folder. Once copying is complete, go back to your Pi. Press Start , choose Game Settings , then Update Game Lists . Your games will now appear in the EmulationStation menu. Note: If \\BATOCERA does not connect, try \\batocera.local instead. If that also fails, use the IP address you noted in Step 5 — for example \\192.168.1.50 . Method B — Copy by USB Drive Format a USB drive as FAT32 or exFAT on your Windows PC: right-click the drive in File Explorer, choose Format , pick FAT32 or exFAT from the file system drop-down, and click Start . On the USB drive, create a folder called roms . Inside it, create sub-folders matching the console names (for example nes , snes , megadrive ). Copy your ROM files into the correct sub-folder. Safely eject the USB drive from Windows, then plug it into one of the Pi's USB ports while Batocera is running. Batocera will detect the USB drive and ask if you want to import games from it. Confirm, and your games will be copied to the microSD card. Once the import finishes, you can unplug the USB drive. The games are now stored on your Batocera card. Common ROM File Extensions Console Folder name in Batocera Typical file extension(s) Nintendo NES nes .nes Super Nintendo (SNES) snes .sfc or .smc Sega Mega Drive / Genesis megadrive .md or .bin Game Boy / Game Boy Colour gb / gbc .gb / .gbc Game Boy Advance gba .gba Sony PlayStation 1 psx .bin + .cue Nintendo 64 n64 .z64 or .n64 Sega Saturn saturn .bin + .cue Dreamcast dreamcast .gdi or .chd Arcade (MAME) mame .zip Note: PlayStation 1 (and Saturn) games usually come as a pair of files — a .bin file (the actual game data) and a .cue file (a short text file that describes the disc layout). You need both files in the same folder for the game to work. If you are missing either one, the game will not launch. About BIOS Files Some older consoles require a special file called a BIOS before their emulator will work. A BIOS is a tiny program that was stored inside the original hardware and that the emulator needs to mimic the console accurately. In plain words: A BIOS file is a small program that was built into the original console's chips. The emulator needs a copy of it to start up, in the same way a real console did. Without it, games for that system simply will not launch. Consoles that require a BIOS include: PlayStation 1 — needs scph1001.bin (or a similar SCPH model file). Sega Saturn — needs a Saturn BIOS file. Sega CD / Mega CD — needs a Mega CD BIOS file. Game Boy Advance — the GBA BIOS improves compatibility (not always required, but recommended). Dreamcast — needs a Dreamcast BIOS set (a small folder of files). Consoles that do not need a BIOS include the NES, SNES, Mega Drive, Game Boy, Game Boy Colour, Nintendo 64, and most arcade games. These will work without any extra files. Careful: BIOS files are copyrighted by the companies that made the original consoles. Distributing or downloading them without owning the original hardware is technically illegal in most jurisdictions. You can legally dump BIOS files from hardware you own using specialist tools. This guide does not provide or link to BIOS file downloads. To install BIOS files in Batocera, copy them to the bios folder visible in the Samba share at \\BATOCERA\share\bios . The exact filenames and folder structure expected by each emulator are listed in Batocera's official documentation (visit the Batocera website and search for "BIOS"). Step 7 — Playing a Game On the EmulationStation main screen, use the left and right arrows (or the left stick) to scroll through systems until you reach the one you want. Press A (or Enter on a keyboard) to open the game list for that system. Scroll up and down to highlight a game. Press A to launch it. The emulator will load — usually in just one or two seconds. Play as normal. Your controller buttons correspond to the original console's layout (as you mapped them in Step 4). Saving and Loading Your Progress Retro consoles originally used battery-backed memory in cartridges, or removable memory cards. Emulators offer a far more convenient system called save states — an instant snapshot of the exact moment in the game, saved at any point you choose. In plain words: A save state is like pressing a pause button that freezes the entire game — the screen, your position, your health, your score, everything — exactly as it is. You can come back to that frozen moment later, even if you died immediately afterwards. In-Game Save vs Save State Some games have their own built-in save system (you will see a "Save" option in the game's own menu). This works in emulators just as it did on real hardware. Save states are a separate, additional feature provided by the emulator — they work even in games that have no built-in save. Hotkey Shortcuts While a game is running, hold the Hotkey button (by default the Select button on your controller) and press another button to trigger a shortcut: Action Default shortcut (Hotkey = Select) Save state (slot 1) Hotkey + R1 Load state (slot 1) Hotkey + L1 Next save-state slot Hotkey + R2 Previous save-state slot Hotkey + L2 Open RetroArch menu Hotkey + B Quit game and return to EmulationStation Hotkey + Start Take a screenshot Hotkey + Y Fast-forward (hold) Hotkey + X Rewind (if enabled) Hotkey + Left Note: Save states are numbered — slot 1 is the default. You can maintain up to 999 separate save slots per game. Use Hotkey + R2 / L2 to cycle through slots before saving or loading, if you want to keep multiple snapshots of the same game at different points. Opening the RetroArch Menu If you need deeper options — changing screen filters, switching the emulator core, or viewing your save files — press Hotkey + B while a game is running. This opens the RetroArch overlay menu, a darker screen with many settings. To close it and return to your game without changing anything, press B a few times until the game is back. To quit the game entirely, choose Close Content from the RetroArch menu, or simply use Hotkey + Start . Performance — What to Expect on the Pi 5 The Pi 5's quad-core Arm Cortex-A76 processor running at 2.4 GHz is significantly faster than any previous Raspberry Pi. Here is a realistic guide to what runs at full speed in Batocera: System Era Pi 5 performance Atari 2600 / 7800 Late 1970s–80s Perfect. Near-zero CPU use. NES / Game Boy / Master System 1980s Perfect. Runs effortlessly. SNES / Mega Drive / Game Boy Colour Early 1990s Perfect. No issues at all. Game Boy Advance Early 2000s Excellent. Full speed on all games. PlayStation 1 / Sega Saturn Mid 1990s Excellent. Full speed on virtually all games. Nintendo 64 Late 1990s Very good. Nearly all games at full speed. Dreamcast Late 1990s Good. Most games playable; a few demanding titles may stutter. PlayStation 2 Early 2000s Mixed. Simpler games work well; complex 3D titles may need speed tweaks. GameCube / Wii 2000s Experimental. Some titles work; many are still too demanding. PlayStation 3 / Xbox 360 2005–2013 Not feasible. Far too demanding for the Pi 5. Tip: If a game runs slowly, open the RetroArch menu (Hotkey + B) and try Quick Menu → Core Options — many emulators have a resolution or rendering option that can improve speed. Alternatively, try a different emulator core for that system under Quick Menu → Core . Audio — No Headphone Socket on the Pi 5 Unlike the Pi 4, the Pi 5 has no 3.5 mm headphone socket . Game audio comes through your HDMI cable to your monitor or TV's built-in speakers. If you would like to use headphones or external speakers, you have three options: HDMI audio: plug headphones into the headphone socket on your monitor or TV (if it has one). USB audio adapter: a small USB dongle with a 3.5 mm socket (costs around £5–10 / €6–12) plugged into any USB port on the Pi. Batocera detects these automatically. Bluetooth headphones or speaker: pair them via Main Menu → Controller & Bluetooth Settings , just as you would pair a controller. Scraping Cover Art Batocera can automatically download cover art, descriptions, and ratings for your games, turning a plain list of filenames into a beautiful visual library. This process is called scraping . In plain words: Scraping means Batocera looks up each of your game files in an online database (by filename and file size), then downloads the matching box art, description, release year, and ratings automatically. Make sure your Pi is connected to the internet. From the EmulationStation main menu, press Start to open the Main Menu. Choose Scraper . Select your source. ScreenScraper is the recommended choice — it is free, covers almost every console, and has high-quality artwork. Optionally create a free account at the ScreenScraper website (search for "ScreenScraper" in your browser) to increase your daily download limit from 20 to several hundred images. Press Scrape Now . Batocera will work through each game and download artwork. This may take several minutes if you have many games. When it finishes, exit the menus. Your game lists will now show box art and descriptions rather than plain filenames. Troubleshooting Common Problems Here are the most common issues beginners encounter, and how to fix them. Games Not Showing Up in the Menu Wrong folder: check the ROM file is in the exact sub-folder for its system (for example nes for NES, not a folder you created yourself with a different name). Wrong file extension: some emulators are strict about file extensions. Check the table in the "Common ROM File Extensions" section above. Need to refresh: press Start → Game Settings → Update Game Lists after copying any new files. Compressed wrong: some ROMs are double-compressed (a .zip inside another .zip ). Batocera can open a single .zip , but not one nested inside another. Unzip the outer layer first. Controller Not Working In-Game If a controller that works in EmulationStation does not work once a game loads, the mapping may not have transferred to that specific emulator core. Open the RetroArch menu ( Hotkey + B ), go to Settings → Input , and remap your buttons for that core. Bluetooth controllers can occasionally disconnect. If this happens, re-pair them (Step 4) or switch to a USB cable. Game Runs Too Slowly Open the RetroArch menu (Hotkey + B) and check Core Options — lowering the internal resolution for 3D systems (PS2, N64) often helps significantly. Make sure no other applications are running on the Pi at the same time. For Dreamcast and PS2, try switching to a different emulator core (Quick Menu → Core) — some cores are better optimised for the Pi 5 than others. No Sound Check the volume on your monitor or TV. In Batocera, press Start → Sound Settings and confirm the correct audio output device is selected (HDMI, USB, or Bluetooth as appropriate). If you are using a USB audio adapter, unplug it and re-insert it, then update the sound output setting. Black Screen After Selecting a Game The game may need a BIOS file that is missing. Check the "About BIOS Files" section above. The ROM file may be corrupted. Try a different copy. Try launching the RetroArch menu straight after the black screen appears (press Hotkey + B) and check the log under Information → Log Viewer for a specific error message. Useful Tips for the Best Experience Use a wired controller for zero lag. Bluetooth is convenient, but a USB connection gives the lowest possible input delay — important for fast action games where timing matters. Try CRT filters. In the RetroArch menu (Hotkey + B), go to Shaders . A CRT shader adds a scanline effect that makes pixel-art games look exactly as they did on an old television. Many people find this more atmospheric than the sharp, chunky pixel look on a modern screen. Enable rewind. RetroArch can let you hold a button to rewind a game by a few seconds — very useful if you just died. Enable it in the RetroArch menu under Settings → Frame Throttle → Rewind . Note that it uses extra memory and is not available for every emulator. Two players. Simply plug a second USB controller into another USB port before launching the game. EmulationStation assigns it as Player 2 automatically. Storage space tip. A 32 GB card comfortably holds a large library of 8-bit and 16-bit games (which are tiny — a few kilobytes each). PlayStation 1 and N64 games are bigger (a few hundred megabytes each), and PlayStation 2 games can be several gigabytes. If you want a large PS2 or Dreamcast library, consider a 64 GB or 128 GB card. Switch back to Pi OS. When you want to use your main Pi OS card again, power off the Pi, swap the card, and power back on. The two systems are completely independent — neither one can affect the other. Using RetroPie Instead (Advanced Option) If you prefer to keep everything on one card — adding gaming on top of your existing Raspberry Pi OS rather than using a separate card — RetroPie is the alternative. The steps below assume you have Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm already running on your Pi. A desktop (GUI) installation is fine, though Raspberry Pi OS Lite (no desktop) leaves more resources free for gaming. Note: This section is entirely optional. If you followed the Batocera path above, you do not need to do this. Skip ahead to the Key Terms section if Batocera is working for you. Installing RetroPie on Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm Open a terminal on your Pi (click the black terminal icon on the taskbar, or connect via SSH as described in Chapter 9). Update your system to make sure all existing packages are current: sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y sudo — runs the command with administrator (superuser) privileges, which are needed to install software. apt update — downloads the latest list of available software packages from the internet. It does not install anything yet. && — "only run the next command if the previous one succeeded without errors". apt full-upgrade -y — installs all available updates. full-upgrade (rather than just upgrade ) is used here because RetroPie's dependencies sometimes require packages to be removed and replaced; -y automatically answers "yes" to any confirmation prompts so you do not have to type Y each time. Install the helper tools that RetroPie's installer needs: sudo apt install -y git dialog unzip xmlstarlet sudo apt install -y — installs the listed packages, automatically confirming any prompts. git — a tool for downloading code from the internet (specifically from GitHub, where the RetroPie installer lives). dialog — provides the text-based, mouse-free menu screens you will see during the RetroPie installation. unzip — unpacks .zip compressed files, which several emulators use during their installation. xmlstarlet — reads and edits XML configuration files that some of RetroPie's components rely on. Download the RetroPie setup script from GitHub: git clone --depth=1 https://github.com/RetroPie/RetroPie-Setup.git git clone — downloads a complete copy of the RetroPie setup files from the internet and puts them in a new folder called RetroPie-Setup in your current directory. --depth=1 — tells git to download only the most recent version of the files, not the full change history. This is faster and uses far less storage. https://github.com/RetroPie/RetroPie-Setup.git — the official, verified address of the RetroPie setup repository on GitHub. Move into the newly downloaded folder and run the installer: cd RetroPie-Setup sudo bash retropie_setup.sh cd RetroPie-Setup — moves you into the RetroPie-Setup folder that was just downloaded. (cd stands for "change directory".) sudo bash retropie_setup.sh — runs the RetroPie setup script with administrator privileges. A text-based menu will appear on screen with several options. In the menu that appears, choose Basic Install . This compiles and installs dozens of emulators from source code — a process that can take 30 to 90 minutes on a Pi 5. Let it run; you can do something else in the meantime. The screen will show progress as each emulator is compiled. When the installation finishes, choose Perform Reboot from the menu. After rebooting, EmulationStation will start automatically. Careful: RetroPie on Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm is a community effort and is actively developed. Some emulators may fail to compile on a 64-bit Bookworm system. If an emulator fails during the Basic Install, you can skip it and install other emulators individually from the Manage Packages menu later. The RetroPie forum at retropie.org.uk/forum is an excellent resource — search for your specific error message and you will almost always find a solution. Once RetroPie is running, you add ROMs by placing files in the /home/pi/RetroPie/roms/ folder on the Pi. This folder is also accessible as a Samba network share from Windows at \\RETROPIE\roms — browse to it in File Explorer just as you did with Batocera. Keeping Batocera Up to Date Batocera receives regular updates that add new emulator cores, fix bugs, and improve performance. Updating is simple and never deletes your games or save files. Make sure your Pi is connected to the internet. Press Start from the EmulationStation main menu, then go to System Settings . Select Updates & Downloads . Choose Start Update . Batocera will download and apply the latest update, then reboot automatically. Note: Your games, save states, BIOS files, and scraped artwork are stored in a separate share partition on the card and are never affected by a system update. You can update with confidence. Key terms Emulator — a program that mimics an old games console in software, allowing games designed for that console to run on different hardware. ROM — a digital copy of a game cartridge or disc; the file the emulator loads and plays. EmulationStation — the graphical menu system that organises your game library by console and lets you launch games. RetroArch — the engine that runs underneath EmulationStation, managing the individual emulators (called "cores") and providing features like save states, shaders, and rewind. Core — in RetroArch, a single emulator plugin; for example, the SNES emulator is one core, the Game Boy emulator is another. Multiple cores can exist for the same console. Batocera — a dedicated, standalone gaming operating system for the Raspberry Pi that combines EmulationStation and RetroArch in a ready-to-use package. RetroPie — an alternative that adds emulation software on top of an existing Raspberry Pi OS installation, keeping both on the same card. Save state — an instant snapshot of a running game that can be saved and restored at any point, allowing you to resume from exactly the frozen moment. Hotkey — a special button on your controller (usually Select) that, when held together with other buttons, triggers emulator shortcuts like saving, quitting, or opening the menu. Samba share — a network folder on the Pi that appears in Windows File Explorer, allowing you to copy files from your PC to the Pi over your home network. BIOS file — a small program originally built into a console's hardware chips, which certain emulators need in order to work correctly. Scraping — the process of automatically downloading cover art, descriptions, and game metadata from an online database to make your game library look polished. Homebrew — games created independently by hobbyists and often released free of charge; a legal and widely available source of ROM files. IP address — a unique numerical address (like 192.168.1.50) that identifies your Pi on the home network, used when Windows cannot find the Pi by name. Chapter summary Your Pi 5 can emulate dozens of classic game systems — from the Atari 2600 right through to the PlayStation 2 — with excellent performance thanks to its powerful quad-core processor. Batocera is the recommended beginner choice: flash it to a spare microSD card with Raspberry Pi Imager, insert the card, and boot into a ready-made games console. Keep your two cards clearly labelled and swap them in the Pi's microSD slot to switch between Raspberry Pi OS and Batocera — the two systems are entirely independent. ROMs are subject to copyright; you may only legally use files for games you personally own, or games released as freeware or homebrew. Some consoles (PlayStation 1, Saturn, Dreamcast, GBA) require BIOS files to work; place them in the \\BATOCERA\share\bios network folder. Copy games to Batocera via the Samba network share at \\BATOCERA\share\roms from Windows, or by importing from a USB drive. Connect a USB or Bluetooth controller and map your buttons on first boot; most modern USB gamepads and Xbox/PlayStation controllers are detected automatically. Save states (Hotkey + R1 to save, Hotkey + L1 to load) let you snapshot your progress at any moment; Hotkey + Start quits back to the EmulationStation menu. The Pi 5 has no headphone socket; game audio comes through HDMI or via a USB audio adapter or Bluetooth headphones. The scraper feature downloads cover art and descriptions automatically, turning a list of filenames into a visual games library. RetroPie is an advanced alternative that sits on top of Raspberry Pi OS on the same card, but requires more setup time and technical patience.

title: Block Ads with Pi-hole
headings: How the internet "looks up" websites — and how Pi-hole exploits that
Before you start: what you need
Step 1 — Give your Pi a fixed IP address
Step 3 — Complete the initial setup in the web dashboard
Step 4 — Point your router's DNS at Pi-hole
Step 5 — Confirm that it is working
Resetting or changing the admin password
Allowing a domain when something breaks
Honest limits: what Pi-hole cannot block
Useful Pi-hole commands at a glance
text: Adverts and tracking scripts slow down web pages, clutter your screen, and quietly follow you around the internet. In this chapter you will turn your Raspberry Pi into a network-wide ad blocker called Pi-hole — a free, open-source tool that protects every phone, tablet, laptop, and smart TV in your home without installing anything on those devices. How the internet "looks up" websites — and how Pi-hole exploits that Before you install anything, it helps to understand the clever trick that makes Pi-hole work. DNS: the internet's phone book In plain words: DNS stands for Domain Name System. When you type www.bbc.co.uk into your browser, your computer does not actually know where that is. It first asks a special server — called a DNS resolver — to translate the human-readable name into a numerical address (like 151.101.0.81 ). That numerical address is an IP address — the internet's equivalent of a postal code for a computer. Only once your device has that number can it actually connect to the site. Every time you load a web page, dozens of these look-ups happen in the blink of an eye — one for the main site, and more for every advert, tracking pixel, and analytics script the page tries to load. Your home router normally forwards all of these look-up requests out to a DNS server run by your internet provider (or Google, or Cloudflare). What Pi-hole does differently Pi-hole installs itself as your home network's DNS server. Instead of forwarding every request straight to the internet, it first checks each domain name against a list of known advertising and tracking domains. If the name is on the list, Pi-hole returns a harmless "not found" answer — so the advert or tracker simply never loads. If the name is legitimate (like bbc.co.uk ), Pi-hole forwards the request normally and your browser gets the page. The beauty of this approach is that nothing needs to be installed on your phone, tablet, or smart TV . As long as those devices use your Pi as their DNS server, they are automatically protected. Pi-hole also keeps detailed logs, so you can see exactly what domains are being blocked — or which device in your home is the chattiest tracker-loader. Pi-hole network flow diagram Diagram showing home devices (phone, laptop, TV) sending DNS queries to the Pi-hole. Pi-hole blocks ad domains and forwards legitimate requests to the internet (upstream DNS). Your home network Phone DNS query Laptop DNS query Smart TV DNS query Pi-hole (Raspberry Pi 5) Checks blocklist forwards safe queries legitimate domains only BLOCKED ad/tracker domains Upstream DNS Internet sites Every device on your network sends DNS look-up requests to the Pi-hole. Pi-hole blocks known ad and tracker domains outright (shown in red) and only forwards legitimate requests to the real internet (shown in teal). Before you start: what you need Your Raspberry Pi 5, already set up with Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm and connected to your home network (wired Ethernet is strongly recommended — a Pi running a network service works best with a cable, not Wi-Fi). Your Pi's current IP address. You can find this by opening a terminal and typing hostname -I — write it down, you will need it throughout this chapter. Access to your router's settings page (usually by opening a browser and visiting 192.168.0.1 or 192.168.1.1 ). If you do not know your router's address, look for it printed on the back of the router. Your router's admin username and password (also usually on a sticker on the router). Tip: Running Pi-hole over a wired Ethernet connection is much more reliable than over Wi-Fi. If your router is in a different room, a powerline adapter (a pair of plugs that send network data through your house's mains wiring) is a cheap way to get a wired connection without running a cable across the floor. Note — Pi-hole version: This chapter covers Pi-hole version 6 , which became the default install from 2025 onwards and is the version you will get when following the instructions below on Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm. Pi-hole v6 has a modernised command-line interface and a refreshed web dashboard. If you find older guides online that use commands beginning with pihole -a , pihole -g , or pihole -up , those are Pi-hole v5 commands and will not work on a fresh install today. Step 1 — Give your Pi a fixed IP address Pi-hole is going to act as your network's DNS server. Every device in your home will be told to send its DNS requests to a specific IP address — the address of your Pi. If that address ever changes (which it can, because home routers normally hand out addresses at random), all those devices would suddenly lose the ability to look up websites. So the first job is to make sure your Pi always gets the same IP address. There are two common ways to do this: Option A — Reserve the address in your router (recommended) Most home routers let you look at the list of connected devices and "reserve" (or "pin") an address to a specific device's network identity (called its MAC address — a unique identifier permanently built into every network adapter). Once reserved, the router always gives that device the same address. This is called a DHCP reservation or a static lease . In plain words: DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) is the system your router uses to automatically give IP addresses to devices that join the network. By default it hands them out however it likes, but you can tell it "always give this device this address". That is a DHCP reservation. The exact steps depend on your router's brand, but in general: Log in to your router's admin page in a browser (for example http://192.168.1.1 ). Look for a section called "Connected Devices", "LAN", "DHCP", or "IP & MAC Binding". Find your Raspberry Pi in the list (it may be labelled "raspberrypi" or show its current IP). Click the option to reserve or pin that IP address to the Pi's MAC address. Save the settings. Your Pi will keep that address from now on. Note: If your router does not have this feature (some very basic models do not), you can set a static IP directly on the Pi itself using the Raspberry Pi OS network settings. Right-click the network icon in the top-right corner of the desktop, choose "Wireless & Wired Network Settings", select your connection, and fill in a fixed IP address, the router's address as the gateway, and a DNS server (use 8.8.8.8 temporarily — you can update this later once Pi-hole is running). Check your router's documentation or look at the addresses your router is currently handing out to choose an address that will not clash with other devices. Option B — Set a static IP on the Pi using the terminal (alternative) If you prefer to configure the static IP from the Pi's terminal rather than the router interface, open a terminal and use the NetworkManager command-line tool. Type each of the following commands one at a time, pressing Enter after each. nmcli con show Lists all network connections that NetworkManager knows about on your Pi. Look for the name of your wired connection (typically something like Wired connection 1 ) — you will use that exact name in the next command. Note: The long command below is split across several lines using the \ backslash character at the end of each line. This just means "the command continues on the next line" — it is one single command. Type it exactly as shown, including the backslashes, or paste it all in one go. sudo nmcli con mod "Wired connection 1" \ ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.100/24 \ ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1 \ ipv4.dns 8.8.8.8 \ ipv4.method manual sudo — runs the command with administrator (superuser) privileges, which are needed to change network settings. nmcli con mod "Wired connection 1" — tells NetworkManager to modify the named connection. Replace the name in quotes with whatever your connection is actually called (as shown by the previous nmcli con show command). ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.100/24 — sets the fixed IP address you want. Replace 192.168.1.100 with an address that is on your network but not already in use. The /24 is the network mask — it means this is a typical home network where the first three numbers are shared and the last can range from 1 to 254. ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1 — tells the Pi the address of your router (the gateway to the wider internet). Adjust this to match your actual router address. ipv4.dns 8.8.8.8 — sets a temporary DNS server (Google's public DNS) so the Pi can look up websites during the Pi-hole installation. You will point this at Pi-hole itself later. ipv4.method manual — switches this connection from "automatic" (DHCP) to "manual" (static), meaning it will use the values you just provided instead of asking the router for an address. sudo nmcli con up "Wired connection 1" Activates the updated connection settings so the change takes effect immediately, without needing to reboot the Pi. Replace the name in quotes with the actual name of your connection if it is different. Careful: If you change the Pi's IP address while connected remotely over SSH, your SSH session will disconnect because the Pi is now at a different address. You will need to reconnect using the new IP address. If you are working directly at the Pi with a keyboard and screen attached, this is not a problem. Step 2 — Install Pi-hole Pi-hole has an official automated installer. It is a shell script — a file containing a sequence of commands — that is downloaded from the internet and run on your Pi. The installer handles everything: it installs all the required software, sets up Pi-hole as a background service, and prepares the web dashboard. In plain words: A shell script is simply a text file full of commands, just like the ones you type in a terminal. Instead of typing them one by one, you run the whole file at once. The Pi-hole installer is a very long shell script maintained by the Pi-hole team. Note — should you trust piping a script to bash? The install command below uses a pattern called "piping to bash": it downloads a script and immediately runs it. You should only ever do this for software from a project you trust, from its official website, and over a secure https:// connection. Pi-hole is a well-known, open-source project maintained by a large community; its installer is publicly readable on GitHub; and the download uses HTTPS. If you are uneasy, you can download the script first with curl -O https://install.pi-hole.net/install.sh , inspect it with nano install.sh , and then run it manually with bash install.sh . For most beginners, running the one-liner from the official documentation is perfectly reasonable. Open a terminal on your Raspberry Pi (or SSH into it from your Windows machine — see Chapter 10 if you need a reminder of how to do this). Make sure your Pi's software is up to date before installing: sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y sudo apt update — refreshes the list of available software packages from the internet. && — means "only run the next command if the previous one succeeded". sudo apt full-upgrade -y — installs all available updates. The -y flag answers "yes" automatically to any prompts, so you do not have to watch it. Run the Pi-hole installer: curl -sSL https://install.pi-hole.net | sudo bash curl — a command-line tool for downloading files from the internet. -sSL — three options combined: -s runs silently (hides the progress bar), -S still shows errors if something goes wrong, -L follows any web redirects automatically. https://install.pi-hole.net — the official Pi-hole installer URL, served securely over HTTPS. | — the "pipe" symbol; it takes the output of the command on the left (the downloaded script text) and passes it directly as input to the command on the right. sudo bash — runs the received script as an administrator using the bash shell. Administrator access is necessary because the installer needs to change system settings, install packages, and configure background services. The installer will print progress messages as it works — downloading components, configuring the DNS service, and setting up the web interface. This usually takes two to five minutes depending on your internet speed. You do not need to interact with it during this time. Note: Pi-hole version 6 (the current version) runs its installer entirely in the background without interrupting you with dialogue boxes. When it is finished, it will print a short summary including your Pi's IP address and a temporary admin password. Copy or write down that password immediately — you will need it to log in to the dashboard for the first time. When the installer finishes, it prints something like this (with your actual IP address and a different password): [✓] Installation complete! Pi-hole Web Interface: http://192.168.1.100/admin Admin password: AbCd1234XyZ This is a summary message printed by the installer — not a command you type. It tells you the address of your Pi-hole dashboard and the randomly generated password for the admin account. Write both down now. Tip: If you miss the password or scroll past it, do not worry — you can reset it at any time using pihole setpassword in the terminal, which is covered later in this chapter. Step 3 — Complete the initial setup in the web dashboard Pi-hole v6 completes its configuration through its own web interface rather than during the installer. Open a browser on any device on your home network and go to: http://192.168.1.100/admin Replace 192.168.1.100 with the actual IP address of your Pi — the one you noted down or fixed in Step 1. This opens Pi-hole's administration dashboard in your browser. Log in with the temporary password shown by the installer. Once logged in, the dashboard will walk you through a short setup wizard. Here is what each step asks and what to choose: Setup step What it is asking What to choose Network interface Which network connection should Pi-hole listen on? Choose eth0 for wired Ethernet (recommended). If you are using Wi-Fi only, choose wlan0 . Upstream DNS provider When a domain is not blocked, which DNS server should Pi-hole forward requests to? Choose Cloudflare ( 1.1.1.1 — fast and privacy-respecting) or Google ( 8.8.8.8 ). Either works well; you can change this later in Settings. Blocklists Which default list of ad/tracker domains should Pi-hole use? Leave the default list enabled (StevenBlack's unified list) — it is a well-maintained, comprehensive starting point blocking around 150,000 known ad and tracker domains. Query logging Should Pi-hole keep a log of every DNS look-up? Leave this on — it is very useful for spotting what is being blocked and why, and for troubleshooting when a site stops working. Privacy mode How much detail should the log show about individual clients? Choose Show everything — since this is your own home network, full detail is helpful for troubleshooting. After the wizard, you may also want to change the admin password to something more memorable. Go to Settings → Web Interface (or use the terminal command described later in this chapter). Step 4 — Point your router's DNS at Pi-hole Pi-hole is now installed and running on your Pi, but your other devices do not know it exists yet. You need to tell your router to use the Pi as its DNS server. Once you do that, the router will pass on the Pi's address to every device on the network, so they all automatically use Pi-hole. In plain words: Your router acts like a post room for your home network. When a device joins, the router tells it several things: "Here is your address, here is where the gateway to the internet is, and here is the phone-book server (DNS) you should use." By changing that last item to your Pi's address, all devices automatically use Pi-hole as their phone book — without you needing to do anything on each device individually. Log in to your router's admin page (for example http://192.168.1.1 ) using your router's admin username and password. Find the DHCP settings. These are often under a section called "LAN", "DHCP Server", "Network Settings", or "Advanced". Find the field labelled "Primary DNS" (sometimes called "DNS Server 1"). Change that field to your Pi's fixed IP address (for example 192.168.1.100 ). For the "Secondary DNS" (or "DNS Server 2") field, consider leaving it blank. If you enter a secondary DNS server (such as 8.8.8.8 ), some devices may bypass Pi-hole and use the secondary server directly — especially if your Pi is slow to respond. Leaving it blank means every DNS request goes through Pi-hole, though it also means that if your Pi is powered off, internet browsing will stop working for all devices until the Pi comes back on. Save and apply the settings. Some routers need a restart. Wait a minute, then test that the internet still works on another device (your phone, for example). Note: Changes to DHCP settings only take effect on a device after it renews its "lease" — essentially, after it asks the router for its settings again. This usually happens automatically within a day, but you can speed it up immediately: on Windows, open a Command Prompt and type ipconfig /release followed by ipconfig /renew . On a phone, turn Wi-Fi off and back on, or forget the network and reconnect. Alternative: set DNS per device instead If you do not have access to your router (for example if it belongs to a landlord or a shared household), you can instead set the DNS server individually on each device you want to protect. On Windows 11, go to Settings → Network & Internet → Wi-Fi → [Your network] → Properties and set DNS to "Manual" with your Pi's IP. On iPhone/iPad, tap the (i) next to your Wi-Fi network, then tap "Configure DNS" and switch to "Manual". On Android, go to Wi-Fi settings, long-press your network, and look for "Advanced options" where you can set a Static IP and DNS. Step 5 — Confirm that it is working On any device on your home network, open a browser and go to http://192.168.1.100/admin (using your Pi's IP address). The Pi-hole admin dashboard should appear. Log in with the admin password. Browse to a few websites on your phone or laptop. Return to the Pi-hole dashboard and watch the query counter go up and the live graph begin to show activity — this confirms those devices are now routing their DNS look-ups through Pi-hole. If nothing appears in the dashboard, the device has not yet received the new DNS setting from the router. Try turning Wi-Fi off and on, or use the ipconfig /release / ipconfig /renew trick on Windows. Tip: On the Pi-hole dashboard home page you will see a figure like "23% of queries blocked" after a few minutes of browsing. Most homes settle somewhere between 15% and 40%, depending on which sites and apps are in use. The higher the percentage, the more ads and trackers were silently trying to reach your devices. Using the admin dashboard The Pi-hole admin dashboard at http://<your-pi-ip>/admin is your control centre. Here is a quick tour of the main sections: Dashboard section What it shows / lets you do Summary (home page) Total queries today, percentage blocked, number of domains on the blocklist, and a live traffic graph. Query Log A real-time list of every DNS look-up made by every device. Green = allowed, red = blocked. Click any entry to add that domain to your allowlist or denylist instantly. Top Blocked Domains The ad/tracker domains being blocked most often — often reveals hundreds of hidden trackers you never knew about. Allowlist / Denylist Manually add domains you want to always allow (allowlist, formerly "whitelist") or always block (denylist, formerly "blacklist"), beyond the automatic blocklists. Group Management Create groups of devices and apply different blocklists to each group — for example, a stricter content-filtering list for a child's tablet. Lists Add additional blocklists (many are maintained by the community) and update or disable existing ones. Settings Change the upstream DNS provider, manage Pi-hole's own IP, configure logging, change the admin password, and more. Resetting or changing the admin password If you lose the password or just want to set something more memorable, open a terminal on the Pi and run: pihole setpassword pihole — the Pi-hole command-line management tool, installed automatically as part of the Pi-hole setup. setpassword — prompts you to type a new password for the web admin interface (you will be asked to type it twice to confirm). If you just press Enter twice without typing anything, Pi-hole removes the password requirement entirely — useful on a private home network where you are not concerned about other household members accessing the dashboard. Note: You can also change the password through the dashboard itself: go to Settings → Web Interface and look for the password change option. Allowing a domain when something breaks Occasionally Pi-hole will block a domain that a website or app genuinely needs, and things will stop working in an unexpected way. Symptoms include: a website that loads with missing images or buttons, a video service that will not start, or an app that cannot connect to its servers. When this happens, Pi-hole is the first thing to check. How to diagnose and fix a blocked domain Open the Pi-hole dashboard and click Query Log . Try using the broken website or app again, then immediately look at the query log. Filter by your device's IP address if needed. Look for red (blocked) entries that appeared at the same moment as the problem. The domain name shown is the one being blocked. To allow that domain, click the green circle-with-plus icon next to it in the query log, or go to Allowlist , type the domain, and click "Add to Allowlist". Refresh the page or restart the app that was broken — it should now work normally. You can also add a domain to the allowlist from the command line: pihole allow example.com pihole — the Pi-hole management tool. allow — adds the specified domain to the allowlist (the list of domains that will always be permitted through, regardless of any blocklist). example.com — replace this with the actual domain name you want to permit, for example cdn.somesite.com . To permanently block a specific domain that is not on any blocklist (for example, a distracting social media site): pihole deny example.com pihole — the Pi-hole management tool. deny — adds the specified domain to the denylist, which means Pi-hole will always block it, even if it does not appear on any of the subscribed blocklists. example.com — replace this with the domain you want to block, for example www.tiktok.com . Tip: If you suspect Pi-hole is causing a problem but are not sure, you can temporarily pause it from the dashboard by clicking Disable on the home page (options include 10 seconds, 30 seconds, 5 minutes, or indefinitely). If things start working with Pi-hole disabled, Pi-hole is responsible — use the query log to find out which domain to add to the allowlist. Keeping Pi-hole up to date The list of ad and tracker domains that Pi-hole blocks is constantly being updated by the community, and Pi-hole itself receives software improvements. Updating is a single command: pihole update pihole — the Pi-hole management tool. update — checks for a newer version of Pi-hole itself and installs it if available. It will print progress messages as it works and usually finishes within a minute or two. To refresh your blocklists (making Pi-hole download the latest versions of all the ad-domain lists you have subscribed to): pihole gravity pihole — the Pi-hole management tool. gravity — runs Pi-hole's "gravity" process: it downloads the latest version of every blocklist you have subscribed to, combines them, removes duplicate entries, and builds an efficient lookup database. Pi-hole calls this process "gravity" because it pulls in all your lists and compresses them into one. Pi-hole runs this automatically on a weekly schedule, but you can run it manually at any time — for example after adding a new blocklist. Tip: Pi-hole automatically updates its blocklists on a schedule, so you do not need to run pihole gravity every day. Running pihole update once a month is plenty to keep the core software current. Adding more blocklists The default blocklist (StevenBlack's unified list) is a solid starting point. But the community maintains many more lists you can add for broader or more specific protection: OISD Big list — a very comprehensive, actively maintained list. URL: https://big.oisd.nl HAGEZI DNS Blocklists — multiple tiers from light to ultra-aggressive. Find them at https://github.com/hagezi/dns-blocklists Malware and phishing domain lists — many lists exist that block known malicious sites, adding a useful security layer on top of ad blocking. To add a list, go to Lists in the Pi-hole dashboard, paste the URL into the "Address" field, and click "Add". Then run the gravity update to download the new list and incorporate it into the blocklist: pihole gravity Same as above — downloads and merges all your subscribed blocklists into the active blocking database. Any new list you just added in the dashboard will be included. Careful: Adding very large or very aggressive blocklists can accidentally block websites or services you legitimately use. Start with one or two extra lists and monitor the query log for unexpected breakage before adding more. Honest limits: what Pi-hole cannot block Pi-hole is genuinely impressive, but it is important to understand what it cannot do, so you are not disappointed: YouTube adverts: YouTube (and the YouTube app on phones and TVs) serves its adverts from the same domain as the actual videos. Pi-hole cannot block those adverts without also blocking the videos themselves. For YouTube ad-blocking you need a browser extension like uBlock Origin (in a desktop browser) or a modified app on mobile devices. Adverts embedded in apps: Some apps serve adverts from their own servers on the same domain as their content, making it impossible for Pi-hole to tell an advert from legitimate app data. Encrypted DNS (DNS over HTTPS / DoH): Newer devices and apps can sometimes use DNS over HTTPS, which routes DNS requests through an encrypted channel that bypasses Pi-hole entirely. You can configure your router to block DoH if this becomes a concern, though it requires additional steps beyond this chapter. It is not a VPN or firewall: Pi-hole only operates on DNS look-ups. It does not encrypt your internet traffic, hide your IP address, or block non-DNS connections to tracking servers. Brand-new advertising domains: Domains that have not yet been added to any blocklist will slip through until the community adds them and you run a gravity update. Note: Despite these limits, most users find that Pi-hole blocks 20–30% of all network requests in their home. Pages load noticeably faster, many types of cross-site tracking are stopped entirely, and some smart-TV channels that previously interrupted viewing with adverts become much cleaner. It is not a silver bullet, but it is one of the most effective and easy-to-maintain privacy tools available. Useful Pi-hole commands at a glance All of these commands are typed in a terminal on the Raspberry Pi itself. Command What it does pihole status Shows whether Pi-hole is running and actively blocking, or has been paused. pihole enable Re-enables blocking if you previously disabled or paused it. pihole disable Disables blocking indefinitely (DNS requests are still answered, but nothing is blocked). Use pihole enable to turn blocking back on. pihole disable 5m Disables blocking for 5 minutes, then automatically re-enables. Replace 5m with 30s for 30 seconds or 1h for one hour. pihole setpassword Set or reset the admin dashboard password. pihole allow domain.com Add a domain to the allowlist (always let it through, even if it is on a blocklist). pihole deny domain.com Add a domain to the denylist (always block it, even if it is not on any blocklist). pihole update Update the Pi-hole software itself to the latest version. pihole gravity Download and apply the latest versions of all subscribed blocklists. pihole tail Show a live stream of DNS queries in the terminal as they happen (press Ctrl+C to stop). pihole restartdns Restart the Pi-hole DNS service — useful if you have changed settings and want them to take effect immediately. Troubleshooting common problems The internet stopped working after setting up Pi-hole First, check that the Pi is powered on and connected to the network. Open a terminal on the Pi and run pihole status — if Pi-hole itself is not running, restart it with pihole restartdns or reboot the Pi with sudo reboot . If the Pi is powered off, any device that has no secondary DNS server configured will lose the ability to browse the internet until the Pi comes back. As a short-term fix, you can temporarily put your router's original DNS address back in the router's DHCP settings while you investigate. Devices are still not using Pi-hole Force a DHCP renewal: on the affected device, disconnect from Wi-Fi and reconnect. On Windows, run the following two commands in a Command Prompt (not a terminal on the Pi — this is done on the Windows machine): ipconfig /release ipconfig /renew These are Windows commands, not Pi commands — type them into a Command Prompt on your Windows PC. ipconfig /release — tells Windows to give up its current IP address and network settings (including the DNS server address). ipconfig /renew — asks the router to issue fresh network settings, which should now include your Pi's IP address as the DNS server. After renewing, open the Pi-hole query log in your browser — if queries from that device now appear there, it is correctly using Pi-hole. A specific website is partially broken Open the Pi-hole query log and search for your device's IP address in the client column. Look for red blocked entries that appeared at the same moment you loaded the broken page. Whitelist — or in Pi-hole v6, allow — the blocked domain and reload the page. Many news and media sites rely on sub-domains (for example cdn.example.com ) that can end up on blocklists even though they serve legitimate content rather than adverts. I forgot the Pi-hole admin password Open a terminal on the Pi and run pihole setpassword to set a new one. Pi-hole says it is running but blocking percentage stays at 0% This usually means your devices are not yet using Pi-hole as their DNS server. Check the router's DHCP settings again to make sure the Pi's IP address is set as the Primary DNS, and force a DHCP renewal on your devices as described above. Key terms DNS (Domain Name System) — the internet's phone book; it translates human-readable domain names (like bbc.co.uk ) into numerical IP addresses that computers use to find each other on the internet. IP address — a numerical label (such as 192.168.1.100 ) that uniquely identifies a device on a network, like a postal address for a computer. Pi-hole — free, open-source software that acts as a DNS server for your home network, automatically blocking known advertising and tracking domains before they can load on any device. Blocklist — a list of domain names that Pi-hole refuses to answer look-up requests for, causing ads and trackers that use those domains to simply never load. Allowlist (formerly whitelist) — a list of domains that Pi-hole always allows through, even if they appear on a blocklist; used to restore access to sites accidentally broken by over-enthusiastic blocking. Denylist (formerly blacklist) — a list of domains you manually tell Pi-hole to always block, even if they do not appear on any subscribed blocklist. DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) — the system your router uses to automatically assign IP addresses and settings (including the DNS server address) to devices that connect to your network. DHCP reservation (static lease) — a router setting that always gives a specific device the same IP address, identified by the device's unique MAC address. MAC address — a permanent, unique identifier built into every network adapter (Wi-Fi card or Ethernet socket), used by the router to recognise individual devices. Upstream DNS — the external DNS server that Pi-hole forwards legitimate (non-blocked) queries on to; common choices are Cloudflare ( 1.1.1.1 ) or Google ( 8.8.8.8 ). Gravity — Pi-hole's term for the process of downloading and combining all subscribed blocklists into a single, efficient local lookup database. DNS over HTTPS (DoH) — a modern protocol that encrypts DNS requests so they are invisible to intermediate servers including Pi-hole; some devices and browsers use it automatically, potentially bypassing Pi-hole. Shell script — a text file containing a sequence of terminal commands that can be run all at once; the Pi-hole installer is a shell script. Chapter summary Pi-hole works by placing itself between your home devices and the internet as a DNS server, silently blocking look-ups for known advertising and tracking domains before they even reach the internet. Every device on your network benefits automatically once you point your router's DNS setting at the Pi's IP address — nothing needs to be installed on phones, tablets, or smart TVs. Giving the Pi a fixed (static) IP address — either via a DHCP reservation in the router or by setting a static IP on the Pi itself using nmcli — is essential before installing Pi-hole. The official installer is launched with a single curl -sSL https://install.pi-hole.net | sudo bash command; note the randomly generated admin password it displays when it finishes. Pi-hole v6 (the current version on Bookworm) uses a web-based setup wizard at http://<pi-ip>/admin and a modernised command line: pihole allow , pihole deny , pihole update , pihole gravity , and pihole setpassword . The admin dashboard provides real-time graphs, a query log showing every DNS look-up, and tools for managing allowlists, denylists, and additional blocklists. Pi-hole cannot block YouTube in-app adverts or ads served from the same domain as legitimate content, but it typically blocks 20–30% of all home network requests, noticeably speeding up page loads. When a site breaks, check the Query Log for red entries at the time of the breakage and use pihole allow domain.com to restore access to that domain.

title: Your Own Home Server & Private Cloud
headings: Part A — A Home File Server with Samba
Part B — Your Own Private Cloud with Nextcloud
text: Your Raspberry Pi 5 is on all day and all night, quietly sipping just a few watts of electricity — so why not put it to work as a proper home server? In this chapter you will turn your Pi into a network file share that every Windows PC in your home can see, and then go a step further by installing your very own private cloud — your files, your photos, your calendar, all stored on hardware you own and control. Note: This chapter has two independent parts. You can follow Part A (Samba file sharing) without ever doing Part B (Nextcloud), or do both. Read through a whole section before typing anything. Part A — A Home File Server with Samba What is a file server, and why do you want one?
