Right now, if you want to move a photo from your Windows laptop to your Pi, you probably copy it to a USB stick and carry it across the room. A file server fixes that. Once it is running, a shared folder on the Pi appears inside Windows Explorer just like any other drive — you drag files in, you drag files out, across the home network, with no cable required. In plain words: A file server is a computer that holds files and lets other computers on the same network open, save, and copy those files as if they were on a local drive. "Server" just means "the one that serves the others". The software that makes this possible on Linux is called Samba . Samba speaks the same file-sharing language that Windows uses (called SMB, or "Server Message Block"), so your Windows PC and your Pi understand each other perfectly. In plain words: Samba is free, open-source software that lets a Linux computer speak Windows' own file-sharing language. It has been around since 1992 and is rock-solid. What you will need Your Pi 5, connected to the same home router as your Windows PC (by Ethernet cable or Wi-Fi — either works, but a cable is faster and more reliable for a file server). A USB hard drive or USB stick to use as the shared storage (optional but recommended — keeps the shared data off the microSD card and allows much larger capacity). A terminal window open on the Pi (or an SSH connection from Windows — see Chapter 12). Tip: Using a USB hard drive rather than the microSD card for shared storage is strongly recommended. microSD cards are not designed for constant read/write activity and can wear out faster. A cheap USB hard drive or a good-quality USB SSD will last far longer and hold far more. Step 1 — Attach and mount a USB drive Plug your USB drive into one of the Pi's blue USB 3.0 ports. Wait five seconds, then find out what name the Pi gave it: lsblk lsblk — "list block devices". It prints a tree of all storage devices the Pi can see. You are looking for your USB drive, which will appear as something like sda with a partition below it called sda1 . You should see output a bit like this: NAME MAJ:MIN RM SIZE RO TYPE MOUNTPOINT sda 8:0 1 119.2G 0 disk └─sda1 8:1 1 119.2G 0 part mmcblk0 179:0 0 59.6G 0 disk ├─mmcblk0p1 179:1 0 512M 0 part /boot/firmware └─mmcblk0p2 179:2 0 59.1G 0 part / sda — your USB drive (the whole physical device). sda1 — the first partition on the USB drive. This is the part that actually holds files. mmcblk0 — your microSD card. Leave this alone. The MOUNTPOINT column shows where (if anywhere) the drive is currently accessible. sda1 may already be mounted automatically by Raspberry Pi OS. Note: If your USB drive already has a MOUNTPOINT shown (such as /media/pi/MY-DRIVE ), Raspberry Pi OS has already mounted it for you and you can skip the manual mount step below. Note the exact path shown — you will need it when configuring Samba. If the MOUNTPOINT column for sda1 is blank, create a folder to attach it to and mount it manually: sudo mkdir -p /mnt/usbdrive sudo mount /dev/sda1 /mnt/usbdrive sudo mkdir -p /mnt/usbdrive — creates a new empty folder at /mnt/usbdrive . The -p flag means "create any missing parent folders too; do not error if it already exists". sudo is needed because /mnt is a system folder. sudo mount /dev/sda1 /mnt/usbdrive — "attaches" the USB partition to that folder. After this, any file you put into /mnt/usbdrive is actually written to the USB drive. Now create the folder that you will actually share over the network, and give it the right permissions: sudo mkdir -p /mnt/usbdrive/shared sudo chown -R $USER:$USER /mnt/usbdrive/shared sudo chmod 775 /mnt/usbdrive/shared sudo mkdir -p /mnt/usbdrive/shared — creates a folder called shared inside the USB drive. sudo chown -R $USER:$USER /mnt/usbdrive/shared — makes your Pi user account the owner of the folder. $USER is a variable that automatically fills in your current username (e.g., pi ), so you do not need to type it manually. sudo chmod 775 /mnt/usbdrive/shared — sets the folder's permissions so that the owner and group can read and write files, and others can read. This is the right balance for a home file server. Careful: Some guides suggest chmod 777 for shared folders. This gives every account on the Pi (including any that might be compromised) full read/write access. Using chmod 775 combined with correct Samba user settings (which we set up next) is more secure and is the right approach for a home server. Step 2 — Install Samba sudo apt update sudo apt install samba -y sudo apt update — refreshes the Pi's list of available software from the internet. Always do this before installing something new. sudo apt install samba -y — downloads and installs Samba. The -y flag automatically answers "yes" to the "do you want to continue?" question, so you do not have to type it. Confirm it installed correctly: samba --version Prints the Samba version number. If you see something like Version 4.17.x or higher, the install succeeded. On Bookworm the version will be 4.17 or newer. Step 3 — Configure the shared folder Samba's configuration lives in a single text file: /etc/samba/smb.conf . You are going to add a section at the very bottom of that file describing your share. First, take a backup of the original file so you can always restore it: sudo cp /etc/samba/smb.conf /etc/samba/smb.conf.bak Copies the original configuration file to a backup file called smb.conf.bak . If anything goes wrong, you can restore the original with sudo cp /etc/samba/smb.conf.bak /etc/samba/smb.conf . Now open the file in the Nano text editor: sudo nano /etc/samba/smb.conf Opens the Samba configuration file in Nano, a simple terminal text editor. sudo is required because this is a system file that only the administrator may change. Use the arrow keys to scroll all the way to the very bottom of the file. Then type the following block exactly as shown (spacing does not matter much, but the square brackets, equals signs, and exact keywords do): [PiShare] comment = Raspberry Pi Shared Folder path = /mnt/usbdrive/shared browseable = yes writable = yes guest ok = no valid users = %S force user = pi create mask = 0664 directory mask = 0775 [PiShare] — the name of the share. This is what Windows shows (for example, \\raspberrypi\PiShare ). You can name it anything you like, but do not use spaces. comment — a friendly description that Windows shows when browsing the network. path — the actual folder on the Pi that this share points to. browseable = yes — the share shows up automatically when Windows browses the network. writable = yes — connected users can save and delete files, not just read them. guest ok = no — anonymous access is not allowed; a password is required. valid users = %S — only the user who authenticated to this share may connect ( %S is a Samba variable meaning "the current share name's user"). You can also write valid users = pi if you prefer to be explicit. force user = pi — any file written through the share is owned by the pi account on the Pi. Replace pi with your actual username if it is different. create mask = 0664 — new files created through the share get sensible read/write permissions. directory mask = 0775 — new folders created through the share also get sensible permissions. Save and close: press Ctrl + O , then Enter to confirm the filename, then Ctrl + X to exit Nano. Note: If your Pi username is not pi , check it by typing whoami in a terminal. Replace pi in the force user line with whatever your username is. Check that your edited file has no typos: testparm testparm — a built-in Samba tool that reads your smb.conf and reports any errors. If it ends with "Loaded services file OK", your configuration is valid. If you see errors, open the file again with sudo nano /etc/samba/smb.conf and check your typing carefully. Step 4 — Set a Samba password Samba keeps its own password list separately from your Linux login password. You need to add your Pi user to that list: sudo smbpasswd -a pi sudo smbpasswd -a pi — adds the user pi to Samba's password database. The -a flag means "add". You will be prompted to type a new password twice. Choose something you will remember — you will need to enter it on Windows when connecting. Replace pi with your actual username if it is different. Tip: Your Samba password does not have to be the same as your Linux login password. Many people keep them the same for simplicity, but they are stored in two separate places by Samba. Step 5 — Restart Samba sudo systemctl restart smbd sudo systemctl enable smbd sudo systemctl restart smbd — stops and starts the Samba service ( smbd stands for "Samba Daemon") so it picks up your new configuration. sudo systemctl enable smbd — tells the Pi to start Samba automatically every time it boots, so you do not need to restart it manually after a reboot. Check it is running: sudo systemctl status smbd Shows whether the Samba service is active. You want to see active (running) highlighted in green. Press q to exit the status view and return to the command prompt. Step 6 — Find your Pi's name or IP address You will need either the Pi's hostname or its IP address to connect from Windows. Run: hostname hostname -I hostname — prints your Pi's network name. By default this is raspberrypi . hostname -I — prints the Pi's IP address on your home network, for example 192.168.1.42 . The first address shown is the one you want. Write it down — you will use it in the next step. Step 7 — Connect from Windows On your Windows PC, open File Explorer (the folder icon in the taskbar, or press Win + E ). Click in the address bar at the top and type one of the following, then press Enter: \\raspberrypi\PiShare — using the hostname (works if your router supports name resolution) \\192.168.1.42\PiShare — using the IP address (always works; replace with your actual IP) Windows will ask for a username and password. Enter pi (or your actual Pi username) and the Samba password you set in Step 4. Tick "Remember my credentials" so you do not need to log in every time. The shared folder opens. You can drag and drop files into it, create folders, and save documents directly from Word or any other Windows application — just as if it were a local drive. Tip: To make the share appear as a permanent drive letter (like Z: ) in Windows, right-click on the share in File Explorer after connecting, choose Map network drive , pick a letter, and tick Reconnect at sign-in . From that moment on, your Pi share appears as a lettered drive every time you start Windows. Windows PC File Explorer Router --> SMB Router Home network Pi --> Wi-Fi / cable Raspberry Pi 5 Samba running \\raspberrypi\PiShare USB drive /mnt/usbdrive/shared Samba lets Windows see the Pi's shared folder as if it were a network drive A home Samba file server: the Windows PC and the Pi communicate over your existing home router. No extra hardware needed. Making the USB drive mount automatically on boot At the moment, if the Pi restarts the USB drive may not mount automatically, and Samba will not be able to find the shared folder. Fix this by adding the drive to the Pi's startup mount list. First, find the drive's unique identifier (called a UUID): sudo blkid /dev/sda1 sudo blkid /dev/sda1 — prints details about the partition, including its UUID, which looks something like UUID="A1B2-C3D4" for a FAT32 drive or UUID="a1b2c3d4-e5f6-..." for a Linux-formatted drive. Copy this string carefully — you will need it in the next step. The output also shows the filesystem type (e.g., TYPE="vfat" , TYPE="ntfs" , TYPE="exfat" , TYPE="ext4" ). Note: Make a note of both the UUID and the TYPE shown by blkid . You will need both for the next step. Common types you might see: vfat = FAT32 (typical for drives formatted on Windows up to 32 GB), exfat = exFAT (Windows drives over 32 GB), ntfs = NTFS (Windows drives formatted for large files), ext4 = Linux format. If your drive is exFAT formatted, install the tools to support it (they are not installed by default on Bookworm): sudo apt install exfatprogs -y Installs the exfatprogs package, which gives the Pi the ability to read and write exFAT-formatted drives. Only needed if your drive is exFAT. Skip this step if your drive is FAT32, NTFS, or ext4. If your drive is NTFS formatted, install the NTFS support package: sudo apt install ntfs-3g -y Installs ntfs-3g , the open-source driver that lets Linux read and write NTFS drives (the format used by most Windows drives). Only needed for NTFS drives. Now open the file system table to add the drive to the boot-time mount list: sudo nano /etc/fstab /etc/fstab — the "file system table". This is the list of drives the Pi mounts automatically on startup. You are adding your USB drive to this list so it is always available when the Pi boots. Add a new line at the very bottom of the file. Use the correct TYPE you noted above. Examples for each format are shown — use only the one that matches your drive: # FAT32 drive (vfat): UUID=XXXX-XXXX /mnt/usbdrive vfat defaults,nofail,uid=1000,gid=1000 0 0 # exFAT drive: UUID=XXXX-XXXX /mnt/usbdrive exfat defaults,nofail,uid=1000,gid=1000 0 0 # NTFS drive: UUID=XXXXXXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXX /mnt/usbdrive ntfs-3g defaults,nofail,uid=1000,gid=1000 0 0 # Linux ext4 drive: UUID=XXXXXXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXX /mnt/usbdrive ext4 defaults,nofail 0 0 # FAT32 drive (vfat): — lines beginning with # are comments (ignored by the system). These are just labels to help you pick the right line. UUID=XXXX-XXXX — replace this with your actual UUID from the blkid output. This identifies the drive by its permanent ID rather than its device name (which can change). /mnt/usbdrive — the folder where the drive will be mounted (you created this earlier). vfat / exfat / ntfs-3g / ext4 — the filesystem type. Use the one that matches your drive. Note that NTFS uses ntfs-3g (not just ntfs ) so that the full-featured driver is used. defaults,nofail — use standard settings; nofail is critical — it means "if the drive is missing at boot, do not panic or halt — just continue booting normally". uid=1000,gid=1000 — makes the drive's files owned by the main user account (user ID 1000 is the first user created on Raspberry Pi OS, which is your account). This option applies to FAT32, exFAT, and NTFS — not ext4, which stores ownership in the filesystem itself. 0 0 — tells the Pi not to dump or automatically check this drive at startup. Add only the one line relevant to your drive type, replacing XXXX-XXXX with your actual UUID. Save with Ctrl + O , Enter, Ctrl + X . Then test the entry without rebooting: sudo mount -a sudo mount -a — attempts to mount everything listed in /etc/fstab that is not already mounted. If there is a typo in your fstab entry, this command will show an error immediately so you can fix it before rebooting. If it runs silently with no errors, your entry is correct. Careful: A typo in /etc/fstab can prevent the Pi from booting into a full desktop. Always run sudo mount -a immediately after editing to test for errors. If you do accidentally break the boot, remove the USB drive and reboot — with nofail set, the Pi should boot anyway without that drive and let you log in to fix the file. Part B — Your Own Private Cloud with Nextcloud What is Nextcloud and why would you want it? Samba is brilliant for accessing files on your home network, but it has one limitation: it only works when you are connected to that same network at home. Nextcloud is a full personal cloud platform — think of it as a self-hosted version of Dropbox or Google Drive. It gives you: A web browser interface to upload, download, and manage files from any device. Automatic photo backup from your phone (Android and iPhone both supported). A shared calendar and contacts that sync to your phone and PC. Notes, tasks, and dozens of optional add-on apps. Total privacy — your data lives on your hardware, not on anyone else's servers. In plain words: Nextcloud is free, open-source software that gives you all the features of Google Drive or Dropbox, but stores everything on your own Pi. Nobody else can access your files. Samba vs Nextcloud — which should you use? Feature Samba (Part A) Nextcloud (Part B) Access from home network Yes — fast and seamless Yes Access from outside home No (not without complex setup) Yes (with port forwarding — see Chapter 20) Phone app / auto photo backup No Yes (iOS and Android) Calendar and contacts sync No Yes Browser-based file manager No Yes Difficulty to set up Easy Medium (we use the easiest route) Resource usage Very light Moderate (perfectly fine on a Pi 5 with 16 GB RAM) Best for Simple local file sharing Full personal cloud, remote access, phone backup Note: You can run both Samba and Nextcloud at the same time on the same Pi. They do not conflict with each other. Many people use Samba for everyday local file access and Nextcloud for phone backups and browser-based access. The easiest installation route: Snap There are several ways to install Nextcloud. The simplest for beginners is a snap package — a self-contained bundle that installs Nextcloud and everything it needs (a web server, a database, background workers) in one single command, without you having to configure any of those pieces separately. In plain words: A snap is a type of software package that bundles an application together with all the extra software it depends on, so you do not have to install or configure those pieces yourself. Think of it as buying a ready-made meal rather than cooking from scratch. First, make sure the snap system is installed and up to date: sudo apt update sudo apt install snapd -y sudo apt update — refreshes the package list. sudo apt install snapd -y — installs the snap package manager. If it is already present, this does nothing harmful. Careful: After installing snapd for the first time, you must reboot before installing any snap package. Snap will not work correctly until the Pi has restarted. Run sudo reboot now and wait for the Pi to come back up before continuing. sudo reboot Restarts the Pi. Wait about 30 seconds for it to come back up, then open a new terminal or reconnect via SSH before continuing. This reboot is required for snapd to fully initialise itself. After the Pi has restarted, install Nextcloud: sudo snap install nextcloud Downloads and installs the Nextcloud snap package. This will take several minutes as it is a large download (several hundred megabytes). You will see a progress indicator. When it finishes you will see a message like nextcloud 28.x.x from Nextcloud✓ installed . Note: The snap version of Nextcloud is maintained by the Nextcloud team themselves and is regularly updated. It bundles the Apache web server, a MySQL-compatible database, and PHP — all the parts Nextcloud needs — so you do not have to install or configure any of them separately. Step 1 — Create your admin account The snap installs Nextcloud but waits for you to choose an administrator username and password before it starts. Run the following command, replacing the placeholders with your choices: sudo nextcloud.manual-install admin YourStrongPasswordHere sudo nextcloud.manual-install — runs the Nextcloud first-run installer that is included in the snap. admin — the administrator username you will use to log in. You can change this to anything you like (for example, your first name). YourStrongPasswordHere — your admin password. Choose something strong — at least 12 characters with a mix of upper and lower case letters, numbers, and symbols. This is what protects your entire cloud. Careful: Do not use the example password shown above. Choose your own strong password and write it down somewhere safe. If you lose the admin password, recovering access is a technical process and can result in losing access to your files. Step 2 — Allow your home network to access Nextcloud By default Nextcloud only accepts connections from the Pi itself (called "localhost"). You need to tell it to also accept connections coming from your home network, using the Pi's IP address. First, check your Pi's IP address if you have not done so already: hostname -I Prints the Pi's IP address on your local network. Note the first address shown — it will be something like 192.168.1.42 . Use your actual address in the commands below. Now add your Pi's IP address as a trusted domain for Nextcloud: sudo nextcloud.occ config:system:set trusted_domains 1 --value=192.168.1.42 sudo nextcloud.occ — the Nextcloud command-line management tool, included in the snap. occ stands for "ownCloud Console" — Nextcloud evolved from a project called ownCloud and kept the tool name. config:system:set trusted_domains 1 — adds a second trusted domain entry (slot 0 is already set to localhost ). Slot 1 is the first one you are adding. --value=192.168.1.42 — replace this with your Pi's actual IP address. This tells Nextcloud "it is safe to serve web pages to browsers that connect using this address". Also add your Pi's hostname so you can connect using either the name or the IP address: sudo nextcloud.occ config:system:set trusted_domains 2 --value=raspberrypi Adds raspberrypi (the Pi's default hostname) as a third trusted domain (slot 2). After this you can reach Nextcloud at either http://192.168.1.42 or http://raspberrypi from any device on your home network. Step 3 — Point Nextcloud at your USB drive for storage By default the Nextcloud snap stores all uploaded files on the microSD card. For a home server holding photos and documents, you almost certainly want it to use your larger, more durable USB drive instead. Do this now — before you upload any files — because moving the data directory after files have been added is more complex. Make sure your USB drive is mounted at /mnt/usbdrive (as set up in Part A). Then create a dedicated folder for Nextcloud's data: sudo mkdir -p /mnt/usbdrive/nextcloud-data Creates a folder on the USB drive that Nextcloud will use to store all uploaded files, photos, and documents. The -p flag prevents an error if the folder already exists. Set the correct permissions on that folder so the Nextcloud snap can write to it: sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /mnt/usbdrive/nextcloud-data sudo chmod 750 /mnt/usbdrive/nextcloud-data sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /mnt/usbdrive/nextcloud-data — sets the owner and group of the folder to www-data . This is the user account that the Nextcloud snap's web server runs as. Without this, Nextcloud cannot write files there. sudo chmod 750 /mnt/usbdrive/nextcloud-data — sets permissions so that www-data has full access, other accounts in the same group can read, and everyone else is locked out. This is the correct, secure setting for a Nextcloud data folder. Careful: The ownership ( www-data ) matters. If you used chown root:root or your own username, Nextcloud will fail silently and uploads will not work. Use www-data exactly as shown. Now tell Nextcloud to use this folder as its data directory: sudo nextcloud.occ config:system:set datadirectory --value=/mnt/usbdrive/nextcloud-data Updates Nextcloud's configuration to point its data storage at the new folder on the USB drive. From now on, every file you upload through Nextcloud will be saved there. Restart Nextcloud to apply all changes: sudo snap restart nextcloud Stops and restarts all the components bundled in the Nextcloud snap — the web server, database, and background job workers. This is necessary for the new configuration to take effect. Step 4 — Open Nextcloud in a browser On any device on your home network (your Windows PC, your phone, your tablet), open a web browser. Type your Pi's IP address into the browser's address bar and press Enter: http://192.168.1.42 (use your actual IP address). The Nextcloud login page appears. Log in with the admin username and password you chose in Step 1. Nextcloud may show a short "first run" wizard — follow the prompts or click Skip to go straight to your files. You are inside your private cloud. Click the Files icon to see your file storage. Click the + (upload) button to upload your first file. Tip: Nextcloud works on any device with a modern web browser — Windows, Mac, Android, iPhone. There is nothing to install on the other devices to use the web interface. Just open a browser and go to your Pi's address. Step 5 — Install the Nextcloud phone app The real power of having a personal cloud on your phone is automatic photo backup — every photo you take is silently copied to your Pi in the background, giving you a private alternative to iCloud or Google Photos. On your Android phone, open the Play Store and search for Nextcloud . On iPhone, open the App Store . Install the free official Nextcloud app (blue icon). Open the app. Tap Log in . When asked for the server address, enter: http://192.168.1.42 (your Pi's IP address). Note that you must be on the same home Wi-Fi network as the Pi for this to work. Tap Next . Log in with your admin username and password. To enable auto backup: on Android, tap the three-line menu, then Auto upload . On iPhone, tap the Photos tab. Enable automatic upload and choose Wi-Fi only to avoid using mobile data. From this point on, every photo or video you take will automatically back itself up to your Pi the next time your phone is connected to your home Wi-Fi network. Tip: The Nextcloud app also lets you access all your Pi files from your phone — you can open documents, play music, and view photos stored on the Pi without them taking up space on your phone's internal storage. Keeping Nextcloud updated Because you installed Nextcloud as a snap, updates are handled automatically in the background by the snap system. If you ever want to check for or apply an update manually: sudo snap refresh nextcloud Checks whether a newer version of the Nextcloud snap is available and installs it if so. This is safe to run at any time. If Nextcloud is already up to date, it will tell you so and do nothing. Security: keep your cloud private Careful: The setup in this chapter makes Nextcloud accessible only on your home network . Do not open your router's firewall to expose Nextcloud to the internet without first reading Chapter 20, which covers HTTPS encryption certificates, firewall rules, and using a reverse proxy or VPN tunnel. Exposing a web service to the open internet without those protections could allow strangers to attempt to log in to your cloud or access your files. As long as Nextcloud is reachable only on your home Wi-Fi (the default after following this chapter), it is protected by your router's built-in firewall. Visitors to your home cannot reach it unless they are connected to your Wi-Fi. Keeping everything backed up A home server is only as useful as its backups. The Pi and the USB drive are in your home — a power surge, a flood, or a fire could wipe everything out. Always follow the 3-2-1 backup rule: In plain words: The 3-2-1 rule says: keep 3 copies of your data, on 2 different types of storage, with 1 copy stored somewhere physically separate (offsite or in the cloud). For example: original on the Pi's USB drive (copy 1), a second USB drive stored in a cupboard (copy 2), and a copy uploaded to a free cloud service or held at a family member's house (copy 3). A simple way to back up the Nextcloud data folder to a second USB drive (which you would mount at /mnt/backup-drive ): sudo rsync -av /mnt/usbdrive/nextcloud-data/ /mnt/backup-drive/nextcloud-backup/ sudo rsync — "remote sync", a powerful and efficient tool for copying files. It only copies files that have changed since the last run, so after the first full copy, subsequent runs are very fast. -a — "archive mode": preserves file permissions, ownership, timestamps, and copies all subdirectories recursively. -v — "verbose": prints the name of each file as it copies it, so you can see what is happening. /mnt/usbdrive/nextcloud-data/ — the source folder (your Nextcloud data). The trailing slash is important — it means "copy the contents of this folder", not the folder itself. /mnt/backup-drive/nextcloud-backup/ — the destination folder on a second USB drive. You would need to mount that second drive at /mnt/backup-drive first. You can automate this backup to run every night using cron — the scheduling tool covered in Chapter 15. Keeping the Pi powered safely Careful: A home server needs reliable power. If the Pi loses power while writing files, those files can become corrupted. Consider plugging the Pi's power supply into a small UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply) — a battery backup box available for around £30–60 that keeps the Pi running for 10–30 minutes during a power cut, giving it time to finish what it is doing and shut down gracefully. Note: When you want to switch the Pi off properly, always shut it down from the desktop menu or by typing sudo shutdown -h now in a terminal, then wait for the activity light to stop blinking before unplugging the power. Never just pull the power cable — this is the most common cause of microSD card corruption. Troubleshooting common problems Windows cannot see the Pi on the network Make sure both devices are on the same network (same router, same Wi-Fi network name). Try connecting by IP address ( \\192.168.1.42\PiShare ) rather than by hostname — some routers do not pass hostnames between devices. Check Samba is running: sudo systemctl status smbd Check whether the Pi's firewall is active and blocking Samba: sudo ufw status . If it shows as active, allow Samba through with: sudo ufw allow samba On Windows, make sure "Network discovery" is turned on. Open Settings → Network & Internet → Advanced network settings → Advanced sharing settings and enable network discovery. Nextcloud shows a warning about "insecure connection" or "not secure" This is expected when using plain http:// rather than encrypted https:// . Within your home Wi-Fi, the connection is acceptable — your router already encrypts the Wi-Fi signal itself. If you want a proper padlock in the browser bar (which is especially important before enabling access from outside your home), Chapter 20 explains how to add a proper HTTPS certificate. Nextcloud is very slow Check the Pi is not overheating: run vcgencmd measure_temp in a terminal. If the temperature is above 80°C, improve ventilation around the Pi or check the active cooler fan is spinning. Make sure the USB drive is plugged into one of the blue USB 3.0 ports (the two at the back of the board), not the black USB 2.0 ports. USB 3.0 is around ten times faster for large file transfers. The first time Nextcloud scans the data folder or processes a large photo album, it will be briefly slow — this is normal and will speed up after the initial indexing is complete. Nextcloud shows "Could not connect to database" The snap's internal database service may not have started yet. Wait 60 seconds after a reboot and try again, or manually restart the snap: sudo snap restart nextcloud The shared USB drive does not appear after a reboot Check the /etc/fstab entry you added. Open it with sudo nano /etc/fstab and look for typos. Run sudo mount -a and watch for any error messages — they will tell you exactly what is wrong. Make sure you have the correct filesystem type. If in doubt, run sudo blkid /dev/sda1 again to check. Remember to use ntfs-3g (not just ntfs ) for NTFS drives, and make sure ntfs-3g is installed. How Nextcloud, Samba, and your storage fit together USB Drive /mnt/usbdrive/ Samba shared/ → \\pi\PiShare Nextcloud nextcloud-data/ Windows PC File Explorer \\pi\PiShare Phone Nextcloud auto backup Any browser http://192.168.x.x web interface Tablet Nextcloud app or browser Both services share the same USB drive but use separate folders Architecture overview: Samba and Nextcloud both read from the same USB drive but serve different types of clients. You can run both at the same time. Key terms Samba — free software that lets a Linux computer speak Windows' file-sharing language (SMB), making the Pi's folders appear as network drives in Windows Explorer. SMB (Server Message Block) — the network protocol Windows uses to share files and printers across a local network. Samba implements this protocol on Linux. File server — a computer whose main job is to store files and make them available to other computers on the same network. Nextcloud — free, open-source personal cloud software that gives you a private Dropbox/Google Drive on your own hardware, with browser access, phone backup, and calendar sync. Snap — a self-contained software package that bundles an application with all its dependencies, simplifying installation and updates. Mount / mounting — attaching a storage device (like a USB drive) to the Linux file system at a specific folder, so the operating system can read and write it. UUID (Universally Unique Identifier) — a permanent identifier assigned to a storage partition. Using a UUID in /etc/fstab ensures the correct drive is always mounted, even if device names change between reboots. fstab — the file /etc/fstab that tells Linux which drives to mount automatically at startup, and how. nofail — an fstab option that tells the Pi to continue booting normally even if a listed drive is missing or cannot be mounted. www-data — the user account that web servers on Linux (including Nextcloud's bundled Apache server) run as. Files that a web server needs to write must be owned by this account. trusted_domains — a Nextcloud security setting that lists the addresses from which it will accept web connections. Addresses not on this list are refused. rsync — a command-line tool for efficiently copying and synchronising files, only transferring data that has changed since the last run. 3-2-1 backup rule — keep three copies of your data, on two different media types, with one copy stored offsite or in a separate physical location. UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply) — a battery backup box that keeps a device running for a short time during a power cut, preventing file corruption from sudden shutdowns. Chapter summary Samba turns the Pi into a Windows-compatible file server: install it with apt , add a share block to /etc/samba/smb.conf , set a Samba password with smbpasswd , restart the service, and connect from Windows Explorer using the Pi's IP address. A USB hard drive connected to the Pi's blue USB 3.0 port gives the shared folder far more space and longevity than the microSD card alone. Adding the USB drive to /etc/fstab with the nofail option ensures it mounts automatically on every boot without risking startup failures if the drive is absent. Use the correct filesystem type in fstab: vfat for FAT32, exfat for exFAT (install exfatprogs first), ntfs-3g for NTFS (install ntfs-3g first), or ext4 for Linux-formatted drives. After installing snapd , you must reboot the Pi before installing any snap package — this is a required step often missed by beginners. Nextcloud, installed as a single snap package, gives you a full personal cloud: browser-based file access, phone photo backup, and calendar and contacts sync — all stored on your own hardware. The Nextcloud data folder must be owned by the www-data user — not root or your own account — for the snap to write files correctly. The Nextcloud phone app (free, iOS and Android) can automatically back up every photo you take to the Pi whenever your phone is on home Wi-Fi. Keep Nextcloud accessible only on your home network until you have read Chapter 20 on HTTPS and firewall security — never expose it directly to the internet without those protections. Always shut the Pi down gracefully before unplugging it, and consider a UPS to protect against sudden power cuts corrupting your files. Follow the 3-2-1 backup rule — at least one copy of your important data should be stored offsite or on a separate physical drive.

title: A Private Smart-Home Hub
headings: The two ways to install Home Assistant
Step 1 — Flash Home Assistant OS with Raspberry Pi Imager
Step 3 — Onboarding: set up your account in the browser
Accessing Home Assistant from your phone
Privacy and local control — why this matters
text: Imagine controlling every smart bulb, plug, sensor, thermostat, and door lock in your home — from any brand — through a single app that runs entirely on your Raspberry Pi, never sending your data to any company's server. That is exactly what Home Assistant does, and this chapter walks you through installing it, connecting your first device, and creating your first automation from scratch. What is Home Assistant? Home Assistant is free, open-source software that acts as the brain of a smart home. Instead of juggling five different apps for five different brands of smart devices, you open one page in your web browser and everything is there: lights, heating, door sensors, cameras, weather, energy monitors, robot vacuums — thousands of different products from hundreds of brands all talking to each other. In plain words: "Open-source" means the software's code is written by volunteers and is freely available for anyone to inspect or improve. There is no company charging you a subscription, and no one can shut it down remotely. The biggest advantage over commercial smart-home systems (Amazon Alexa, Google Home, Apple HomeKit) is local control . Most of those systems send your commands up to a cloud server owned by a company, which then sends the instruction back down to your device. If the company's server goes offline, or if the company decides to shut down the product, your devices stop working. Home Assistant runs entirely on your Raspberry Pi, inside your home network. Your light-switching command travels: phone → Pi → light bulb, all within your own house. The internet is not involved at all. Note: Home Assistant does offer optional cloud features (called "Nabu Casa") for a small monthly fee, which lets you control your home remotely from outside your house. That is entirely optional. The core local system is completely free and works without it. In plain words: A "port" (the number after the colon in an address like :8123 ) is like a door number inside a computer. A single device can run many different services at the same time — each on its own door number. Port 8123 is the door Home Assistant listens on. You will see this number throughout the chapter. The two ways to install Home Assistant There are two main approaches, and it is worth understanding both before you choose. Approach What it is Pros Cons Best for Home Assistant OS (HAOS) A complete, dedicated operating system you flash to your microSD card (or SSD). The Pi boots directly into Home Assistant and nothing else. Simplest setup. Automatic updates. Full access to the Add-on Store. Best performance. Officially recommended. The Pi is dedicated — you cannot also use it as a normal Raspberry Pi OS desktop at the same time. Anyone who wants Home Assistant as the Pi's main job. Recommended for beginners. Home Assistant Container (Docker) Home Assistant runs as a "container" (an isolated software box) inside Raspberry Pi OS, which you already know from this book. You keep the normal Raspberry Pi OS desktop and can run other software alongside it. More complex to set up. The Add-on Store is not available (add-ons must be managed manually). Updates require more steps. Users who specifically need to keep a normal desktop and run Home Assistant on the same Pi. Tip: If you have a second microSD card or a spare SSD (via the Pi 5's PCIe slot), you can have both: one card for Raspberry Pi OS and one for Home Assistant OS, and simply swap them when you want to switch roles. This is a very popular approach. This chapter follows the Home Assistant OS route — it is the path the Home Assistant project itself recommends, it is the simplest, and it gives you the full feature set including the Add-on Store. What you will need Your Raspberry Pi 5 (already assembled with its cooler and case). A microSD card, 32 GB or larger (the 64/128/256 GB card from your kit is perfect). Note: this will erase whatever is currently on the card, including Raspberry Pi OS if it was pre-installed. If you want to keep Raspberry Pi OS, use a second card. The USB card reader that came with your kit. A Windows 11 PC (your everyday computer) to flash the card. A monitor, keyboard, and mouse connected to the Pi for the very first boot (after that, you manage everything from your PC's web browser). An Ethernet cable or your Wi-Fi credentials (network name and password). Ethernet is strongly preferred for the first boot. Careful: Flashing a new image to the microSD card completely erases all existing data on it. If your card came with Raspberry Pi OS pre-installed and you have files on it you want to keep, copy them to your Windows PC first before continuing. Step 1 — Flash Home Assistant OS with Raspberry Pi Imager The process is almost identical to flashing Raspberry Pi OS in Chapter 4 — you use the same Raspberry Pi Imager tool on your Windows PC. Insert the microSD card into the USB card reader, then plug the card reader into your Windows 11 PC. Open Raspberry Pi Imager . (If you do not have it, download it free from raspberrypi.com/software — it is the same tool from Chapter 4.) Under "Raspberry Pi Device", click Choose Device and select Raspberry Pi 5 . Under "Operating System", click Choose OS . Scroll down and click Other specific-purpose OS . Click Home assistants and home automation . Click Home Assistant OS . Then select the version listed for Raspberry Pi 5 (it will be labelled something like "Home Assistant OS 14.x (RPi5)" — choose the highest version number available). Under "Storage", click Choose Storage and select your microSD card. Double-check the name and size match your card — do not select your Windows PC's internal drive by mistake. Click Next . When asked "Would you like to apply OS customisation settings?", click No — Home Assistant has its own first-run setup wizard and does not need anything entered here. Click Yes to confirm you want to erase and write the card. The Imager will download the image and flash it. This typically takes 5–10 minutes depending on your internet speed. When it says "Write Successful", click Continue and remove the card reader from your PC. Note: Raspberry Pi Imager downloads the Home Assistant OS image directly from the internet. Make sure your PC is connected to the internet before starting. The file is roughly 1–2 GB. Step 2 — First boot Insert the freshly flashed microSD card into the slot on the underside of your Raspberry Pi 5. Connect the micro-HDMI cable from the Pi to your monitor, and plug in your keyboard and mouse. If you have an Ethernet cable, plug it in now — this is the most reliable option for the first boot, because Home Assistant can get a network address immediately without needing to know your Wi-Fi password. If you only have Wi-Fi, that is fine — you will enter your Wi-Fi details using the HAOS console menu (see the note below). Plug in the 27 W USB-C power supply. The Pi will start automatically. Watch the monitor. You will see text scrolling past (this is the system starting up). After a minute or two, the screen will show a simple text display — not a desktop. It will look something like this: Home Assistant http://homeassistant.local:8123 hostname: homeassistant IPv4: 192.168.1.45 This screen is just a status display — you do not normally type anything here. It is telling you: Home Assistant is running, and you can reach it from any browser on your home network by going to the address shown. The IP address (the numbers like 192.168.1.45) will be different on your network — every router assigns its own addresses. Tip: The very first boot takes longer than usual — often 5 to 20 minutes — because Home Assistant is setting itself up internally. If the screen shows the address but your browser says "site can't be reached", wait a few more minutes and try again. Note — Setting up Wi-Fi via the HAOS console: Home Assistant OS is not a normal Linux desktop. Its text console is a special menu-driven system, not a regular command prompt. If you need to configure Wi-Fi from the console (because you have no Ethernet cable), press Enter on the console screen after boot. You will see a menu. Navigate to Network using the arrow keys, then Update , choose your wireless interface (usually wlan0 ), and enter your Wi-Fi name (SSID) and password. Press Enter to save and the Pi will connect. Once it has an IP address, you can proceed with all remaining steps from your PC's browser. Step 3 — Onboarding: set up your account in the browser Everything from this point onwards happens in a web browser on your Windows 11 PC (or any phone, tablet, or laptop on the same home network). You do not need to type anything on the Pi itself. On your Windows PC, open any web browser (Edge, Chrome, Firefox). In the address bar, type exactly: http://homeassistant.local:8123 and press Enter. If that does not work, use the IP address shown on the Pi's monitor screen instead (for example: http://192.168.1.45:8123 ). You will see a welcome page titled "Welcome to Home Assistant" . Click Create my smart home . Fill in the form to create your owner account: Name: your first name (e.g. "Alex"). Username: a login name, no spaces (e.g. "alex"). Password: choose a strong password and remember it — this protects your entire smart home. Click Create account . Next, you are asked for your home location. Type your town name — Home Assistant uses this to calculate sunrise and sunset times for automations. Set your time zone (e.g. Europe/London, Europe/Paris, Europe/Zurich), unit system (Metric for Europe), and currency. Click Next . Home Assistant will now show you a list of devices it has already found on your home network — smart TVs, printers, Philips Hue bridges, Sonos speakers, and so on. This is auto-discovery at work. You can add them now or skip and do it later. Click Finish . You arrive at the Home Assistant Dashboard — your smart home control centre. Congratulations! In plain words: "Auto-discovery" means Home Assistant scans your home network and recognises known devices all by itself, without you having to manually enter IP addresses or codes. It uses standard network protocols like mDNS and SSDP to find them. Home Assistant Setup Flow 1. Flash card HAOS via Imager 2. Boot Pi Wait up to 20 min 3. Open browser :8123 4. Create account Name + password 5. Set location Town + timezone 6. Auto-discover Devices found 7. Dashboard You're live! Your Home Assistant Dashboard is live All control happens at http://homeassistant.local:8123 in any browser on your phone, tablet, or PC — anything connected to the same home Wi-Fi No internet connection required for day-to-day use The seven steps from flashing the card to your live Home Assistant dashboard. Step 4 — Add your first integration In plain words: An "integration" in Home Assistant is a plug-in that teaches Home Assistant how to talk to a specific brand or type of device. There are over 3,000 integrations included out of the box — no extra downloads needed for most popular products. If Home Assistant already found some of your devices during onboarding (Step 6 above), you may already have integrations set up. Here is how to add or manage them manually: In the Home Assistant dashboard, click the three-line menu icon in the top-left corner (it looks like three stacked horizontal lines), then click Settings . Click Devices & Services . You will see any integrations already active, plus any discovered devices waiting to be added. To add a new integration, click the blue Add Integration button in the bottom-right corner. Type the name of your device brand in the search box — for example, "Philips Hue", "TP-Link Kasa", "IKEA TRÅDFRI", "Shelly", "Tasmota", "Tuya", "Sonos", or "Nest". Click the matching result and follow the on-screen instructions. For most popular brands, this means entering your hub's IP address, or simply clicking a button on the hub itself to authorise the connection. Once added, your devices appear automatically in the dashboard. Tip: Philips Hue users — make sure your Hue Bridge is connected to your router by Ethernet, then press the round button on top of the Bridge when Home Assistant asks you to. That is all the authentication it needs. Note: If your smart devices use Zigbee or Z-Wave radio protocols (common in professional-grade smart home gear), you will need a USB Zigbee/Z-Wave dongle plugged into one of the Pi's USB ports. Recommended dongles include the Sonoff Zigbee 3.0 USB Dongle Plus and the HUSBZB-1. Home Assistant will detect them and offer to set up the ZHA (Zigbee Home Automation) or Z-Wave JS integration automatically. In plain words: "Zigbee" and "Z-Wave" are short-range radio protocols designed specifically for smart home devices. They use very little power (so sensor batteries last years) and the devices form a "mesh" — each device helps pass signals to others, extending the network's range through walls and floors. Home Network Topology: Your Pi as Smart-Home Hub Home Router Internet gateway Raspberry Pi 5 Home Assistant OS USB Zigbee Dongle (optional, for Zigbee devices) Zigbee sensor Zigbee bulb Smart plug (Wi-Fi) Philips Hue Bridge Smart thermostat IP camera Wi-Fi / Ethernet Zigbee radio Ethernet (router→Pi) Your Raspberry Pi 5 sits between your router and all your smart devices. Wi-Fi and Ethernet devices connect over your home network; Zigbee/Z-Wave devices need a small USB dongle. Step 5 — Build your first automation Automations are the magic of Home Assistant — rules that make things happen automatically. Let's create one everyone finds useful: turn a lamp on at sunset every day . In plain words: An "automation" is a simple "if this, then that" rule. Home Assistant handles the "if" (the trigger) and the "then" (the action) for you through a visual editor — no programming required. In the sidebar, go to Settings → Automations & Scenes . Click the blue Create Automation button, then choose Create new automation . You are now in the automation editor. At the top, click on the automation name field and type a friendly name like Lamp on at sunset . Under Triggers (the "when" section), click Add trigger → Sun . Set Event to Sunset . You can optionally add an offset, for example -00:30 to trigger 30 minutes before actual sunset. Scroll down to Actions (the "then do this" section). Click Add action → Device . Click Pick a device and select your lamp from the list. Then choose the action Turn on . If your lamp supports brightness or colour, you can set those here too. Click Save in the top-right corner. Your automation is now active and will run every evening. Note: Home Assistant knows your local sunset time because you entered your home location during onboarding. The sunset time adjusts automatically throughout the year — you never need to update it. Once you are comfortable with that, you can explore much more powerful automations: turn heating off when a door is left open, flash a light when someone rings the doorbell, send a notification to your phone when motion is detected while you are away, or turn everything off with one "Goodnight" button. The Add-on Store One of the biggest advantages of Home Assistant OS (compared to the Docker container approach) is the Add-on Store . Add-ons are extra software packages you can install with one click, running safely alongside Home Assistant on the same Pi. Popular add-ons include: Mosquitto Broker — runs an MQTT server on your Pi. MQTT is a lightweight messaging system used by a huge range of IoT devices. Node-RED — a powerful visual programming tool for building complex automations by dragging and connecting blocks on screen. ESPHome — lets you create your own custom smart sensors using cheap ESP32/ESP8266 microcontroller boards and have them talk directly to Home Assistant over Wi-Fi. Let's Encrypt — automatically sets up secure HTTPS access to your Home Assistant from outside your home (works together with the Nabu Casa remote access service or your own domain name). Samba share — makes the Home Assistant configuration folder visible as a shared network drive on your Windows PC, so you can edit configuration files easily without any technical tools. File editor — lets you view and edit configuration files directly in the browser. Zigbee2MQTT — an alternative to the built-in ZHA integration for Zigbee devices; preferred by many advanced users for its wider device support. To browse the Add-on Store: go to Settings → Add-ons → click Add-on Store in the bottom-right corner. Search for what you want, click it, then click Install . In plain words: "MQTT" stands for Message Queuing Telemetry Transport. It is a very lightweight messaging system that lets small, battery-powered devices send tiny data packets to a central server (called a "broker") efficiently. Many cheap sensors and smart home gadgets use it. Keeping Home Assistant updated Home Assistant releases updates frequently — often every month — adding new integrations, features, and security fixes. On Home Assistant OS, updating is straightforward and safe: When an update is available, you will see a notification icon in the bottom-left corner of the Home Assistant dashboard (a downward-pointing arrow with a number). Click it, read the release notes, then click Update . Home Assistant downloads and applies the update in the background and restarts itself. The whole process usually takes just a few minutes. Careful: Before every update, make a backup first. Go to Settings → System → Backups → Create backup . This creates a snapshot of all your settings, automations, and integrations. The backup file can be downloaded to your PC or saved to a USB drive. If an update ever causes a problem, you can restore from the backup in just a few clicks. Make backups a regular habit — ideally before any major change. Accessing Home Assistant from your phone Home Assistant has official apps for Android and iPhone. Search for "Home Assistant" in the Google Play Store or Apple App Store and install the free official app (the publisher is "Home Assistant"). Open it, tap Add server manually , type in your Home Assistant address ( http://homeassistant.local:8123 ), then log in with your username and password. You now have a full smart-home control panel on your phone — as long as your phone is on the same home Wi-Fi. Tip: The mobile app also supports companion features : Home Assistant can read your phone's GPS location, battery level, Wi-Fi network name, and more, and use those as triggers for automations. For example: "turn the heating on when my phone's GPS shows I am within 2 km of home", or "switch on the hall light when I disconnect from my office Wi-Fi network". Privacy and local control — why this matters Every major smart-home platform — Amazon Alexa, Google Home, Apple HomeKit, Samsung SmartThings — requires its servers to work. When their servers are down (which does happen), your smart home stops working. When a company discontinues a product line (which also happens), devices you paid for become useless. Some platforms have raised subscription prices or removed features after users were already deeply invested. Home Assistant on your Raspberry Pi eliminates all of that: All processing happens inside your house, on your Pi. No subscription fee. No account required with any third-party company. Your usage data — which lights you turn on, when you come and go, your camera footage — stays on your hardware and goes nowhere. Even if the Home Assistant project shut down tomorrow, the software would keep running forever on your Pi, because it is already installed locally. You can integrate devices that have been officially discontinued or abandoned by their manufacturers, as long as someone has written a Home Assistant integration for them. The Docker container route (brief overview) If you specifically want to keep using Raspberry Pi OS as your main operating system and also run Home Assistant, the Docker container method is the way to do it. Docker is a system that runs self-contained software packages (containers) on top of a regular operating system, so multiple programs can share the same Pi without interfering with one another. Careful: These steps are more advanced than the HAOS route above. If you are not already comfortable with the Terminal from earlier chapters, use Home Assistant OS on a second microSD card instead. The end result (the web interface at :8123 ) looks exactly the same — only the installation method differs. Installing Docker and the Home Assistant container requires typing commands in the Terminal. Open a Terminal on Raspberry Pi OS and type the following commands: First — install Docker using the official install script: curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com -o get-docker.sh sudo sh get-docker.sh sudo usermod -aG docker $USER Line 1: Downloads the official Docker installation script from Docker's website and saves it to a file called get-docker.sh in the current folder. ( curl is a tool for downloading files from the internet; -fsSL means "fail quietly on errors, follow redirects, and work in silent mode".) Line 2: Runs that installation script with administrator privileges ( sudo ). The script detects that you are on Raspberry Pi OS (Debian Bookworm) and installs the latest version of Docker from Docker's own servers — this is the correct, supported way to install Docker on Bookworm. Line 3: Adds your current user account to the "docker" group. $USER automatically fills in your username. This means you will be able to run Docker commands in the future without needing to type sudo each time. You must log out and log back in (or reboot) for this change to take effect. Note: After running those three commands, reboot the Pi ( sudo reboot ) before continuing, so the group membership takes effect. When you log back in, open a new Terminal and proceed. Second — create the folder for Home Assistant's settings and start the container: mkdir -p /home/$USER/homeassistant docker run -d \ --name homeassistant \ --privileged \ --restart=unless-stopped \ -v /home/$USER/homeassistant:/config \ -e TZ=Europe/London \ --network=host \ ghcr.io/home-assistant/home-assistant:stable Line 1: Creates the folder /home/<your-username>/homeassistant where Home Assistant will store all its settings, automations, and data. The -p flag means "create any missing parent folders too; do not error if it already exists". Using $USER ensures the path uses your actual username automatically. Line 2 (the backslash \ ): The backslash at the end of several lines is just a line-continuation character — it tells the Terminal that the command continues on the next line. This is purely for readability; it is all one single command. docker run -d : Tells Docker to start a new container and run it in the background ( -d stands for "detached"), so you get your Terminal prompt back immediately. --name homeassistant : Gives the container a friendly name so you can refer to it later with commands like docker stop homeassistant or docker logs homeassistant . --privileged : Gives Home Assistant full access to the Pi's hardware, including USB ports. This is required for Zigbee/Z-Wave dongles and other hardware integrations to work. --restart=unless-stopped : Tells Docker to automatically restart the Home Assistant container whenever the Pi reboots — so your smart home comes back online automatically after a power cut. -v /home/$USER/homeassistant:/config : Maps (links) the folder you just created on the Pi's storage to the /config folder inside the container. This means all your settings are saved outside the container on your real storage, so they survive container updates or re-creation. -e TZ=Europe/London : Sets the time zone inside the container. Change this to match your location — for example: Europe/Paris , Europe/Berlin , Europe/Zurich , Europe/Brussels , Europe/Amsterdam . A full list is available at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones . --network=host : Uses your Pi's actual network connection directly, rather than a private virtual network inside Docker. This is required for Home Assistant's auto-discovery to work — it needs to "see" the same network as your other devices. ghcr.io/home-assistant/home-assistant:stable : The address of the official Home Assistant container image, hosted on GitHub's container registry. The word "stable" at the end means "use the latest stable release". After this command completes (it may take a few minutes to download the container image on first run), you access Home Assistant at the same address: http://homeassistant.local:8123 or http://<your-pi-ip>:8123 . The onboarding steps are identical to the HAOS route. Careful: With the Docker container route, the Add-on Store is not available . Add-ons like Mosquitto, Node-RED, and ESPHome must each be run as separate Docker containers and configured manually — this is significantly more complex. For most users, Home Assistant OS is the better choice. To update the Home Assistant container in future, run these two commands in Terminal: docker pull ghcr.io/home-assistant/home-assistant:stable docker restart homeassistant Line 1: Downloads the newest version of the Home Assistant container image from the internet. "Pull" is Docker's word for "download the latest version of an image". Line 2: Stops and restarts the running container so it uses the newly downloaded image. Your settings in /home/$USER/homeassistant are unaffected because they live outside the container. Troubleshooting common first-boot issues Problem Likely cause Fix Browser says "site can't be reached" at homeassistant.local:8123 Pi still starting up, or your PC does not support mDNS name resolution Wait 10 more minutes and try again. If still failing, use the IP address shown on the Pi's monitor screen instead (e.g. http://192.168.1.45:8123 ). Pi's monitor shows no IP address Pi not connected to the network yet Check the Ethernet cable is firmly plugged into both the Pi and your router. If using Wi-Fi only, press Enter on the HAOS console to open the network menu, navigate to Network → Update , select wlan0 , and enter your Wi-Fi name and password. Pi shows a blank screen or no video output Wrong micro-HDMI port or cable not fully inserted The Pi 5 has two micro-HDMI ports — try the other one. Make sure the tiny connector clicks firmly into the Pi. Also check the cable is fully pushed into your monitor. Onboarding page asks you to restore a backup instead of setting up fresh You accidentally opened the restore prompt Click Create new home or use the back button. You have not damaged anything — start again from the welcome screen. A device is not auto-discovered Device uses a protocol requiring a hub or dongle; or it is on a separate guest Wi-Fi network Add the integration manually: Settings → Devices & Services → Add Integration . Make sure the device and the Pi are on the same Wi-Fi network — most routers isolate guest networks, preventing discovery. After a Home Assistant OS update, the dashboard is not loading Update still in progress; browser cache stale Wait 5 minutes and do a hard refresh (press Ctrl + Shift + R in your browser). If it still fails, restore from your backup via Settings → System → Backups . Key terms Home Assistant — free, open-source smart-home software that controls devices from many brands in one place, running locally on your Pi. Home Assistant OS (HAOS) — a complete, dedicated operating system you flash to a card; the recommended and simplest install method. Local control — commands that travel only within your home network, without going through the internet or any company's server. Integration — a plug-in that teaches Home Assistant to communicate with a specific brand or type of device. Auto-discovery — Home Assistant automatically scanning your network and recognising compatible devices without manual entry. Automation — an "if this, then that" rule that makes devices act automatically (e.g. turn a light on at sunset). Add-on — an extra software package (like an MQTT broker or Node-RED) you install alongside Home Assistant OS with one click from the Add-on Store; not available with the Docker container route. Zigbee / Z-Wave — short-range low-power radio protocols used by many smart home sensors and switches; require a USB dongle plugged into the Pi. MQTT — a lightweight messaging protocol widely used by IoT devices to send small data packets to a central server (broker). Docker — a system for running self-contained software packages (containers) on top of a regular operating system; used in the alternative Home Assistant Container install method. Port — a numbered "door" on a networked device. Home Assistant listens on port 8123, which is why you always include :8123 in its address. Nabu Casa — the optional paid cloud service from the Home Assistant team that enables remote access from outside your home; not required for local smart-home control. Chapter summary Home Assistant is free, open-source software that unifies smart devices from thousands of brands into one private, local control system running entirely on your Raspberry Pi. The recommended install method is Home Assistant OS — flash it with Raspberry Pi Imager (under "Other specific-purpose OS → Home assistants and home automation") exactly as you would Raspberry Pi OS. First boot takes up to 20 minutes; once ready, all setup and daily use happens in a web browser at http://homeassistant.local:8123 — no keyboard on the Pi required after that. The onboarding wizard creates your account, sets your location (for accurate sunrise/sunset times), and auto-discovers devices already on your network. Integrations (over 3,000 included) connect Home Assistant to specific device brands; most require only a few clicks — no technical knowledge needed. Automations are visual "if this, then that" rules — no programming needed — and can use triggers like time of day, sunrise/sunset, sensor values, or your phone's GPS location. The Add-on Store (HAOS only) lets you install extra services like MQTT brokers, Node-RED visual programming, and ESPHome custom sensors with a single click. The Docker container route lets you run Home Assistant alongside Raspberry Pi OS, but the Add-on Store is unavailable and setup is more complex — always make a backup before updating. Everything runs locally: no subscription, no cloud dependency, no company can disable your smart home — your data stays in your house, on your hardware, forever.

title: Host a Website & Self-Host with Docker
headings: What Is a Web Server, Really?
Part A — Serve a Simple Web Page
Part B — The Modern Way: Docker and Containers
Reaching Your Pi from Outside Your Home Network
Quick Reference: Ports Used in This Chapter
text:
Your Raspberry Pi 5 can do far more than run programs you use yourself — it can serve things to other devices on your home network, acting as a tiny, always-on web server or running powerful self-hosted applications. This chapter shows you two practical paths: the quick-and-simple way with a built-in Python trick, and the modern, tidy way using Docker containers. What Is a Web Server, Really? When you type a web address into your browser, your browser sends a request over the network asking "Please send me that page." A web server is simply a program sitting on another computer, waiting for those requests and then sending back the web page (an HTML file) in reply. The word "server" just means "something that serves requests" — it has nothing to do with the size or power of the computer. Your Pi 5 is perfectly capable of being a web server for every device on your home Wi-Fi. In plain words: A web server is a program that listens for browsers asking for pages and hands them back, the same way a library assistant hands you a book when you ask for one. Every device on your home network has a local address called an IP address — a set of four numbers like 192.168.1.42 . Once your Pi is running a web server, any other device on the same Wi-Fi can open a browser and visit http://192.168.1.42 to see whatever page the Pi is serving. (Finding your Pi's IP address was covered in Chapter 5; the quick reminder is to open a Terminal on the Pi and type hostname -I .) Note: Everything in this chapter works on your home network only, until you deliberately open it to the outside world. That is the safe default — we discuss the outside internet at the end of the chapter. Part A — Serve a Simple Web Page There are two easy approaches. The first uses a tool that is already installed; the second installs the professional-grade web server software called Nginx . Both end with you viewing a page from another device. Method 1: The One-Command Python Server Python 3 is already installed on Raspberry Pi OS and includes a tiny built-in web server. It takes one command and serves every file in a folder. This is great for a quick demo or sharing files on your home network — but it is not meant to run permanently or to handle heavy traffic. Open a Terminal on your Pi. Create a test folder and move into it: mkdir ~/my-website cd ~/my-website mkdir ~/my-website — creates a new folder called my-website inside your home directory. The ~ is a shortcut that always means "my home folder" (usually /home/pi ). cd ~/my-website — changes your current location to that new folder so the next commands work there. Create a simple web page: nano index.html nano index.html — opens the Nano text editor to create a new file called index.html . A file named index.html is the conventional "home page" that web servers look for first when a visitor arrives at the address without asking for a specific file. Type (or paste) this into Nano: My Pi Website

Hello from my Raspberry Pi 5!

This page is being served by my Pi.

This is a minimal HTML web page. The declaration tells the browser this is a modern HTML5 document.

creates a large heading;

creates a paragraph. The browser will display both. You can write anything you like here — it is your page. Press Ctrl + O then Enter to save, then Ctrl + X to exit Nano. Start the web server: python3 -m http.server 8080 python3 -m http.server 8080 — tells Python 3 to run its built-in web server module ( http.server ) and listen on port 8080 . A port is like a numbered door on your Pi — different services listen on different door numbers. The standard web port is 80, but we use 8080 here to avoid needing extra administrator permissions. You will see a message like Serving HTTP on 0.0.0.0 port 8080 . The Terminal is now busy running the server — leave it open. On any device on your home network (phone, laptop, another computer), open a web browser and go to: http://:8080 Replace with the actual IP address shown by hostname -I on the Pi (for example http://192.168.1.42:8080 ). The :8080 tells the browser which port to knock on. You should see your "Hello from my Raspberry Pi 5!" page. When you are done, go back to the Terminal and press Ctrl + C to stop the server. Tip: While the server is running, look back at the Terminal — it prints a line every time a device visits the page, showing the visitor's IP address, the time, and what file was requested. This is exactly what a real web server access log looks like. Method 2: Nginx — The Proper Web Server Nginx (pronounced "engine-ecks") is a fast, professional web server used by millions of websites worldwide. Unlike the Python one-liner, it runs as a background service that starts automatically when your Pi boots. This is the right choice if you want a page that is always available. In plain words: A service (also called a daemon ) is a program that runs quietly in the background all the time, without needing a Terminal window open. Your Pi starts its services automatically when it boots up, so you never have to remember to start them. Open a Terminal and install Nginx: sudo apt update sudo apt install nginx -y sudo apt update — refreshes the list of available software packages from the internet. Always do this before installing something new to make sure you get the latest version. sudo apt install nginx -y — downloads and installs Nginx. The -y answers "yes" automatically to the "do you want to continue?" question, so you do not have to type it yourself. When the installation finishes, Nginx starts automatically and is immediately listening for web traffic. Check that it is running: sudo systemctl status nginx sudo systemctl status nginx — asks the system service manager ( systemctl ) to report the current status of the Nginx service. You should see the word active (running) highlighted in green. Press Q to exit the status view. On your Pi itself, open the Chromium web browser and go to http://localhost . The word localhost always means "this computer itself". You should see the Nginx welcome page — this confirms it is working. Now replace the default page with your own. The web files Nginx serves live in /var/www/html/ . Edit the default page: sudo nano /var/www/html/index.html sudo nano /var/www/html/index.html — opens the existing index file in the Nano editor. sudo is needed because the folder is owned by the system, not your user account, and without it Nano would not be able to save your changes. Select all the existing text (hold Ctrl + K repeatedly to delete line by line) and replace it with your own HTML — you can use the same simple page from Method 1, or write something new. Save with Ctrl + O , Enter , then Ctrl + X . From any device on your home network, open a browser and visit: http:// No port number is needed — Nginx listens on the standard web port 80, which browsers use automatically when you just type an http:// address without a colon and number. Your page appears! And it will still be there the next time you visit, even after you restart the Pi. Tip: You can drop any number of HTML files, images, or CSS files into /var/www/html/ and Nginx will serve them all. Create sub-folders for different pages and link between them with normal HTML links — you are building a real website. How a home network web server works Diagram showing a browser on a laptop sending an HTTP request to the Raspberry Pi, which has Nginx running and returns a web page. Both are connected through a home Wi-Fi router. Raspberry Pi 5 Nginx (web server) 192.168.1.42 : 80 /var/www/html/ GET http://192.168.1.42/ Here is index.html → Your Laptop / Phone Web browser Displays the page Home Wi-Fi Router (same network) A browser on any device on your home network asks the Pi's Nginx web server for a page. Nginx reads the HTML file from disk and sends it back. The whole conversation stays inside your home network, through the router. Part B — The Modern Way: Docker and Containers Serving a static HTML page is satisfying, but the real fun begins when you run complete self-hosted applications on your Pi — things like a home dashboard, a private notes app, an uptime monitor, or a media server. The cleanest way to do this in 2025 is with Docker . What Is Docker? In plain words: A container is like a pre-packed lunchbox for a program. It contains the program itself plus every library, tool, and configuration file it needs to run — all bundled together. You can drop the lunchbox onto any compatible computer and it just works, without touching or interfering with anything else on the machine. Docker is the most popular tool for creating and running these containers. Before Docker, installing a server application on Linux could mean following a long list of steps, installing dozens of extra packages, editing configuration files, and hoping nothing clashed with other software already on the machine. With Docker: You pull a ready-made container image from the internet (think of an image as the sealed lunchbox before you open it). Docker runs it in an isolated environment — it cannot accidentally break other things on your Pi. Removing an app is as simple as deleting its container and image — no leftover files scattered everywhere. The same container works the same way every time, on every machine that runs Docker. Docker containers on a Raspberry Pi Diagram showing Raspberry Pi OS at the base, Docker Engine on top of it, and three separate containers sitting side by side inside Docker, each with their own libraries and a port number. Raspberry Pi OS (Bookworm) — the base system Docker Engine Container A Uptime Kuma Port 3001 (its own libraries) Container B Memos (Notes) Port 5230 (its own libraries) Container C Any other app Port 9000 (its own libraries) Three containers run side by side on the same Pi, each isolated with its own set of files and libraries. They share the underlying hardware through Docker but cannot interfere with each other or with the main Raspberry Pi OS. Installing Docker The official and recommended way to install Docker on Raspberry Pi OS is to use a script provided by Docker themselves. Here is how. Careful: The installation command below downloads a script from the internet and runs it with administrator rights on your Pi. This is only safe because it comes directly from Docker's own website, which is a trusted source. As a rule, never paste commands that run downloaded scripts unless you trust where they come from. In this case, Docker's official documentation recommends exactly this method for Linux systems. Open a Terminal and download the installer script: curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com -o get-docker.sh curl — a command-line tool for downloading files from the internet. -fsSL — a combination of flags: -f makes curl fail quietly on server errors, -s hides the download progress bar, -S still shows error messages even in silent mode, and -L follows any redirects automatically. https://get.docker.com — the official Docker installation script URL. -o get-docker.sh — saves the downloaded content to a file called get-docker.sh on your Pi rather than running it immediately, so you can inspect it first if you wish. Run the installer: sudo sh get-docker.sh sudo sh get-docker.sh — runs the downloaded script with administrator privileges ( sudo ). This installs the Docker Engine and all its dependencies. You will see a lot of text scrolling past — that is normal. It will take a few minutes. Add your user account to the docker group. By default, only administrators can run Docker commands. Adding yourself to the docker group means you can run them without typing sudo every time: sudo usermod -aG docker $USER sudo usermod — modifies a user account. -aG docker — appends ( -a ) the user to the group ( -G ) called docker . Using -a is critical: without it, the command would replace all your existing groups instead of adding to them, which could lock you out of things. $USER — the shell automatically replaces this with your own username (for example pi ). Careful: Being in the docker group is effectively the same as having administrator access, because Docker can manipulate system files. Only add trusted users to this group on your Pi. This group change does not take effect in your current Terminal session. You must log out and log back in, or simply reboot: sudo reboot sudo reboot — restarts the Pi. After it comes back on (give it about 30 seconds), open a Terminal and your user account will have Docker permissions. After rebooting, open a Terminal and verify Docker is working: docker --version docker run hello-world docker --version — prints the installed Docker version number. A successful output confirms Docker is installed correctly. docker run hello-world — downloads a tiny test container image called hello-world from the internet and runs it. The container prints a friendly success message and then exits on its own. This confirms Docker can pull images from the internet and run containers on your Pi's ARM64 processor. You should see a message that includes "Hello from Docker!" — Docker is ready. Essential Docker Commands Before running a real app, here are the key commands you will use day-to-day.
