These are worth bookmarking — you will reach for them often. Command What it does docker ps Lists all running containers — their names, what image they are based on, and which ports they are listening on. docker ps -a Lists all containers, including stopped ones. docker stop Gracefully stops a running container. Replace with the container's name. docker start Starts a container that has been stopped. docker restart Stops then immediately starts a container — useful after changing settings. docker logs Prints the recent output (messages and errors) from a container — the first place to look when something is not working. docker logs -f Follows the logs in real time as they are written. Press Ctrl + C to stop watching. docker rm Deletes a stopped container. Your data in volumes is kept safe — only the container itself is removed. docker images Lists all downloaded images (the "sealed lunchboxes") on your Pi, with their sizes. docker rmi Deletes a downloaded image from disk to free up storage space. docker pull Downloads an image from Docker Hub without running it yet. docker system prune Cleans up all stopped containers, unused images, and unused networks in one go — useful for reclaiming disk space. It asks for confirmation before deleting anything. In plain words: A Docker image is the recipe — a sealed, downloadable package. A Docker container is what you get when you actually run that recipe — a live, running instance of the app. You can run the same image multiple times to get multiple separate containers, just as you can bake the same recipe multiple times to get multiple cakes. Running Your First Real App: Uptime Kuma Uptime Kuma is a beautiful, free self-hosted monitoring dashboard. You give it a list of websites or services to watch, and it checks them regularly and shows you whether they are up or down — with a clean visual interface and optional alerts. It is a perfect first Docker app because it installs in one command and needs nothing else. Run Uptime Kuma: docker run -d \ --name uptime-kuma \ --restart unless-stopped \ -p 3001:3001 \ -v uptime-kuma-data:/app/data \ louislam/uptime-kuma:1 docker run — the command to create and start a new container. -d — runs the container detached , meaning it runs in the background. You get your Terminal prompt back immediately. --name uptime-kuma — gives this container a human-readable name so you can use it in other commands (like docker stop uptime-kuma ) instead of a random ID. --restart unless-stopped — tells Docker to automatically restart this container if the Pi reboots or if the container crashes, unless you manually stop it with docker stop . This is what makes it feel like a real always-on service. -p 3001:3001 — maps port 3001 on your Pi to port 3001 inside the container . The format is always Pi-port:container-port . This is what lets your browser reach the app from outside the container. -v uptime-kuma-data:/app/data — creates a named storage area managed by Docker called uptime-kuma-data and links it to the folder inside the container where Uptime Kuma stores its data. Without this, all your settings and monitoring history would be lost every time the container is restarted. louislam/uptime-kuma:1 — the image to use. Docker downloads it automatically from Docker Hub (the main public library of images) if it is not already on your Pi. louislam is the developer's account, uptime-kuma is the image name, and :1 is the version tag — the latest version in the 1.x series, which supports ARM64 (your Pi's processor type). The backslash \ at the end of each line simply means "this command continues on the next line" — it is there for readability. You could write the whole thing on one line if you preferred. Docker will download the image (this may take a minute or two the first time, depending on your internet speed) and then start the container. You will see a long container ID printed — that means it is running. Check that it is running: docker ps docker ps — shows all currently running containers. You should see uptime-kuma in the list with a status of Up and the port 0.0.0.0:3001->3001/tcp shown, which means port 3001 on your Pi is connected to port 3001 inside the container. On your Pi's browser, or on any device on your home network, open a browser and go to: http://:3001 Replace with your Pi's actual local IP address — for example http://192.168.1.42:3001 . The :3001 is the port number you mapped in the -p flag. The Uptime Kuma setup page appears. Create an admin account and start adding websites or services to monitor. Tip: The --restart unless-stopped flag means Uptime Kuma will automatically start again every time you reboot your Pi. You never need to remember to start it manually. To stop it permanently, run docker stop uptime-kuma . Docker Compose — Managing Multi-Part Apps Some apps are made of several containers working together — for example, a web application plus a separate database container. Typing a long docker run command for each one is tedious and error-prone. Docker Compose solves this with a single text file that describes all the containers, and one command to start them all. In plain words: A docker-compose.yml file is a recipe card that lists all the containers an app needs, their settings, and how they connect to each other. Running docker compose up reads the card and starts everything in one go. Note: Modern Docker (version 20 and later, which is what you just installed) includes Compose built-in. The command is docker compose (two words, no hyphen). If you see older tutorials using docker-compose (with a hyphen), that is an older separate tool — the built-in version works the same way. Here is an example using Memos , a lightweight private notes app. You type notes into a clean interface and they are stored entirely on your Pi — no third-party server involved. Create a folder for this app and move into it: mkdir ~/memos && cd ~/memos mkdir ~/memos — creates a folder called memos in your home directory. && — runs the second command only if the first one succeeded (a safety check). cd ~/memos — moves into that new folder so the next commands work there. Create the Compose file: nano docker-compose.yml Opens Nano to create a new file called docker-compose.yml . The name and the .yml extension are important — Docker Compose looks for exactly this filename in the current folder. Paste in this content exactly. Indentation matters in YAML files — use spaces, not tabs, and keep the spacing exactly as shown: services: memos: image: neosmemo/memos:stable container_name: memos restart: unless-stopped ports: - "5230:5230" volumes: - ./data:/var/opt/memos services: — the top-level section that lists all the containers this Compose file manages. memos: — the name we give to this service within Compose. It can be anything you like. image: neosmemo/memos:stable — the Docker image to use, pulled automatically from Docker Hub. The :stable tag means the latest stable release. container_name: memos — the name Docker will give the running container, so you can use commands like docker logs memos . restart: unless-stopped — auto-restart on reboot, same as before. ports: - "5230:5230" — maps port 5230 on the Pi to port 5230 inside the container. volumes: - ./data:/var/opt/memos — maps a folder called data in the current directory ( ./data ) to the data folder inside the container. Docker will create the data sub-folder for you automatically the first time. This is where your notes are permanently stored — they survive container restarts and updates. Save and exit Nano: Ctrl + O , Enter , Ctrl + X . Start the app: docker compose up -d docker compose up — reads the docker-compose.yml file in the current folder and creates and starts all the services listed in it. Docker downloads the image if it is not already on your Pi. -d — runs everything in the background (detached), so your Terminal is free again. Visit it on your network by opening a browser on any device and going to: http://:5230 The Memos sign-up page appears. Create an account and start writing private notes — they are stored on your Pi, not on anyone else's server. To stop everything in the Compose file (run this from inside the ~/memos folder): docker compose down docker compose down — stops and removes all the containers defined in the Compose file. Your notes and data stored in the ./data folder are not deleted — they stay safely on your Pi's storage. Run docker compose up -d again at any time to start the app back up. Tip: There is a huge community of self-hosted apps with ready-made Docker Compose files. Good places to discover them are Awesome-Selfhosted (a curated list at github.com/awesome-selfhosted/awesome-selfhosted ) and the r/selfhosted community on Reddit. Home media servers, password managers, recipe organisers, photo libraries, and hundreds more can be running on your Pi in minutes. Updating a Docker Container Docker images are periodically updated by their authors to add features or fix security issues. Updating a container is a three-step process: pull the new image, stop and remove the old container, then run a new container from the updated image. For Compose apps it is even simpler. For a single container (like Uptime Kuma): docker pull louislam/uptime-kuma:1 docker stop uptime-kuma docker rm uptime-kuma docker run -d \ --name uptime-kuma \ --restart unless-stopped \ -p 3001:3001 \ -v uptime-kuma-data:/app/data \ louislam/uptime-kuma:1 docker pull louislam/uptime-kuma:1 — downloads the latest version of the image. Even if the :1 tag has not changed, this fetches any updates published under that tag. docker stop uptime-kuma — gracefully stops the running container. docker rm uptime-kuma — removes the old container. Your data is safe because it lives in the named volume uptime-kuma-data , not inside the container itself. The final docker run block — creates and starts a fresh container from the newly downloaded image, with all the same settings as before. Your data in the volume is automatically reconnected. For a Compose app (like Memos) — from inside the app's folder: cd ~/memos docker compose pull docker compose up -d cd ~/memos — moves into the Memos folder so Docker Compose can find the docker-compose.yml file. docker compose pull — downloads the latest version of every image listed in the Compose file. docker compose up -d — restarts all services using the newly pulled images. Any container whose image has changed is automatically recreated. Your data in the ./data folder is untouched. Tip — Portainer, a graphical Docker dashboard: If you prefer clicking over typing commands, Portainer is a free, self-hosted web interface for managing all your Docker containers, images, and volumes through a browser. You can install it with a single docker run command (search for "Portainer CE install" on their official site at portainer.io ). It makes updating, starting, and stopping containers as easy as clicking a button, and it is a great way to see everything Docker is doing on your Pi at a glance. Reaching Your Pi from Outside Your Home Network Everything so far works only on your home network — devices in your house can reach the Pi, but not anyone on the wider internet. You may wonder: how do I access my Pi when I am away from home, or share something with a friend? Careful — read this before opening your router to the internet. The most obvious method — opening a port on your home router (called "port forwarding") — directly exposes your Pi and everything running on it to the entire internet. Automated bots constantly scan the internet for open ports and attempt to break in. If your Pi is exposed without proper security measures (HTTPS encryption, strong authentication, firewall rules, and regular updates), it is likely to be compromised within hours or days. Do not attempt port forwarding without significant technical knowledge and careful preparation. The good news is that there are modern, safer alternatives that do not require opening any router ports at all. These tools create an encrypted tunnel between your Pi and their servers, so you can reach your Pi securely from anywhere without ever exposing a raw port to the internet. Safer Alternatives to Port Forwarding Tool What it does Free tier? Best for Tailscale Creates a private, encrypted virtual network (a VPN) between your devices. Your Pi gets a stable private IP address accessible from your phone or laptop anywhere in the world, as if they were all on the same home network. No open router ports needed. Yes — free for up to 3 users / 100 devices Personal access to your own Pi from anywhere Cloudflare Tunnel The Pi makes an outgoing connection to Cloudflare's network. Cloudflare gives you a public URL (optionally your own domain name) and routes traffic to your Pi with HTTPS automatically. No open router ports. Yes — free for personal use Sharing a web app publicly with a proper https:// web address Raspberry Pi Connect The Raspberry Pi Foundation's official remote access tool. Lets you reach the Pi desktop or a Terminal through a plain web browser, using your Raspberry Pi account. Very beginner-friendly to set up. Yes — free Remote desktop and Terminal access to the Pi itself Setting Up Tailscale (Recommended for Beginners) Tailscale is the easiest option for personal use — install it on your Pi and on your phone or laptop, sign in with a free account, and your devices can reach each other from anywhere securely, with no technical configuration of your router required. On your Pi, install Tailscale: curl -fsSL https://tailscale.com/install.sh | sudo sh curl -fsSL https://tailscale.com/install.sh — downloads the Tailscale installation script from their official servers. The flags mean the same as before: fail on error, silent, show errors, follow redirects. | sudo sh — the | (called a "pipe") sends the downloaded script directly into sudo sh to run it as administrator. This is the method Tailscale's own documentation recommends for Linux. Connect the Pi to your Tailscale account: sudo tailscale up sudo tailscale up — starts the Tailscale connection and authentication process. It will print a URL in the Terminal. Open that URL on any device — your phone, laptop, or the Pi's own browser — to log in with your Tailscale account (or create a free one). Once you log in, the Pi joins your private Tailscale network immediately. Install Tailscale on your phone or laptop too. Free apps are available for Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android. Visit tailscale.com/download and sign in with the same account you used in the previous step. Find your Pi's Tailscale IP address: tailscale ip -4 tailscale ip -4 — prints your Pi's private Tailscale IP address. It will look something like 100.x.x.x . This address only works when you are connected to Tailscale on both the Pi and the device you are browsing from, but it works from anywhere in the world — your home, a cafe, or another country — through an encrypted connection, with no router ports open. For example, if your Tailscale IP is 100.64.10.5 , you could reach Uptime Kuma from anywhere by visiting http://100.64.10.5:3001 . Note: Tailscale's free tier supports up to 3 users and 100 devices — more than enough for personal and family use. If you ever want to share an app publicly with a real https:// web address that anyone can visit without installing Tailscale, look at Cloudflare Tunnel — but that is a more advanced step beyond this chapter. Quick Reference: Ports Used in This Chapter Service Default port Access URL on your home network Python http.server (temporary) 8080 http://:8080 Nginx (permanent web server) 80 http:// (no port needed) Uptime Kuma (monitoring) 3001 http://:3001 Memos (private notes) 5230 http://:5230 Tip — find your Pi's IP address quickly: Open a Terminal on the Pi and type hostname -I . The first number shown (e.g. 192.168.1.42 ) is your Pi's local IP address. Use that number everywhere you see in this chapter. Key terms Web server — a program that listens for browser requests and sends back web pages in reply. Nginx — a popular, fast, professional web server that runs as a permanent background service on your Pi. IP address — a unique number (like 192.168.1.42 ) that identifies a device on a network. Port — a numbered "door" on a networked device; different services listen on different port numbers so many services can run on the same machine simultaneously. localhost — a special name that always means "this computer itself"; typing http://localhost in a browser on the Pi reaches the Pi's own web server. Docker — software for running applications inside isolated containers on your Pi. Container — a self-contained, isolated running instance of an application, bundled with everything it needs, that cannot interfere with the rest of the system. Image — the sealed, downloadable package from which a container is created; the recipe that Docker runs to produce a container. Docker Hub — the main public online library where Docker images are stored and downloaded from. Volume — a Docker-managed storage area that keeps your data (settings, databases, files) safe even when a container is stopped, updated, or replaced. Docker Compose — a tool that reads a YAML file describing one or more containers and starts them all with a single command. Port forwarding — a router setting that sends incoming internet traffic to a specific device on your home network; risky without expert-level security measures. Tailscale — a free VPN tool that creates a private, encrypted connection between your devices so you can reach your Pi from anywhere without opening any router ports. Cloudflare Tunnel — a free service that gives a Pi-hosted app a public HTTPS web address without opening any router ports. Service / daemon — a program that runs quietly in the background, starting automatically each time the Pi boots, with no Terminal window required. ARM64 — the processor architecture used by the Raspberry Pi 5. When choosing Docker images, look for ones that support linux/arm64 or arm64/v8 — most popular images do. Chapter summary A web server is simply a program that responds to browser requests with web pages — your Pi 5 can be one right now with no special hardware. python3 -m http.server 8080 instantly serves any folder as a temporary website — useful for quick tests but stops when you close the Terminal. Nginx is a proper, always-on web server installed with sudo apt install nginx ; drop HTML files into /var/www/html/ and they are immediately available on your network, even after a reboot. Docker lets you run self-hosted applications as isolated containers — one command installs a complete app without touching anything else on the Pi. Key Docker habits: always use --restart unless-stopped so apps survive reboots; always use a volume ( -v ) so your data is preserved; check docker logs first when something goes wrong. Docker Compose describes multi-container apps in a single docker-compose.yml file and starts everything with docker compose up -d ; updates are as simple as docker compose pull followed by docker compose up -d . Access your apps on the home network at http://: ; use Tailscale, Cloudflare Tunnel, or Raspberry Pi Connect for safe remote access from outside your home — never open raw router ports without expert security knowledge.

title: Run AI on Your Pi
headings: What is an AI language model, in plain English?
How models are measured — and what fits on a Pi
Setting honest expectations before you start
Chatting with a model in the terminal
Controlling the model from a Python script
Using the official Ollama Python library (optional)
Other on-device AI: speech-to-text with Whisper
Simple image recognition with TensorFlow Lite
The Raspberry Pi AI HAT+ — optional hardware for serious speed
Privacy: why running AI locally matters
text: This chapter tackles one of the most exciting things you can do with your 16 GB Raspberry Pi 5: run a genuine artificial-intelligence language model entirely on your own device, with no internet connection required, no cloud subscription, and nothing leaving your home. It is genuinely remarkable — and with honest expectations about speed, completely achievable. What is an AI language model, in plain English? You have probably heard of ChatGPT, Google Gemini, or similar tools that you type questions to and receive surprisingly thoughtful answers. Behind the scenes, each of those services runs a large language model — a piece of software that has been trained to understand and generate human language. In plain words: A "large language model" (LLM) is a program that has read an enormous amount of text — books, websites, articles — and learned the patterns of how words and ideas connect. When you ask it a question, it predicts, word by word, what a useful and sensible answer looks like. It does not truly "think" or "know" things the way a person does, but the results can be remarkably helpful for writing, answering questions, summarising text, and generating code. The difference between what you see on the internet and what you can run on your Pi comes down to model size . The biggest commercial models (the ones powering ChatGPT and Gemini) have hundreds of billions of parameters and require vast data centres filled with specialised hardware. The ones you can run at home are much smaller — but still impressively capable. In plain words: "Parameters" are the millions or billions of internal numbers that a language model learned during training. Think of them like the settings on a very complicated machine. More parameters generally means a smarter model — but also one that needs more memory and runs more slowly. A model with 3 billion parameters is a small, efficient machine; a model with 70 billion parameters is a much larger one that needs far more RAM. How models are measured — and what fits on a Pi Model sizes are described in billions of parameters, written as "B". Common sizes you will encounter include 1B, 3B, 7B, 8B, and 13B. As a rough guide, the bigger the number, the smarter the answers — but also the more RAM needed and the slower it runs. There is a clever technique called quantisation that makes models much more practical for home hardware. In plain words: "Quantisation" is a form of compression applied to an AI model. The original model stores each parameter as a precise 32-bit or 16-bit number. Quantisation rounds those numbers down to 4 bits or 8 bits each — losing a tiny amount of accuracy but shrinking the model to roughly one quarter or one eighth of its original size. A 7B model that would normally need about 14 GB of RAM can, after 4-bit quantisation, fit in around 4–5 GB. The quality difference is usually small enough that you will not notice it for everyday tasks. Your Pi 5 has 16 GB of RAM — four times more than the standard 4 GB model, and twice as much as the 8 GB version. This genuinely matters, because it allows you to run models in the 7B–8B range comfortably, while leaving enough memory for the operating system to run smoothly alongside them. Most other Pis can only manage 1B–3B models without grinding to a halt. Model size Approx. RAM needed (4-bit quantised) Fits on your 16 GB Pi? Speed (tokens/second, approx.) 1B parameters ~1 GB Yes, easily 15–30 tokens/sec (fast) 3B parameters ~2–3 GB Yes, easily 8–15 tokens/sec (comfortable) 7B–8B parameters ~5–6 GB Yes, with room to spare 3–7 tokens/sec (readable) 13B parameters ~9–10 GB Yes, just fits 1–3 tokens/sec (slow but usable) 70B parameters ~45+ GB No — not enough RAM N/A Note: "Tokens per second" is how AI speed is measured. A token is roughly three quarters of a word on average — so 5 tokens per second is about 4 words per second. That is slower than a fast typist but perfectly readable as the text appears on screen, one word at a time. Setting honest expectations before you start Before installing anything, please read this section — it will save you frustration. Speed: Your Pi 5 runs AI on its main processor (CPU), not on a specialised AI chip. Expect text to appear at a readable pace — roughly like watching someone type — not instantly. A 7B model generating a paragraph may take 15–30 seconds. Smaller models are noticeably faster. No image generation: Generating photorealistic images (like Stable Diffusion does) requires a powerful graphics card. The Pi 5 cannot do this at any practical speed. What we cover here is text — asking questions and getting answers. Context length: Small models have a limited "memory" within a conversation. If you have a very long chat, the model may forget what was said at the beginning. Accuracy: Small local models can make mistakes or "hallucinate" (confidently state something false). Always verify important facts from other sources. Privacy: This is the genuine superpower. Everything stays on your device. No company sees your prompts, no data is sent anywhere, and it works with no internet connection at all. For sensitive documents, personal questions, or offline environments, this is a real advantage. Cloud AI (ChatGPT etc.) Your device (prompt typed here) Internet Data Centre Answer returned Your prompts travel over the internet and are processed on remote servers. Requires internet. Data leaves device. Local AI (your Pi 5) Raspberry Pi 5 Prompt ► Ollama ► Model All processing stays here Answer ◄◄◄◄◄◄◄◄ Everything happens inside your Pi. Works offline. Nothing sent anywhere. Private. No subscription needed. Cloud AI sends your prompts across the internet to remote servers. Local AI on your Pi processes everything on your own device — privately, offline, and free. Installing Ollama Ollama is a free, open-source tool that makes running AI models on your own computer as simple as typing one command. It handles downloading models, setting them up, and providing a straightforward way to chat with them. It also runs a small local web server in the background so that programs (like Python scripts) can send it questions and receive answers automatically. Open a Terminal window (click the black screen icon in the taskbar, or go to the Applications menu and look under Accessories). Then type the following command exactly and press Enter: curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh This is a single command split into two parts connected by a pipe ( | ): curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh — curl is a program that fetches content from the internet. The flags -fsSL tell it to fail silently if something goes wrong ( -f ), suppress the progress bar ( -s ), still show errors if they occur ( -S ), and follow any web redirects ( -L ). The result is the Ollama installation script, downloaded directly into memory. | sh — the pipe sends that downloaded script straight to sh (the shell, your command interpreter), which runs it immediately. This is a common one-line installation pattern in Linux. In plain English: download the official Ollama installer and run it. The script detects that you are on a Raspberry Pi (Linux, 64-bit ARM) and installs the correct version automatically. You will see progress messages scrolling past. When you see your terminal prompt ( pi@raspberrypi:~ $ ) again, installation is complete. Careful: Running a script piped directly from the internet grants it full control over your system. Only do this for trusted, well-known projects. Ollama is a reputable open-source project at ollama.com — but as a general rule, always check the URL carefully before running such a command. Confirm the installation was successful by asking Ollama for its version number: ollama --version ollama --version — runs the ollama program with the --version flag, which asks it to print which version is installed. If you see something like ollama version 0.9.x , everything worked. If you see "command not found", close the terminal window, open a fresh one, and try again — a new terminal session picks up the newly installed program. Note: Ollama also installs itself as a background service that starts automatically every time your Pi boots. This means the AI server will always be ready when you want to use it, without any extra steps. Pulling your first model Ollama uses the word "pull" to mean "download a model from the internet and store it on your Pi". You only need to do this once per model — afterwards it lives on your microSD card and works completely offline. In plain words: "Pulling" a model is similar to downloading an app. Once downloaded, you run it locally — no internet needed to use it, only to download it the first time. Start with a small, fast model to make sure everything works. Gemma 3 1B is Google's efficient 1-billion-parameter model, quantised to fit in about 800 MB. It downloads quickly and is a good first test: ollama pull gemma3:1b ollama pull gemma3:1b — tells Ollama to download the Gemma 3 model at the "1b" (1 billion parameter) size. The part after the colon ( :1b ) is the tag , which selects which size or variant you want. Ollama will display a download progress bar. The file is about 815 MB, so on typical home broadband this takes one to three minutes. Once that has downloaded, try a more capable model. Llama 3.2 3B is Meta's 3-billion-parameter model — noticeably smarter than Gemma 1B but still quick on your Pi: ollama pull llama3.2:3b ollama pull llama3.2:3b — downloads Meta's Llama 3.2 model at the 3-billion-parameter size. This is around 2 GB and takes a few minutes. It gives clearly better answers than the 1B model for most everyday tasks, while still running at a comfortable speed. If you want the best quality that fits comfortably in your 16 GB Pi, you can pull an 8-billion-parameter model. This takes longer to download (around 5 GB) and generates text more slowly, but produces impressively thorough answers. The recommended 8B model is Llama 3.1 8B (note: Meta's Llama 3.2 series only goes up to 3B; the 8B model belongs to the Llama 3.1 series): ollama pull llama3.1:8b ollama pull llama3.1:8b — downloads the 8-billion-parameter Llama 3.1 model. At approximately 4.7 GB download size, it uses around 5–6 GB of RAM while running — well within your 16 GB Pi's capacity. Many users find this the best balance of quality and speed for a home device. Expect the download to take 15–30 minutes on typical home broadband. Note: Model names and available tags change over time as new models are released. To see the full catalogue, visit ollama.com/library in your web browser. Popular choices for beginners include gemma3 , llama3.2 , llama3.1 , phi4 (Microsoft — very strong for its size), and mistral (excellent for summarisation). Each model has different strengths; feel free to experiment. To see all the models you have downloaded so far: ollama list ollama list — displays a table of every AI model currently stored on your Pi, including its name, tag, file size, and when it was last used. Use this to keep track of what you have downloaded and how much space each model takes. Chatting with a model in the terminal Now comes the rewarding part. To start a conversation with a model, use ollama run followed by the model name: ollama run llama3.2:3b ollama run llama3.2:3b — loads the Llama 3.2 3B model into your Pi's RAM and starts an interactive chat session right in the terminal. The first time you run a model after a reboot, there may be a short pause of a few seconds while it is loaded into memory. Once you see the >>> prompt appear, the model is ready and waiting for your message. After a brief loading pause, you will see a prompt like this: >>> Send a message (/? for help) The >>> is Ollama's interactive chat prompt. Type your question or message and press Enter. The model will begin generating a response, word by word. When it finishes, the >>> prompt returns and you can ask another question. The model remembers everything said earlier in the session, so you can have a natural back-and-forth conversation. Try typing something like this at the prompt: >>> Explain what a Raspberry Pi is, in two sentences, for someone who has never heard of one. Type this (or any question you like) after the >>> prompt and press Enter. Words will appear one by one at a comfortable reading pace. On a 3B model, a two-sentence answer typically takes about 5–10 seconds. On the 8B model, expect 15–25 seconds for the same question. When you want to end the conversation and return to the normal terminal, type: /bye /bye — a special Ollama command (note the slash at the start, which distinguishes it from a question you would type to the model) that ends the chat session, unloads the model from memory, and returns you to the normal terminal prompt. You can also press Ctrl + D to exit. Tip: Inside an Ollama chat session, type /? and press Enter to see all available slash commands. Useful ones include /clear (start a fresh conversation, making the model forget everything said so far), /show info (display technical details about the currently loaded model), and /set system "..." (give the model a persona or background instructions, for example /set system "You are a friendly French tutor" ). How an Ollama chat session works You type a question Ollama receives prompt AI Model generates reply answer returned, word by word Answer appears Everything stays on your Pi. No internet required. The model remembers your whole conversation until you type /bye. How Ollama processes a chat: your question goes to the local model, which generates a reply word by word — all within your Pi. Controlling the model from a Python script Chatting in the terminal is enjoyable, but the real power comes from writing Python programs that can talk to the AI model automatically. Ollama runs a small web server in the background at all times while it is installed — your programs can send it questions and receive answers using simple web requests. In plain words: A "web server" is a program that listens for requests and sends back responses — just like a website, but running locally on your own Pi. Ollama's built-in server listens at the address http://localhost:11434 . "Localhost" means "this very machine" — the request never leaves your Pi. Your Python script sends a prompt to that address, and Ollama sends back the AI's answer. Open Thonny (the Python editor — find it in the Programming section of the Applications menu). Create a new file, paste in the script below, and save it as ai_chat.py in your home folder. This script uses only Python's built-in libraries, so no extra installation is needed. import urllib.request import json MODEL = "llama3.2:3b" def ask(prompt): url = "http://localhost:11434/api/generate" data = { "model": MODEL, "prompt": prompt, "stream": False } body = json.dumps(data).encode("utf-8") req = urllib.request.Request( url, data=body, headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"}, method="POST" ) with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as response: result = json.loads(response.read().decode("utf-8")) return result["response"] question = "What are three good reasons to learn Python programming?" print("Asking the AI:", question) print() answer = ask(question) print("AI says:") print(answer) Here is what each part of this script does: import urllib.request — loads Python's built-in tool for making web requests. We use this to talk to Ollama's local server. Using the built-in library means no extra packages need to be installed. import json — loads Python's built-in JSON tool. JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a simple text format used to package data — it looks like {"key": "value"} . Ollama communicates using JSON. MODEL = "llama3.2:3b" — stores the model name in a variable so it is easy to change in one place. To use a different model, just update this line. def ask(prompt): — defines a reusable function called ask . You give it a question (the prompt ) and it returns the AI's answer. Everything indented below this line is part of the function. url = "http://localhost:11434/api/generate" — this is Ollama's local web address for text generation. localhost means "this Pi", 11434 is the port Ollama listens on (a port is like a numbered door on a server), and /api/generate is the specific endpoint that accepts prompts. data = {...} — creates a Python dictionary (a collection of labelled values) containing the request. model tells Ollama which model to use, prompt is the question, and "stream": False tells Ollama to wait until the full answer is ready before sending it back all at once (rather than word by word). body = json.dumps(data).encode("utf-8") — converts the Python dictionary into a JSON-formatted text string, then encodes it into bytes (the raw binary format needed for sending over a network). req = urllib.request.Request(...) — builds a web request object specifying the URL, the data to send, a header telling Ollama the data is in JSON format, and POST as the HTTP method (meaning "send data to this address and expect a response"). with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as response: — sends the request to Ollama and opens the response. The with keyword ensures the network connection is cleanly closed when we are done reading. result = json.loads(response.read().decode("utf-8")) — reads the raw bytes of the response, decodes them into a text string, and parses the JSON into a Python dictionary we can work with. return result["response"] — extracts just the AI's text answer from the dictionary and returns it. Ollama's reply contains several fields; the actual generated text is under the key "response" . question = "What are three good reasons..." — stores the question we want to ask. Change this to anything you like. print("Asking the AI:", question) — prints the question to the screen so you can see what was sent. answer = ask(question) — calls our ask function, sending the question to Ollama and waiting for the answer. This may take 10–30 seconds depending on the model and question length. print("AI says:") / print(answer) — prints the AI's response to the output panel at the bottom of Thonny. Note: Before running this script, make sure Ollama is running in the background. Because Ollama installs as a system service, it starts automatically when your Pi boots. You can verify it is running by opening a terminal and typing ollama list — if it shows your models without an error, the server is ready. To run the script in Thonny, click the green Run button (the triangle) in the toolbar, or press F5 . After a wait of 10–30 seconds, you should see the AI's answer printed in the panel at the bottom of Thonny. Tip: Change the question variable to anything you like — ask it to summarise a paragraph of text you paste in, suggest a recipe, explain a concept, or help you draft an email. To use a smaller, faster model, change MODEL to "gemma3:1b" . For more thoughtful answers at the cost of extra waiting time, change it to "llama3.1:8b" . Using the official Ollama Python library (optional) The script above uses only Python's built-in libraries, which is great for learning. However, if you want a cleaner way to work with Ollama in Python, there is an official ollama library that simplifies the code considerably. Because Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm manages system Python packages carefully, the safest way to install it is inside a virtual environment . In plain words: A "virtual environment" is a self-contained folder that holds a private copy of Python and any extra libraries you install into it. It keeps your project's packages separate from the rest of the system, avoiding conflicts. Think of it as a clean, isolated workbench just for one project. Open a terminal and create a folder for your AI project, then create a virtual environment inside it: mkdir ~/ai-project cd ~/ai-project python3 -m venv venv mkdir ~/ai-project — creates a new folder called ai-project in your home directory ( ~ is a shortcut for your home folder). cd ~/ai-project — moves into that new folder. python3 -m venv venv — creates a virtual environment in a subfolder called venv . The -m venv part tells Python to run its built-in virtual environment tool. Activate the virtual environment and install the Ollama library: source venv/bin/activate pip install ollama source venv/bin/activate — activates the virtual environment. Your terminal prompt will change to show (venv) at the start, confirming it is active. While active, any pip install commands install packages only inside this private environment, not system-wide. pip install ollama — downloads and installs the official Ollama Python library from the Python Package Index (PyPI). This is safe inside a virtual environment. Create a new Python file called ai_simple.py in the same folder with the following content: import ollama response = ollama.generate( model="llama3.2:3b", prompt="Explain in two sentences what the Raspberry Pi 5 is good for." ) print(response["response"]) import ollama — loads the Ollama library you just installed. response = ollama.generate(...) — sends a prompt to your locally running Ollama server and waits for the full answer. The model and prompt arguments work just like in the manual version earlier. print(response["response"]) — prints the AI's text answer to the screen. Run the script from the terminal (make sure the virtual environment is still active): python3 ai_simple.py python3 ai_simple.py — runs your Python script. After 10–30 seconds, the AI's answer will be printed in the terminal. When you have finished working in the virtual environment, type deactivate and press Enter to return to the normal terminal. Note: When you return to this project in the future, you will need to activate the virtual environment again before running your scripts: navigate to the folder ( cd ~/ai-project ) and then run source venv/bin/activate . Your prompt will show (venv) to confirm it is active. Managing your models — saving space Each AI model takes up significant space on your microSD card — anywhere from 800 MB to 5 GB or more. To see how much space is currently used, run: ollama list ollama list — shows all downloaded models with their sizes. Use this to decide which models to keep and which to remove. If you want to remove a model you no longer use, simply run: ollama rm llama3.1:8b ollama rm llama3.1:8b — deletes the specified model from your Pi, freeing up the disk space it was using. Replace llama3.1:8b with whichever model name you want to remove. You can always re-download it later with ollama pull . Tip: If your microSD card is getting full, start by removing larger models you do not use regularly. The 8B model takes nearly 5 GB, while the 1B model is under 1 GB. Keep whichever model you use most, and re-download others as needed. Other on-device AI: speech-to-text with Whisper Language models are not the only AI you can run locally. Whisper , made by OpenAI and released as open-source software, is a speech-to-text system — it listens to an audio recording and converts it to written text. A fast compiled version called whisper.cpp runs well on the Pi 5 CPU without needing any cloud service. In plain words: "Speech-to-text" means automatically turning spoken words into written ones — like live captions or a dictation tool. "Compiling from source code" means downloading the program as raw instructions and building it into a runnable application on your own computer. It takes a few minutes but is a one-time step. Installing whisper.cpp requires building it from source code. Here are the full steps: Install the build tools needed to compile the program: sudo apt install -y build-essential git sudo apt install -y build-essential git — installs two packages. build-essential provides the compiler (the tool that turns source code into a runnable program), and git is a tool for downloading source code from the internet. The -y flag automatically confirms all prompts. Download the whisper.cpp source code to your Pi: git clone https://github.com/ggerganov/whisper.cpp git clone https://github.com/ggerganov/whisper.cpp — copies (clones) the entire whisper.cpp project from GitHub onto your Pi into a new folder called whisper.cpp . This is the source code you will compile in the next step. Enter the folder and compile the program: cd whisper.cpp make -j4 cd whisper.cpp — moves into the newly downloaded folder. make -j4 — compiles the source code into a runnable program. The -j4 flag tells make to use all four CPU cores of your Pi 5 simultaneously, which speeds up the build significantly. This step typically takes 2–5 minutes. You will see many lines of output scrolling past — this is normal. Download a small English speech model: bash ./models/download-ggml-model.sh base.en bash ./models/download-ggml-model.sh base.en — runs the download script included with whisper.cpp to fetch the "base" English model. base.en is a fast, reasonably accurate model optimised for English speech. It is about 140 MB. Larger models ( small.en , medium.en ) are more accurate but slower. Transcribe an audio file (it must be in WAV format): ./build/bin/whisper-cli -m models/ggml-base.en.bin -f your_recording.wav ./build/bin/whisper-cli — runs the whisper.cpp transcription program that was built in step 3. The ./ prefix means "in the current folder". -m models/ggml-base.en.bin — tells whisper.cpp which model file to use (the one downloaded in step 4). -f your_recording.wav — specifies the audio file to transcribe. Replace your_recording.wav with the actual filename of your audio file. The file must be in WAV format (you can convert MP3 or other formats using the ffmpeg tool: sudo apt install -y ffmpeg , then ffmpeg -i input.mp3 output.wav ). Note: Whisper can also transcribe other languages and even detect the language automatically, using larger multilingual models (remove the .en from the model name, e.g. base instead of base.en ). It is useful for transcribing voice memos, meeting recordings, or interview audio — entirely on your own device, with no data sent anywhere. Simple image recognition with TensorFlow Lite For basic image recognition (identifying everyday objects in photographs), the Pi 5's VideoCore VII graphics processor can accelerate lightweight models using TensorFlow Lite , which is available directly through the apt package manager. In plain words: "Image recognition" means teaching a computer to identify what is in a photograph — a cat, a car, a banana. TensorFlow Lite is a lightweight version of Google's machine-learning framework, designed specifically for small devices like the Raspberry Pi. It uses pre-trained models, meaning the AI has already been taught to recognise thousands of objects; you just need to give it a photo. sudo apt install -y python3-tflite-runtime sudo apt install -y python3-tflite-runtime — installs TensorFlow Lite for Python 3 directly from the official Raspberry Pi OS software repository. This is the recommended method on Bookworm because it uses the system package manager rather than pip, avoiding any conflicts with the system Python. The -y flag automatically confirms the installation. With TensorFlow Lite installed, you can run pre-trained image classification models to identify everyday objects in photos taken with a Raspberry Pi Camera or loaded from files. The Raspberry Pi Foundation's official documentation at raspberrypi.com/documentation/computers/camera_software.html contains complete step-by-step examples with sample code. Tip: A good beginner project combining TensorFlow Lite and the Pi Camera is a "bird feeder identifier" — a Pi with a camera pointed at a bird feeder that automatically logs which species visit, entirely without a cloud service. The Raspberry Pi AI HAT+ — optional hardware for serious speed If you find that the Pi 5's CPU speed is too slow for your AI ambitions, there is an optional add-on board made by the Raspberry Pi Foundation called the AI HAT+ . It contains a Hailo-8L neural network accelerator chip that connects to the Pi's PCIe slot. In plain words: A "neural network accelerator" is a chip specially designed to perform the mathematical operations that AI models need, far faster than a general-purpose CPU can. Think of it as adding a dedicated AI co-processor to your Pi. The PCIe slot (a small connector on the underside of the Pi 5 board) is a high-speed data connection; the AI HAT+ uses it to communicate at maximum speed. The AI HAT+ provides up to 13 TOPS (Tera Operations Per Second) of AI processing power, which is roughly 10–20 times faster than the Pi 5 CPU alone for vision tasks. It is designed particularly for real-time video analysis — detecting people, vehicles, faces, or objects in a live camera stream at full frame rates. Task type Best approach on Pi 5 Why Chat / text generation (LLMs) Ollama on CPU LLMs run on CPU RAM; AI HAT+ does not accelerate them significantly Real-time object detection in video AI HAT+ (optional) HAT+ is 10–20× faster for vision models; CPU is too slow for real-time video Speech-to-text (Whisper) CPU (whisper.cpp) Works well on Pi 5 CPU; HAT+ does not help here Image classification (TensorFlow Lite) CPU or AI HAT+ CPU fine for single images; HAT+ needed for live video classification Note: The AI HAT+ is available from official Raspberry Pi retailers for approximately £50–70 (around €55–80 in mainland Europe). Installation involves fitting it onto the 40-pin GPIO header and connecting a short ribbon cable to the PCIe slot — straightforward but it adds significant height, so check your case has room (an open-top or tall case works best). Privacy: why running AI locally matters Cloud AI services — ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini, and others — are powerful, but every question you type is sent to servers owned by a company, stored, potentially used to improve future models, and subject to that company's privacy policy, data protection laws, and any future policy changes. When you run AI on your Pi: Your prompts never leave your home network. Your questions are not stored or logged by any company. It works with no internet connection at all — useful on a train, in a remote location, or anywhere connectivity is limited or expensive. There is no subscription fee. Once downloaded, the model is yours to use indefinitely. You are in complete control of what model is running and how it behaves. This makes local AI genuinely useful for tasks involving personal information — summarising private documents, asking questions about medical or financial topics you would rather keep private, or working with confidential text. Tip: If you would like a proper graphical chat interface (similar to the ChatGPT website, but talking to your local models), search for Open WebUI — a free, open-source web application that connects to Ollama and runs on your Pi. You access it by opening a browser on your Pi and going to http://localhost:3000 after installation. Full instructions are at openwebui.com . Troubleshooting common problems Ollama says "command not found" after installation Close your terminal window and open a fresh one. The installation adds Ollama to your PATH (the list of locations the terminal searches for commands), and a new terminal session picks up the change automatically. If the problem persists, type the following and try again: source ~/.bashrc ollama --version source ~/.bashrc — reloads your shell configuration file without closing and reopening the terminal. This picks up any changes made to your PATH during installation. ollama --version — checks whether Ollama is now found and prints its version number. If this still fails, try restarting your Pi ( sudo reboot ) and trying again. The model download is very slow AI models are large files — 1–5 GB is normal. On a typical home broadband connection this takes anywhere from 5 minutes to half an hour. Connect your Pi via an Ethernet cable rather than Wi-Fi for a faster and more reliable download. Downloads can be resumed — if a download is interrupted, just run the same ollama pull command again and it will continue from where it left off. Running a model makes the Pi very sluggish While a large model is generating text, it uses most of the Pi's CPU. This is normal and expected — wait for the response to finish and the Pi will return to its normal responsiveness. If things are uncomfortably slow, switch to a smaller model (for example, gemma3:1b instead of llama3.1:8b ). You can also close other applications while the model is generating. The Python script says "Connection refused" Ollama's background server may not be running. Check its status with: sudo systemctl status ollama sudo systemctl status ollama — checks whether the Ollama background service is currently running. You will see either Active: active (running) highlighted in green, meaning all is well, or a stopped or failed status. If it is not running, start it with the next command. If it is stopped, start it manually: sudo systemctl start ollama sudo systemctl start ollama — starts the Ollama service immediately. To make it start automatically every time the Pi boots (which is the default after installation), run sudo systemctl enable ollama . The model gives wrong or strange answers This is a known limitation of all current language models, especially smaller ones. It is called hallucination — the model confidently produces text that sounds plausible but is factually incorrect. Always verify important information from a reliable source. Smaller models hallucinate more often than larger ones. Providing more context in your prompt often helps: instead of "What is the boiling point of water?", try "You are a physics teacher. Please explain the boiling point of water at sea level." Whisper.cpp build fails with an error Make sure build-essential and git are installed (run sudo apt install -y build-essential git again). Also ensure you have enough free disk space — the build process temporarily needs several hundred megabytes. Run df -h ~ to check how much free space you have on your microSD card. df -h ~ df -h ~ — shows the disk usage of the filesystem where your home folder lives. The -h flag makes the sizes human-readable (showing GB or MB rather than raw bytes). The "Available" column tells you how much free space remains. You need at least 1 GB free for the build, plus space for model files. Key terms Large Language Model (LLM) — a type of AI program trained on vast amounts of text, capable of understanding and generating human language. Parameters — the numerical values learned during AI training; measured in billions (e.g. 7B = 7 billion). More parameters generally means a more capable but larger, slower model. Quantisation — a compression technique that reduces a model's file size and RAM usage by storing its numbers at lower precision, with only a small loss of quality. Ollama — a free, open-source tool for downloading and running AI language models locally on your own device. Tag — the part after the colon in an Ollama model name (e.g. :3b , :8b ) that specifies which size or variant of a model to download. Token — roughly three quarters of a word; the unit AI models use internally. "Tokens per second" measures how fast a model generates text. Localhost — a special network address meaning "this computer itself". Ollama's local server is accessed at http://localhost:11434 , which never leaves your Pi. Port — a numbered "door" on a server that allows different services to listen on the same machine. Ollama uses port 11434. API — Application Programming Interface; a defined way for programs to talk to each other. Ollama provides an API so Python scripts can send prompts and receive answers automatically. Virtual environment — a self-contained folder holding a private copy of Python and its installed packages, keeping a project's dependencies separate from the rest of the system. Hallucination — when an AI model confidently generates text that is factually incorrect. A known limitation of all current language models, more common in smaller models. Whisper / whisper.cpp — an open-source speech-to-text AI made by OpenAI; whisper.cpp is a fast compiled version that runs efficiently on the Pi 5 CPU. TensorFlow Lite — a lightweight machine-learning framework for small devices, used for image classification and other AI tasks on the Pi without a cloud service. AI HAT+ — an optional Raspberry Pi add-on board containing a Hailo neural network accelerator chip, dramatically speeding up real-time vision AI tasks. PCIe — a high-speed hardware connection on the Pi 5 used by add-on boards like the AI HAT+ to communicate at fast data rates. TOPS — Tera Operations Per Second; a measure of AI chip performance. The AI HAT+'s Hailo chip delivers up to 13 TOPS. Chapter summary A large language model (LLM) is an AI program trained on text; it generates answers word by word based on patterns it learned during training. Model size is measured in billions of parameters (1B, 3B, 7B, 8B…); larger models give better answers but need more RAM and run more slowly. Quantisation compresses models to roughly a quarter of their original size with minimal quality loss, making 7B–8B models practical on home hardware. Your 16 GB Pi 5 can comfortably run 7B–8B quantised models — far more capable than what fits in the 4 GB or 8 GB versions. Ollama installs with a single terminal command and handles downloading, storing, and running models automatically; it also starts as a background service on every boot. Use ollama pull <name> to download a model, ollama run <name> to chat interactively, and ollama list to see what is stored. Note that Llama 3.2 only comes in 1B and 3B sizes; the recommended 8B model is llama3.1:8b . A Python script using only built-in libraries can send prompts to Ollama's local API and display the AI's answers; the optional ollama Python library simplifies this further when used inside a virtual environment. Whisper.cpp provides offline speech-to-text; TensorFlow Lite enables image recognition — both run on the Pi CPU without any cloud service. The optional Raspberry Pi AI HAT+ (Hailo accelerator) dramatically speeds up vision tasks like real-time object detection; it does not significantly help text generation. Running AI locally means complete privacy — your prompts never leave your device, no subscription is needed, and it works with no internet connection. Expect text to appear at a readable but modest pace; small models can hallucinate (state incorrect facts confidently), so always verify important information elsewhere.

title: Security & Good Habits
headings: Step One: Change the Default Password
Step Two: Keep the System Updated
Step Three: SSH Keys — Log In Without a Password
Step Four: A Simple Firewall with ufw
Step Five: Do Not Expose the Pi Directly to the Internet
Step Six: fail2ban — Blocking Repeated Bad Login Attempts
Step Seven: Disable Unused Interfaces with raspi-config
Step Eight: Backups as a Security Measure
text: Your Raspberry Pi 5 is a capable little computer — and like any computer connected to a network, it deserves a few sensible precautions. This chapter walks you through the most important habits: locking down access, keeping software fresh, adding a firewall, and protecting the hardware itself. None of it requires a security background — just a few minutes of your time and a willingness to follow the steps. Why Bother with Security? A Raspberry Pi running on your home network is unlikely to be attacked within minutes of being switched on. But over time, a few real risks build up: Anyone on your Wi-Fi — a guest, a compromised smart TV, or a neighbour who knows your password — could log in to the Pi if it still uses the default password. If you ever open the Pi to the internet, even for a few minutes, automated scanners called "bots" will find it and try common passwords within hours. An out-of-date system may have known security holes that are trivially exploited. The good news is that a handful of straightforward steps make the Pi extremely resistant to the vast majority of threats, without turning your life into a cybersecurity course. Step One: Change the Default Password When you first set up Raspberry Pi OS, the installer asked you to create a username and password. If you skipped that step or used something obvious like raspberry , now is the time to fix it. Careful: The old default username was pi and the old default password was raspberry . Many automated attack scripts try this combination first. If your Pi still uses them, change both immediately. What makes a strong password? A strong password is long, random, and unique — used nowhere else. You do not need to memorise a string of symbols; a passphrase made of four or five random words is both memorable and very secure. For example: kettle-purple-moon-46-fence is far stronger than P@ssw0rd! . In plain words: A passphrase is a password made of several words strung together. Length beats complexity — a 30-character passphrase of common words is harder to crack than an 8-character mix of symbols. To change your password, open a Terminal on the Pi (or connect via SSH) and run: passwd This command opens the "change password" tool for your own user account. It will ask you to type your current password, then ask you to type the new password twice to confirm it. The characters you type will not appear on screen — this is normal and deliberate. Tip: Use a password manager (such as Bitwarden, which is free) to generate and store a strong, unique password. You only need to remember one master password, and the manager handles everything else. Checking for other user accounts On a freshly set-up Pi 5 running Bookworm there should only be your own user account (plus the system root account that runs in the background). It is worth confirming no unexpected accounts exist: awk -F: '$3 >= 1000 && $1 != "nobody" { print $1 }' /etc/passwd This command reads the file /etc/passwd (which lists every user account on the system) and prints only the ones with a user ID of 1000 or above. Those are the "real" human user accounts. On a fresh Pi you should see just your own username. If you see names you do not recognise, investigate before continuing. Note: The root account is a special all-powerful administrator account built into Linux. On Raspberry Pi OS, the root account does not have a password set and cannot be logged into directly — you use sudo instead. Do not set a root password unless you have a specific reason to. Step Two: Keep the System Updated Software updates fix security vulnerabilities — holes that attackers could use to take control. Running apt regularly is one of the single most effective things you can do. In plain words: apt is the Raspberry Pi OS package manager — the tool that downloads and installs software and updates from the official Raspberry Pi and Debian servers. We covered this in detail in Chapter 6. As a recap, run these two commands: sudo apt update sudo apt full-upgrade -y Line 1 — sudo apt update : Downloads the latest list of available packages and versions from the internet. It does not change anything on your system yet — it only refreshes the catalogue. Line 2 — sudo apt full-upgrade -y : Installs every available update, including updates that require removing or replacing existing packages (which is what full-upgrade does that plain upgrade does not). The -y flag answers "yes" automatically to any confirmation prompts. Tip: Make this a habit — run it once a week, or at least once a month. It takes only a minute or two on a fast connection. Automatic security updates If you want the Pi to install security-related updates on its own in the background, you can install the unattended-upgrades package: sudo apt install unattended-upgrades -y sudo dpkg-reconfigure --priority=low unattended-upgrades Line 1: Installs the unattended-upgrades tool, which can apply security updates automatically without you needing to run apt manually. Line 2: Opens a simple text-based configuration screen asking whether you want automatic updates enabled. Choose Yes . The tool will then download and apply official security patches in the background each day. Note: Unattended-upgrades only installs security updates automatically. Major version upgrades and new software still require your manual approval. Step Three: SSH Keys — Log In Without a Password In Chapter 11 you learned to connect to the Pi remotely using SSH (Secure Shell). By default, SSH asks for your password every time. There is a smarter, more secure method: SSH keys . Once set up, you never type a password to SSH in — and you can disable password login entirely, which blocks automated attackers completely. What is an SSH key pair? In plain words: An SSH key pair is a pair of matching digital files — a public key (like a padlock) and a private key (like the only key that opens that padlock). You put the public key (the padlock) on the Pi. You keep the private key (the opening key) on your Windows PC. When you connect, your PC proves it holds the matching key — without ever sending the key itself over the network. No password is needed. The private key must stay on your Windows PC and never be shared. The public key can be placed on any number of servers — it is safe to share because it can only be used to verify the private key, never to impersonate it. Windows PC Private Key (secret) Keep this file safe! proves match (no password) Raspberry Pi Public Key (padlock) ~/.ssh/authorized_keys You keep this Pi stores this How SSH key authentication works: your PC holds the private key; the Pi holds the matching public key. A connection is granted only when the two match — no password is transmitted. Generating a key pair on Windows 11 Windows 11 comes with a built-in SSH client, so you do not need to install anything extra. Open a PowerShell window on your Windows PC (press Win + X and choose "Terminal" or "PowerShell"). In the PowerShell window, type the following and press Enter: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "my-pi-key" ssh-keygen : The key-generation program built into Windows 11. -t ed25519 : Tells it to use the Ed25519 algorithm — a modern, fast, secure algorithm that produces short keys. This is the recommended choice over the older RSA algorithm. -C "my-pi-key" : Adds a comment label to the key so you can identify it later (you can use any text you like here). The program asks: Enter file in which to save the key . Press Enter to accept the default location ( C:\Users\YourName\.ssh\id_ed25519 ). Two files will be created: id_ed25519 — your private key. Never share this file. id_ed25519.pub — your public key. This is the one you will copy to the Pi. The program then asks for a passphrase . This is an optional extra layer of protection: if someone steals the private key file, they still cannot use it without this passphrase. You can press Enter twice to skip it, but setting a passphrase is recommended — Windows will remember it for you via a feature called the SSH Agent, so you only type it once per Windows session. Note: If you already have a key pair from a previous project (you see a message like "already exists"), you can reuse it — just press n when asked to overwrite, and skip to the next section. Copying the public key to the Pi Now you need to place the public key into a special file on the Pi called ~/.ssh/authorized_keys . There are two ways to do this. In plain words: The tilde ( ~ ) is a shortcut that means "your home folder". So ~/.ssh/authorized_keys means the file named authorized_keys inside the hidden .ssh folder inside your home folder on the Pi. Method A — using ssh-copy-id (easiest, from Git Bash on Windows) Windows 11's built-in PowerShell does not include ssh-copy-id , but if you have Git for Windows installed (which gives you Git Bash), you can use: ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub yourname@raspberrypi.local ssh-copy-id : A helper tool that reads your public key and appends it to the authorized_keys file on the remote machine automatically. -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub : Tells it which public key file to use. yourname@raspberrypi.local : Replace yourname with the username you chose when you set up the Pi, and raspberrypi.local with the Pi's hostname or IP address. It will ask for your Pi's password one last time to authenticate and copy the key. Method B — paste it manually (works from plain PowerShell on Windows) In PowerShell on your Windows PC, display the contents of your public key: Get-Content "$env:USERPROFILE\.ssh\id_ed25519.pub" This PowerShell command reads and prints the contents of your public key file to the screen. The output is one long line starting with ssh-ed25519 . Select it all and copy it to your clipboard (Ctrl+C). Now SSH into the Pi using your password as normal: ssh yourname@raspberrypi.local Opens an SSH session to the Pi, logging in with your password as before. Replace yourname and raspberrypi.local with your actual username and Pi address. On the Pi, create the .ssh directory if it does not already exist, and open the authorized_keys file: mkdir -p ~/.ssh chmod 700 ~/.ssh nano ~/.ssh/authorized_keys Line 1 — mkdir -p ~/.ssh : Creates the hidden .ssh folder in your home directory. The -p flag means "don't complain if it already exists". Line 2 — chmod 700 ~/.ssh : Sets the folder's permissions so that only your own user account can read or write it. SSH refuses to work if the folder permissions are too open. Line 3 — nano ~/.ssh/authorized_keys : Opens the nano text editor to create (or edit) the authorized_keys file. In the nano editor, paste the public key you copied from Windows (right-click in the terminal window to paste, or use Ctrl+Shift+V). It must be all on one single line. Press Ctrl + X , then Y , then Enter to save and exit. Set correct permissions on the file: chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys Sets the authorized_keys file to be readable and writable only by your own user. SSH will refuse to use the file if anyone else can read it — this permission setting satisfies that requirement. Testing the key login Without closing your current SSH session (keep it open as a safety net in case something goes wrong), open a new PowerShell window and try connecting: ssh yourname@raspberrypi.local If the key is set up correctly, the Pi will log you in without asking for a password — it silently verified your private key against the stored public key. If it still asks for a password, re-check that you pasted the key correctly on a single line with no extra spaces, and that the file permissions on the Pi are exactly 700 for ~/.ssh and 600 for ~/.ssh/authorized_keys . Optionally disabling password login (advanced — read carefully first) Once key login is confirmed to be working, you can disable password authentication entirely. This means only computers that hold the correct private key can log in via SSH — brute-force password guessing becomes impossible. Careful: If you disable password login and then lose your private key (for example, your Windows PC fails and you had no backup), you will be permanently locked out of SSH. Before doing this, either back up your key files to a USB drive or cloud storage, or make sure you have a keyboard and monitor you can plug into the Pi so you can still log in locally. Confirm key login works perfectly before taking this step. On the Pi, open the SSH server configuration file: sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config Opens the SSH server configuration file in the nano text editor with administrator ( sudo ) privileges. This file controls how the SSH server behaves. Find the line that says PasswordAuthentication . If it starts with a # , that means it is commented out (ignored). Remove the # and change the line to read exactly: PasswordAuthentication no This line tells the SSH server to refuse password-based login attempts. Only key-based authentication will be accepted. Make sure the line does not start with a # character — a # at the start means the setting is ignored. Save the file ( Ctrl + X , then Y , then Enter ), then restart the SSH service: sudo systemctl restart ssh Restarts the SSH server so it reads the new configuration. Your current SSH session stays open — the restart only affects new connections from this point onward. Test immediately by opening a fresh PowerShell window and connecting again. If it works, you are done. If it does not, your existing session is still open so you can undo the change — re-open the file and set PasswordAuthentication yes , then restart ssh again. Tip: You can also change the default SSH port from 22 to a high, non-standard port number (for example 2222 or 51234). This does not stop a determined attacker but does dramatically reduce the number of automated probing attempts that reach the Pi. To do this, add a line Port 2222 to /etc/ssh/sshd_config , then run sudo ufw allow 2222/tcp before restarting ssh . When connecting you would then use ssh -p 2222 yourname@raspberrypi.local . Step Four: A Simple Firewall with ufw In plain words: A firewall is a gatekeeper that decides which network connections are allowed in and which are blocked. ufw stands for "Uncomplicated Firewall" — it is a beginner-friendly tool built on top of Linux's powerful but complex built-in firewall system. For a home Pi, the default Raspberry Pi OS setup is fairly safe already, but adding ufw gives you explicit control and an extra layer of defence if you ever install a new service by accident. Install ufw: sudo apt install ufw -y Downloads and installs ufw from the official Raspberry Pi OS software repository. The -y flag confirms the installation automatically. Allow SSH connections — do this before enabling the firewall, otherwise you will lock yourself out of remote access: sudo ufw allow ssh Tells ufw to always permit incoming connections on the SSH port (port 22). Without this rule, enabling the firewall would immediately cut off your remote access. If you are running a web server on the Pi and want to allow normal web traffic, add these rules too — skip them if you have no web server: sudo ufw allow 80/tcp sudo ufw allow 443/tcp Line 1: Allows unencrypted web traffic (HTTP) on port 80. Line 2: Allows encrypted web traffic (HTTPS) on port 443. Enable the firewall: sudo ufw enable Turns on the firewall immediately and configures it to start automatically every time the Pi boots. It will warn you that existing SSH connections may be disrupted — type y to confirm. Because you added the SSH rule in step 2, SSH connections will continue to work fine. Check the current status and active rules: sudo ufw status verbose Prints a summary of whether ufw is active and lists all the rules currently in effect — which ports are allowed or blocked, and in which direction. You should see Status: active and a rule permitting SSH. Here is what a typical ufw status looks like for a Pi used for SSH access and a web server: To (port) Action From 22/tcp (SSH) ALLOW IN Anywhere 80/tcp ALLOW IN Anywhere 443/tcp ALLOW IN Anywhere Everything else DENY IN Anywhere Note: ufw blocks incoming connections by default while allowing all outgoing connections. This means the Pi can freely browse the web, download updates, and contact external services — only unsolicited connections arriving from outside are filtered. Step Five: Do Not Expose the Pi Directly to the Internet This is one of the most important rules in this chapter. Never open ports on your home router to forward traffic directly to your Pi unless you are an experienced network administrator who understands the implications. Here is why: The moment a port is open to the internet, automated scanners will find it — usually within an hour. Even with a strong password and SSH keys, a misconfigured service or an unpatched vulnerability can be exploited. Home internet connections typically have a dynamic IP address that changes, making direct access unreliable anyway. Instead, use one of these safer approaches: Tool What it does Best for Tailscale Creates a private, encrypted virtual network between your devices. Only your approved devices can reach the Pi. SSH access from anywhere; connecting Pi to your laptop and phone securely. Raspberry Pi Connect Official Raspberry Pi remote desktop and shell service. Free, easy, no router configuration needed. Beginners who want to see the Pi's desktop from another computer. Cloudflare Tunnel Publishes a web service running on the Pi through Cloudflare's network, with HTTPS and DDoS protection built in. Sharing a website or web app running on the Pi with the public. Tip: Tailscale is free for personal use with up to 100 devices and is the simplest way to access your Pi securely from anywhere. Install it on Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm using Tailscale's official installer script — do not use a plain apt install as the package is not in the default Raspberry Pi OS repository. Open a Terminal on the Pi and run: curl -fsSL https://tailscale.com/install.sh | sh This downloads and runs the official Tailscale installation script directly from tailscale.com. The script detects your operating system (Debian Bookworm on a Pi 5), adds the correct package repository, and installs Tailscale. After it completes, run sudo tailscale up and follow the link it shows to sign in and approve the Pi in your Tailscale account. Careful: Running a script piped directly from the internet (the curl … | sh pattern) is only safe when you trust the source completely. Only do this with well-known, reputable services such as Tailscale, and always verify you are typing the URL correctly. Step Six: fail2ban — Blocking Repeated Bad Login Attempts In plain words: fail2ban watches your system's log files for repeated failed login attempts and automatically blocks the IP address of whoever is trying. Think of it as a bouncer who notices someone trying the wrong door code five times in a row and then bars the door to them for an hour. Even if you have SSH keys enabled and password login disabled, fail2ban is good practice: it reduces log clutter and slows down any scanners that probe your Pi. Install fail2ban: sudo apt install fail2ban -y Downloads and installs fail2ban from the software repository. Once installed, it starts running automatically in the background and begins watching the SSH login logs immediately. Create a local configuration file so your settings survive future package updates: sudo cp /etc/fail2ban/jail.conf /etc/fail2ban/jail.local Copies the default configuration file to a new file called jail.local . fail2ban always reads jail.local in preference to jail.conf , so any customisations you make here will not be overwritten when fail2ban is updated. Check that the SSH protection is active: sudo fail2ban-client status sshd Asks the fail2ban service to report the status of its SSH "jail". You should see that the jail is active and a count of currently banned IP addresses (probably zero on a freshly set-up Pi). If the command returns "sshd is not a valid jail", try sudo fail2ban-client status ssh instead. The default settings ban an IP address for 10 minutes after five failed login attempts within 10 minutes. You can adjust these values in /etc/fail2ban/jail.local if you wish, but the defaults are sensible for most home Pi setups. Step Seven: Disable Unused Interfaces with raspi-config The raspi-config tool lets you switch hardware interfaces (SSH, VNC, the camera connector, and so on) on or off. Disabling anything you are not using is good security practice — an interface that is switched off cannot be attacked. In plain words: An interface here means a communication channel — for example, the SSH network service, or the I2C bus used by electronic sensors. If you are not using it, turning it off removes a potential entry point. sudo raspi-config Opens the Raspberry Pi Configuration tool in the terminal. Use the arrow keys to navigate and Enter to select. Go to Interface Options to enable or disable SSH, VNC, the camera connector, I2C, SPI, and other interfaces. Select Finish when done; the Pi may ask you to reboot.
