Think of them like a lock on a filing cabinet — only authorised people have the key. Command What it does sudo <command> Run any command as the system administrator ("superuser"). You will be asked for your password the first time in a session. chmod +x <file> Make a file executable — allows you to run it as a program. chmod 644 <file> Set standard file permissions: owner can read & write; everyone else can only read. chmod 755 <file> Set standard program permissions: owner can read, write & run; everyone else can read & run. chown <user>:<group> <file> Change the owner (and optionally the group) of a file. chown -R <user>:<user> <folder> Give a specific user ownership of a folder and everything inside it ( -R means "recursive"). Replace <user> with your actual username (e.g. pi ). ls -l <file> Show a file's current permissions in detail — the string of r , w , and x letters tells you who can read, write, and execute it. whoami Print the name of the currently logged-in user. groups List all the groups the current user belongs to (useful for checking GPIO and camera access). sudo usermod -aG <group> <user> Add a user to a group (e.g. sudo usermod -aG gpio pi gives the pi user access to GPIO pins). Log out and back in for the change to take effect. Tip: If a command refuses with "Permission denied", try putting sudo in front of it. But only use sudo when genuinely needed — running everything as superuser all the time is risky, like always working as a Windows Administrator. 4 — Installing and Managing Software Raspberry Pi OS uses a tool called apt (Advanced Package Tool) to download and install software from the internet — similar to an app store, but operated entirely from the terminal. In plain words: A package is a bundle containing a program plus everything it needs to run. The package manager ( apt ) handles downloading, installing, and updating packages for you automatically. Command What it does sudo apt update Refresh the list of available packages and their latest versions (does NOT yet install anything). sudo apt full-upgrade Download and install all available updates to packages already on your Pi (preferred over apt upgrade on Raspberry Pi OS). sudo apt install <package> Download and install a specific package (e.g. sudo apt install tree ). sudo apt install <pkg1> <pkg2> Install multiple packages in one command by listing their names separated by spaces. sudo apt remove <package> Uninstall a package, but keep its configuration files. sudo apt purge <package> Uninstall a package and delete its configuration files completely. sudo apt autoremove Remove packages that were installed as dependencies but are no longer needed by anything. apt search <keyword> Search the package list for programs matching a keyword (no sudo needed for searching). apt show <package> Show detailed information about a package before you install it. dpkg -l | grep <name> Check whether a particular package is already installed on your Pi. apt list --installed List every package currently installed on the Pi. Note: Always run sudo apt update before sudo apt full-upgrade or sudo apt install . The update step fetches the current catalogue; without it, apt may try to install an outdated version. One-line Recipe: Update Everything To refresh, upgrade, and tidy up in a single command, you can chain these three instructions together with && (which means "and then, only if the previous step succeeded"): sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y && sudo apt autoremove -y sudo apt update — fetches the latest list of available packages from the internet. && — only runs the next command if the previous one finished without errors. sudo apt full-upgrade -y — installs all available updates; -y automatically answers "yes" to any confirmation prompts. && sudo apt autoremove -y — removes any packages that are no longer needed, keeping your Pi tidy. 5 — Python on Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm Python 3 is pre-installed on Raspberry Pi OS. However, since the Bookworm release (Debian 12), the system Python is externally managed — meaning you cannot install Python libraries into it with plain pip install without extra steps. This protects the operating system from accidentally broken packages. Here is what to use instead. In plain words: A virtual environment (venv) is a private, self-contained copy of Python just for one project. Libraries you install there do not affect anything else on the Pi. Think of it as a separate toolbox for each job. Command What it does python3 --version Show which version of Python 3 is installed. python3 <script.py> Run a Python script file. python3 -m venv <name> Create a new virtual environment in a folder called <name> (e.g. python3 -m venv myenv ). source <name>/bin/activate Activate the virtual environment — your prompt will change to show its name. Now pip install is safe to use. deactivate Leave the virtual environment and return to the normal system Python. pip install <library> Install a Python library — only run this after activating a virtual environment . pip list Show all libraries installed in the current virtual environment. pip freeze > requirements.txt Save the list of installed libraries to a file (useful for recreating the same environment later). sudo apt install python3-<name> Install a Python library as a system package via apt — the safe alternative to pip for the system Python (e.g. sudo apt install python3-pygame ). thonny Launch the Thonny IDE — the beginner-friendly Python editor that comes pre-installed and manages its own Python environment safely. Careful: On Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm, running pip install <library> directly (without activating a virtual environment first) will produce an error: "externally-managed-environment" . This is intentional. Either activate a virtual environment first, or install via sudo apt install python3-<name> . 6 — System Information These commands let you peek under the bonnet of your Pi — checking temperature, memory, disk space, and more. Command What it does df -h Show disk space usage for all storage drives in human-readable sizes (GB/MB). free -h Show how much RAM is being used and how much is still free, in human-readable form. vcgencmd measure_temp Report the current CPU temperature (e.g. temp=47.8'C ) — great for checking if your Active Cooler is working. vcgencmd get_throttled Check whether the Pi is throttling (slowing down) due to overheating or low voltage. 0x0 means all is well; any other value flags a problem. vcgencmd measure_volts core Show the current core voltage — useful for diagnosing under-voltage warnings. hostname -I Show the IP address(es) assigned to your Pi on the local network. uname -a Print detailed information about the operating system kernel version and hardware architecture. cat /proc/cpuinfo Show detailed CPU information including the hardware model — confirm it shows a Raspberry Pi 5. cat /etc/os-release Show which version of Raspberry Pi OS (Bookworm, etc.) is installed. fastfetch Display a colourful system summary (CPU, RAM, OS version, uptime). Install with sudo apt install fastfetch if missing. top Show a live, updating list of running programs and their CPU/memory usage. Press q to quit. htop A friendlier, colour-coded version of top . Install with sudo apt install htop if missing. uptime Show how long the Pi has been running since it was last switched on. lsusb List all USB devices currently plugged in to your Pi. lsblk List all storage devices and partitions (useful for spotting USB drives or NVMe SSDs). lspci List devices connected on the PCIe bus — on the Pi 5 this includes any NVMe SSD fitted to an M.2 HAT. Tip: Run vcgencmd measure_temp a few minutes after the Pi has been on and working hard. A healthy temperature with the Active Cooler fitted is typically 40–60 °C under load. Anything consistently above 80 °C is worth investigating — check that the cooler fan is spinning. Throttling Status Quick-Reference The number returned by vcgencmd get_throttled is a bitmask. Here are the most common values and what they mean: Value Meaning 0x0 All clear — no problems detected. 0x1 Under-voltage currently detected — check your power supply. The official 27 W USB-C supply is recommended. 0x2 Arm frequency is currently being throttled (speed reduced) due to heat or voltage. 0x4 Currently throttled — the Pi is running slower than normal. 0x50000 Under-voltage has occurred since last boot (even if not happening right now). 7 — Managing Services A service (also called a daemon ) is a program that runs in the background — for example the web server, SSH, or your own Python scripts set to start at boot. The systemctl command controls them all. In plain words: A service is a background program that keeps running quietly without a window, doing a job such as serving web pages or listening for SSH connections. systemctl is like the master on/off switch for every background program on the Pi. Command What it does systemctl status <service> Show whether a service is running or stopped, and its recent log messages. sudo systemctl start <service> Start a service immediately (until the next reboot). sudo systemctl stop <service> Stop a running service immediately. sudo systemctl restart <service> Stop then start a service — useful after changing its configuration file. sudo systemctl reload <service> Ask a service to re-read its configuration without fully stopping (not all services support this). sudo systemctl enable <service> Make a service start automatically every time the Pi boots. sudo systemctl disable <service> Stop a service from starting automatically at boot (it can still be started manually). systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running List every service that is currently running — useful when you cannot remember the exact service name. journalctl -u <service> Show the full log history for a specific service — helpful for diagnosing errors. journalctl -u <service> -f Follow a service's log live — new lines appear as they are written. Press Ctrl+C to stop. journalctl -xe Show recent system-wide log messages, jumping to the end — useful when something just went wrong. journalctl --since "1 hour ago" Show all log messages from the last hour. Note: Replace <service> with the actual service name, for example ssh , nginx , or bluetooth . Common services you will encounter: ssh (remote access), NetworkManager (Wi-Fi), cron (scheduled tasks), pigpiod (GPIO daemon). 8 — Networking These commands help you check your network connection, find your Pi's address on the network, and connect to other computers remotely. Command What it does ping <address> Send test packets to a host (e.g. ping google.com ) to check whether it is reachable. Press Ctrl+C to stop. ping -c 4 <address> Send exactly 4 test packets then stop automatically. ip a Show all network interfaces and their IP addresses (the modern replacement for the older ifconfig command). ip route Show the routing table — useful for finding your router's (gateway's) IP address. hostname -I Print just the Pi's own IP address(es) in a clean format — the quickest way to look it up. nmcli device status Show the status of all network interfaces — whether Wi-Fi and Ethernet are connected. nmcli device wifi list List all nearby Wi-Fi networks visible to the Pi. nmcli device wifi connect "<SSID>" password "<pass>" Connect to a Wi-Fi network from the terminal. Replace <SSID> with the network name and <pass> with its password. ssh <user>@<address> Open a secure remote terminal session to another computer (e.g. ssh pi@192.168.1.42 ). ssh -p <port> <user>@<address> Connect via SSH on a non-standard port number. scp <file> <user>@<address>:<path> Securely copy a file to a remote computer over SSH. scp <user>@<address>:<file> . Securely copy a file FROM a remote computer to your current local folder (the dot at the end means "here"). curl -I <url> Fetch only the headers from a web URL — a quick way to check whether a web server is responding. wget <url> Download a file from the internet to the current folder. Note: The older iwconfig command (for Wi-Fi details) is deprecated on Bookworm and may not be installed. Use nmcli device status or nmcli device wifi list instead — these work correctly with Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm's NetworkManager. One-line Recipe: Find Your Pi's IP Address from Windows If you are on Windows and want to find your Pi without logging in to it, open a Command Prompt on your Windows PC and type: ping raspberrypi.local ping raspberrypi.local — sends a test packet to the hostname raspberrypi.local . If the Pi is on the same network, it will reply and Windows will show its IP address in the output. You can then use that IP to connect via SSH or a web browser. If you changed the hostname in raspi-config , substitute your custom name — e.g. ping mypihostname.local . 9 — Power and Configuration These commands control the Pi's power state and open the main configuration tool. Careful: Always shut the Pi down gracefully with one of the commands below before cutting the power. Yanking the power cable while the Pi is running can corrupt the microSD card, just like pulling a USB drive out of a Windows PC while files are being written to it. Command What it does sudo reboot Safely restart the Pi — it will shut everything down and then boot up again. sudo shutdown -h now Safely shut the Pi all the way down to a powered-off state immediately ( -h means "halt"). sudo shutdown -h +5 Schedule a safe shutdown in 5 minutes — gives others time to save their work. sudo shutdown -r 22:00 Schedule a reboot at 10 pm tonight ( -r means "reboot"). sudo shutdown -c Cancel a scheduled shutdown or reboot before it happens. sudo raspi-config Open the Raspberry Pi Configuration tool — a text menu for changing settings such as hostname, Wi-Fi country, SSH, locale, and display resolution. sudo raspi-config nonint do_ssh 0 Enable SSH from the command line without entering the menu ( 0 = enable, 1 = disable). Tip: The Pi 5 has a small physical power button on the board (next to the USB-C socket). A short press initiates a safe shutdown; once the green LED stops flashing, it is safe to disconnect the power. Press again to switch it back on. 10 — Helpful Keyboard Shortcuts in the Terminal These shortcuts work in almost any Linux terminal and will save you enormous amounts of time once they become habit. Shortcut What it does Tab Auto-complete a filename or command. Press twice to see all possibilities if there is more than one match. ↑ / ↓ Scroll through your command history — press Up to repeat the previous command, Down to move forward again. Ctrl+C Cancel (stop) a running command immediately. Ctrl+D Close the terminal session (sends an end-of-input signal, equivalent to typing exit ). Ctrl+L Clear the terminal screen (same as typing the clear command). Ctrl+A Jump to the beginning of the current line. Ctrl+E Jump to the end of the current line. Ctrl+U Delete everything from the cursor back to the start of the line — useful for quickly clearing a mistyped command. Ctrl+Z Suspend (pause) the current program and return to the prompt. Type fg to bring it back to the foreground. Ctrl+R Search backwards through your command history — start typing any part of a previous command to find it. history Print a numbered list of your recent commands. !<number> Re-run a command from your history by its number (e.g. !42 runs command number 42). !! Repeat the very last command you ran — extremely useful as sudo !! if you forgot to type sudo . clear Clear all text from the terminal screen (same as Ctrl+L ). exit Close the terminal session (same as Ctrl+D ). 11 — Pipes, Redirects and Other Useful Tricks These are not commands by themselves but special characters you can combine with commands to do more powerful things in a single line. In plain words: A pipe (the | character) connects two commands so that the output from the first flows directly into the input of the second — like connecting garden hoses end-to-end. A redirect ( > ) sends output into a file instead of the screen. Symbol / Example What it does command1 | command2 Pipe — sends the output of command1 as the input to command2 (e.g. ls -la | less lets you scroll a long file listing). command > file.txt Redirect — saves the output of a command into a file, overwriting any existing content. command >> file.txt Append redirect — adds the output to the end of an existing file without overwriting it. command1 && command2 Run command2 only if command1 succeeded without errors. command1 || command2 Run command2 only if command1 failed — useful as a fallback. command1 ; command2 Run command2 after command1 regardless of whether command1 succeeded. command & Run a command in the background so the terminal is free immediately for your next command. grep "text" file | wc -l Count how many lines in a file contain a specific word ( wc -l counts lines). ls -la | grep ".py" List only the Python files in the current folder by filtering the output with grep . 2>/dev/null Silently discard error messages — append this to a command to suppress "Permission denied" noise. One-line Recipe: Quickly Check Temperature Every 2 Seconds watch -n 2 vcgencmd measure_temp watch — runs a command repeatedly and refreshes the display on a fixed interval. -n 2 — sets the interval to 2 seconds. vcgencmd measure_temp — the command being repeated; it reads and reports the CPU temperature. The result is a live temperature display that updates every 2 seconds. Press Ctrl+C to stop. One-line Recipe: Find the Biggest Files Eating Your Disk Space sudo du -sh /home/* /var/* /tmp/* 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head -20 sudo du -sh — estimates disk usage of each listed path; -s gives a summary per item and -h shows sizes in human-readable form (MB, GB). sudo is used so that protected folders are not skipped. /home/* /var/* /tmp/* — the folders most likely to hold large user files and temporary data. 2>/dev/null — silently discards any "Permission denied" error messages so the output stays clean. | sort -rh — pipes the results into sort , ordering them largest-first ( -r reverses, -h handles human-readable sizes). | head -20 — shows only the top 20 results. One-line Recipe: Save a List of All Installed Packages dpkg --get-selections > ~/installed-packages.txt dpkg --get-selections — lists every package installed on the Pi in a format that can be restored later. > ~/installed-packages.txt — redirects the output into a file called installed-packages.txt in your home folder. Useful as a backup record before making big changes. 12 — GPIO Quick-Reference The Pi 5's 40-pin GPIO header lets you connect electronics — LEDs, buttons, sensors, and more. These commands help you work with GPIO from the terminal. All GPIO pins on the Pi 5 operate at 3.3 V logic — never connect a 5 V signal directly to a GPIO pin. In plain words: GPIO (General-Purpose Input/Output) pins are the row of metal pins along the edge of the Pi board. You can program each one to either read a signal coming in (e.g. from a button) or send a signal out (e.g. to light an LED). They are the Pi's way of talking to the physical world. Command / Library What it does pinout Display a colour-coded diagram of the Pi's GPIO pins directly in the terminal — the fastest way to look up which pin is which. gpio readall Show the current state (high/low, in/out) of every GPIO pin — requires the wiringpi package ( sudo apt install wiringpi ). sudo apt install python3-lgpio Install the lgpio library — the recommended GPIO library for Python on Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm. sudo apt install python3-gpiozero Install the gpiozero library — a beginner-friendly Python GPIO library pre-installed on Raspberry Pi OS. sudo apt install rpi.gpio Install the classic RPi.GPIO Python library (still works on the Pi 5 via a compatibility layer). raspi-gpio get Show the current function and level of all GPIO pins. raspi-gpio set <pin> op Set a GPIO pin to output mode (e.g. raspi-gpio set 17 op ). raspi-gpio set <pin> dh Drive a GPIO pin high (turn it on), e.g. to light an LED. raspi-gpio set <pin> dl Drive a GPIO pin low (turn it off). Careful: The Pi 5's GPIO pins use 3.3 V logic and have a maximum current of around 16 mA per pin. Never connect them directly to 5 V, and always use a resistor (typically 330 Ω) in series with an LED to limit the current. Damage to GPIO pins is not covered by warranty. GPIO Pin Number Systems BCM (Broadcom) Used by Python libraries (gpiozero, lgpio) e.g. GPIO 17 = chip's internal signal number Physical (Board) Pin position counted on the header e.g. Pin 11 = 11th hole from top-left of header Quick check Run pinout in the terminal to see both numbering systems side-by-side in a colour diagram There are two pin numbering systems. BCM numbers refer to the chip's internal signal numbers (used by most Python libraries). Physical numbers count the actual pin positions on the header. The pinout command shows both. Key terms Terminal — the text window where you type commands; on Raspberry Pi OS it is the black LXTerminal window. Command — a short text instruction typed at the terminal prompt that makes the Pi do something immediately. Prompt — the text the terminal shows to indicate it is ready for your next command; usually ends with a $ sign. Sudo — stands for "superuser do"; runs the following command with full administrator privileges. Root — the top-level directory of the entire Linux file system, written as / ; also the name for the administrator account. Home folder — your personal folder (e.g. /home/pi ) where your files and settings live. Permissions — the read/write/execute rules attached to each file that control who can access or run it. Package — a bundle of software (program + supporting files) managed by the apt package manager. Package manager (apt) — the tool that downloads, installs, updates, and removes software packages on Raspberry Pi OS. Service / Daemon — a background program that runs without a window, started automatically at boot (e.g. SSH, a web server). systemctl — the command used to start, stop, enable, and check the status of services. journalctl — the command used to read log messages written by services and the system. Virtual environment (venv) — a private, isolated copy of Python for one project so that installed libraries do not affect the rest of the system. Pipe ( | ) — a character that connects two commands so the output of the first feeds into the input of the second. Redirect ( > ) — a character that saves a command's output to a file instead of displaying it on screen. GPIO — General-Purpose Input/Output; the 40 programmable pins on the Pi header used to connect and control electronic components. BCM numbering — the GPIO pin numbering system based on Broadcom's internal chip numbers, used by most Python libraries. IP address — a number (e.g. 192.168.1.42 ) that identifies your Pi on the local network, used for SSH and web connections. SSH — Secure Shell; a way to open a secure remote terminal session on another computer over a network. Throttling — the Pi automatically slowing down its processor to prevent damage when it overheats or the power supply is too weak. Chapter summary Use pwd , ls , and cd to find your way around the file system; Tab auto-completes as you type. mkdir , cp , mv , and rm create, copy, move, and delete files — remember that rm is permanent with no undo. sudo grants temporary administrator power; use it only when a command genuinely needs it. Always run sudo apt update before installing or upgrading software; use sudo apt full-upgrade (not just upgrade ) on Raspberry Pi OS. On Bookworm, do not run plain pip install into the system Python — use a virtual environment ( python3 -m venv ) or install via sudo apt install python3-<name> . vcgencmd measure_temp and df -h are your quickest health checks for temperature and disk space. systemctl controls background services; journalctl reads their logs when something goes wrong. Always shut down gracefully with sudo shutdown -h now (or the physical power button) before cutting power to protect the microSD card. The pipe ( | ), redirect ( > ), and && symbols let you chain commands together into powerful one-liners. Run pinout to see a colour diagram of the GPIO pins; the Pi 5 uses 3.3 V logic — never connect a 5 V signal directly to a GPIO pin.

title: Glossary of Terms
headings: Quick reference: abbreviations at a glance
text: Every technology topic comes with its own vocabulary, and it can feel like everyone else already knows the secret language. This glossary collects every significant term used in this book and explains each one in plain English — no assumed knowledge, no shortcuts. Keep this chapter bookmarked: whenever you encounter an unfamiliar word, flip here first. How to use this glossary Entries are sorted alphabetically from A to Z. If you are looking for a specific term, scan the letter headings or use your browser's or PDF viewer's Find function ( Ctrl + F on Windows). Where two terms are closely related, cross-references appear in italics . Note: Some entries contain a short example in square brackets — these examples use the Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm command line. You do not need to type them right now; they are just there to make the definition feel concrete. A Term Meaning Active Cooler A small metal heatsink combined with a tiny fan that clips directly onto the Raspberry Pi 5's main chip. It draws heat away and blows it into the air, stopping the Pi from slowing itself down when it gets warm. Your iRasptek kit comes with one already fitted. Alias A short nickname you create for a longer command. For example, you might create the alias update to stand for sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade , so you only have to type one word. apt The main tool for installing, updating, and removing software on Raspberry Pi OS. Its full name is "Advanced Package Tool". You use it by typing sudo apt install <name> in the terminal . Think of it as the Pi's official app store, accessed from the keyboard. ARM A family of processor designs (short for "Advanced RISC Machine"). The Raspberry Pi 5 uses an ARM-based chip. ARM processors are popular in phones and single-board computers because they are power-efficient. Most software you install on the Pi is compiled specifically for the ARM architecture. Argument Extra information you pass to a command to tell it what to work on. In ls /home/pi , the folder /home/pi is the argument — it tells the ls command which folder to list. Autostart A setting that makes a program launch automatically when the Pi boots or when a user logs in, without you having to open it manually. B Term Meaning Bash The most common shell (command interpreter) on Linux and Raspberry Pi OS. When you open a terminal and start typing commands, Bash is the program reading your input and running the right programs. The name stands for "Bourne Again Shell". Bluetooth A short-range wireless technology for connecting devices — keyboards, mice, speakers, headphones — without cables. The Raspberry Pi 5 has Bluetooth 5.0 built in, which is reliable up to about 10 metres from the Pi. Boot / Booting The process of switching a computer on and loading the operating system until it is ready to use. When you press the Pi's power button, it "boots". The word comes from the old saying "pulling yourself up by your bootstraps". Bootloader A tiny program that runs before the operating system. On the Raspberry Pi 5 it lives in a chip on the board (the EEPROM ). Its job is to find the operating system on the microSD card (or SSD) and hand control over to it. Bookworm The codename for Debian version 12, which is the foundation of the current Raspberry Pi OS. Software instructions that say "Bookworm" apply to this version. Debian names its releases after characters from the film Toy Story. Breadboard A rectangular plastic board full of small holes used for building electronic circuits without soldering. Components and wires push into the holes and are held in place by friction, making it easy to experiment and rearrange. Perfect for beginners learning about GPIO . C Term Meaning CLI (Command-Line Interface) A way of controlling a computer by typing text commands rather than clicking icons. The opposite of a GUI . On the Pi, the CLI is accessed through the terminal . It feels unfamiliar at first but becomes very powerful once you know a handful of commands. Command A word (or short phrase) you type in the terminal to make the computer do something. For example, ls lists files, and pwd shows your current location. Config file A text file that stores settings for a program. Instead of clicking through menus, you edit the file to change how the program behaves. The most important low-level hardware settings file on the Pi is /boot/firmware/config.txt . Container A lightweight, self-contained package that includes an application and everything it needs to run (libraries, settings), but shares the Pi's operating system kernel. Containers made with Docker are popular for running server software cleanly without cluttering the system. CPU (Central Processing Unit) The main "brain" of the computer — the chip that carries out instructions. The Raspberry Pi 5's CPU has four cores (Arm Cortex-A76) running at up to 2.4 GHz, meaning it can work on up to four things at the same time and executes billions of steps per second. cron / crontab A built-in Linux scheduler that runs commands automatically at times you specify — for example, "back up my files every night at 2 am". You set it up by editing a file called a crontab (cron table) with the command crontab -e . Current The flow of electricity through a circuit, measured in amperes (amps, A) or milliamps (mA). Your Pi 5's power supply provides up to 5 A. GPIO pins can each safely supply only about 8–16 mA, so you usually need a resistor to protect an LED . D Term Meaning Debian A long-established, free Linux operating system maintained by a worldwide community of volunteers. Raspberry Pi OS is built on top of Debian, so it inherits Debian's software tools, package system, and stability. Ubuntu is also based on Debian. Desktop Environment The visual layer on top of Linux that gives you a GUI — windows, icons, a taskbar, and a file manager. Raspberry Pi OS uses a desktop environment called PIXEL (built on LXDE/Openbox). Without it you would only see a text terminal. DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) A service (usually running on your home router) that automatically gives every device on your network an IP address when it connects. You rarely need to configure this yourself — it just works. Directory Another word for folder — a container that holds files and other directories. On Linux, directories are separated by forward slashes: /home/pi/Documents . DNS (Domain Name System) The internet's address book. When you type a website name (like raspberrypi.com ), DNS converts it into a numeric IP address that computers can actually route to. Your router usually handles DNS automatically. Docker A popular tool for creating, running, and managing containers . With Docker you can install a complex application (like a media server or a home-automation hub) as a single command without worrying about dependencies conflicting with other software on your Pi. E Term Meaning EEPROM A tiny memory chip on the Raspberry Pi 5 board that stores the bootloader firmware. Unlike the microSD card, it keeps its contents even when power is removed. You can update it with sudo rpi-eeprom-update . Ethernet A wired networking standard. You plug a standard RJ45 network cable between your Pi and your router to get a fast, reliable internet connection. The Pi 5 supports Gigabit Ethernet (up to 1,000 Mb/s). Wired is always faster and more reliable than Wi-Fi. Environment variable A named value stored in the shell's memory that programs can read. For example, the variable HOME stores the path to your home folder. You can view all of them with the env command. F Term Meaning File A named collection of data stored on a disk — a document, a photo, a program, or a settings file. On Linux, almost everything is treated as a file, including hardware devices. File system The way files and folders are organised on a storage device. The Pi uses the ext4 file system for its main storage. Your Windows computer uses NTFS. They are like different filing systems — you need the right tools to read each one. Firewall Software (or hardware) that blocks or allows network traffic according to rules. On the Pi, ufw (Uncomplicated Firewall) is the friendliest way to set up a firewall. Think of it as a bouncer for your Pi's network connections. Firmware Software that is embedded very deeply in hardware — closer to the machine than the operating system. The Pi's bootloader is firmware. Your router, your printer, and even your keyboard all have firmware. Flag / Option A short switch you add to a command to change its behaviour. Flags usually start with a hyphen: ls -l adds the -l flag to show a detailed list. Some flags use two hyphens: apt install --yes . Folder See Directory . Both words mean the same thing — a container for files. "Folder" is the everyday word; "directory" is the technical one you'll see in Linux documentation. Function In programming, a named block of code that does one specific job. You define it once and can call it by name as many times as you like. In Python: def greet(): starts a function called greet . G Term Meaning GPIO (General Purpose Input/Output) The row of 40 metal pins on the Raspberry Pi that you can connect to electronic components (LEDs, buttons, sensors, motors). Some pins supply power, some are ground (0 V), and the "general purpose" ones can be set as either inputs or outputs by software. The Pi 5 uses 3.3 V logic — never connect 5 V signals directly to GPIO pins. gpiozero The beginner-friendly Python library for controlling GPIO pins on the Raspberry Pi. It comes pre-installed on Raspberry Pi OS. Instead of thinking in raw voltage levels, you work with simple objects like LED , Button , and Buzzer . It is the recommended library for beginners. GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) A chip designed to process graphics and video very efficiently. The Pi 5's GPU is a VideoCore VII, built into the same chip as the CPU. It handles what you see on screen and can accelerate video decoding. Group A collection of user accounts that share the same permissions. For example, the gpio group allows members to access GPIO pins, and the video group allows access to the camera. Adding your user to a group grants those extra permissions. GUI (Graphical User Interface) A visual way of using a computer — windows, buttons, icons, and menus you click with a mouse. The opposite of the CLI . Raspberry Pi OS Desktop is a GUI. Most beginners start here before learning the terminal. H Term Meaning HAT (Hardware Attached on Top) An add-on board that plugs onto the Pi's 40-pin GPIO header and sits on top of it. HATs follow a standard that includes an ID chip so the Pi can recognise what is attached. Examples: a HAT with an M.2 slot for an NVMe SSD, a display HAT, or a motor-driver HAT. HDMI (High-Definition Multimedia Interface) The standard cable for sending video and audio to a TV or monitor. The Raspberry Pi 5 has two micro-HDMI ports — smaller than the full-size HDMI port on your TV, so you need an adapter or a micro-HDMI-to-HDMI cable (included in your kit). Home Assistant An open-source smart-home platform you can run on your Pi. It lets you control smart bulbs, thermostats, door locks, and hundreds of other devices from one dashboard — without sending your data to a third-party cloud. Hostname A human-friendly name for a device on a network. The Pi's default hostname is raspberrypi . You can reach it from another computer on the same network as raspberrypi.local (using mDNS ), which is much easier than remembering an IP address. I Term Meaning I2C (Inter-Integrated Circuit) A simple two-wire communication protocol used to connect sensors, displays, and other small electronic components to the Raspberry Pi via the GPIO header. "I-squared-C" or "I-two-C" is how you say it. You enable I2C in raspi-config under Interface Options. IDE (Integrated Development Environment) A program that makes writing code easier by combining a text editor, error highlighting, and a way to run your code all in one window. Thonny is the IDE pre-installed on Raspberry Pi OS for Python beginners. Image (disk image) A single file that is an exact copy of an entire storage device — every file and every piece of system data. When you "flash" Raspberry Pi OS to a microSD card, you are writing a disk image. The file usually ends in .img or .img.xz . Image (Docker image) In the Docker world, an image is the blueprint for a container — it contains the application and all its dependencies, frozen and ready to run. You download images from Docker Hub and turn them into running containers. Input (GPIO) When a GPIO pin is set to input mode, the Pi reads the voltage on that pin — HIGH (3.3 V) or LOW (0 V) — to detect whether a button has been pressed, a sensor has triggered, or another signal has arrived. The opposite of Output (GPIO) . IP address A unique numerical label assigned to every device on a network. Local addresses look like 192.168.1.42 . Your router assigns one to your Pi automatically via DHCP . An IP address is like a postal address for network traffic. J Term Meaning Jellyfin A free, open-source media server you can run on your Pi. It organises your films, TV shows, and music and lets you stream them to phones, tablets, or smart TVs on your network — similar to a private Netflix. JSON A common text format for storing and exchanging data. Files end in .json . Many configuration files and APIs use JSON because it is easy for both humans and programs to read. K Term Meaning Kernel The deepest, most fundamental part of the operating system. The kernel talks directly to the hardware — the CPU, RAM, storage, and GPIO pins — and lets other programs use them safely. On the Pi, it is a version of the Linux kernel. You rarely interact with it directly. Kodi A popular open-source media centre application. You can install it on your Pi to turn it into a TV set-top box that plays local video files, streaming services, and live TV. LibreELEC is a minimal operating system built entirely around Kodi. L Term Meaning LED (Light-Emitting Diode) A small electronic component that produces light when current flows through it. LEDs are directional — they only work one way round. The longer leg (anode) connects to the positive side. They are the classic first GPIO project: make one blink with Python. Library A collection of pre-written code that your program can use. Instead of writing code to control a GPIO pin from scratch, you import the gpiozero library and use its ready-made functions. Libraries save enormous amounts of time. LibreELEC A tiny, specialised Linux operating system built solely to run Kodi . It boots straight into Kodi, uses minimal resources, and is designed to be very stable. It is a separate OS from Raspberry Pi OS — you flash it to its own card. Linux A free, open-source operating system kernel created by Linus Torvalds in 1991. "Linux" is now used loosely to mean any operating system built on that kernel — including Raspberry Pi OS, Ubuntu, and Debian. It runs most of the world's servers and all Android phones. LLM (Large Language Model) The type of artificial intelligence behind chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude. An LLM is trained on vast amounts of text and learns to predict and generate human-sounding language. You can run small LLMs locally on your Pi using tools like Ollama . localhost A special name (and the IP address 127.0.0.1 ) that always refers to the computer you are currently using. If you run a web server on your Pi and open http://localhost in a browser on the same Pi, you see that server's output. M Term Meaning mDNS / .local mDNS (Multicast DNS) is a technology that lets devices on a local network find each other by name without a central DNS server. Your Pi advertises itself as raspberrypi.local so that other computers on the same Wi-Fi can find it by that name instead of its IP address. microSD card A tiny flash storage card — about the size of a fingernail — used as the main storage for the Raspberry Pi OS. Your iRasptek kit includes one (64/128/256 GB), and Raspberry Pi OS may already be installed on it. The Pi reads it through the microSD slot on the underside of the board. micro-HDMI A smaller variant of the HDMI connector. The Raspberry Pi 5 has two micro-HDMI ports, allowing it to drive two screens simultaneously at up to 4K 60 fps each. You need a micro-HDMI-to-HDMI cable or adapter to connect to a standard TV or monitor. N Term Meaning Nextcloud A free, open-source file-sync and collaboration platform you can self-host on your Pi. It works like a private Dropbox or Google Drive — you store and share files on your own hardware rather than a company's servers. NVMe (Non-Volatile Memory Express) A fast type of SSD that connects via a PCIe slot. An NVMe drive in an M.2 form factor, attached to your Pi 5 via a HAT, can be five to ten times faster than a microSD card and is far more reliable for constant read/write workloads. O Term Meaning Ollama A free, open-source tool that makes it easy to download and run LLMs (AI language models) on your own computer — including the Raspberry Pi 5. With one command you can pull a model and chat with it entirely offline. Open source Software whose source code (the human-readable instructions that make it work) is freely available for anyone to read, use, modify, and share. Raspberry Pi OS, Linux, Python, LibreOffice, and VLC are all open source. It is the opposite of proprietary software like Microsoft Windows. Operating system (OS) The fundamental software that manages all the hardware and lets you run applications. Windows 11 is an operating system. So is Raspberry Pi OS. The OS sits between the hardware and your apps, handling memory, files, networking, and security so apps don't have to. Output (GPIO) When a GPIO pin is set to output mode, the Pi controls its voltage level — pulling it HIGH (3.3 V) or LOW (0 V) — to switch something on or off, such as an LED or a relay. The opposite of Input (GPIO) . P Term Meaning Package A bundle of software — the program itself plus any support files — packaged in a standard format so apt can install, update, or remove it cleanly. Every piece of software you install via sudo apt install is a package. Package manager A tool that handles installing, updating, and removing software automatically, including all the extra pieces a program depends on. On Raspberry Pi OS the package manager is apt . It saves you from manually hunting down and installing software. Path The full address of a file or folder on the file system, written as a series of directory names separated by slashes. /home/pi/Documents/myfile.txt is an absolute path (starts from the very top). Documents/myfile.txt is a relative path (starts from where you are now). PCIe (PCI Express) A high-speed hardware interface used to connect expansion cards to a computer's main board. The Raspberry Pi 5 has a PCIe 2.0 x1 connector that you can use (via an M.2 HAT) to add a fast NVMe SSD. Permissions Rules that control who can read, write, or execute each file or folder. Every file on Linux has permissions for the owning user , the owning group , and everyone else. The command ls -l shows them as a string like -rw-r--r-- . Pi-hole A DNS-based ad blocker you can run on your Pi. It acts as the DNS server for your whole home network, intercepting requests to known ad-serving domains and blocking them before they reach any device. Works on every phone, tablet, and computer in your home without installing anything on them. Pin One individual metal connector on the GPIO header. The Pi 5 has 40 pins. Each has a specific role: power supply (3.3 V or 5 V), ground (0 V), or a programmable GPIO pin. Always check a pinout diagram before connecting anything. pip The standard Python package installer. You use it to add Python libraries not included with Python itself. On Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm, you should use pip inside a virtual environment or install system packages via apt instead of running pip directly into the system Python, which is marked as "externally managed". Port (network) A numbered "door" on a device's network connection. A single IP address can receive many different types of traffic at once by using different ports. Web traffic uses port 80 (or 443 for secure HTTPS), SSH uses port 22, and so on. PWM (Pulse Width Modulation) A technique for simulating a variable voltage on a digital output pin by switching it on and off very rapidly. By changing the ratio of on-time to off-time, you can dim an LED, control the speed of a motor, or set the position of a servo. Supported on several GPIO pins of the Pi 5. Python A beginner-friendly programming language that is enormously popular for Raspberry Pi projects, data analysis, AI, and web development. Its code reads almost like English. Raspberry Pi OS comes with Python 3 pre-installed, and the Thonny IDE is designed for writing Python. Q Term Meaning Quantisation A technique for making LLM (AI) models smaller and faster by storing their internal numbers with less precision. For example, a "Q4" quantised model uses 4-bit numbers instead of 32-bit, shrinking it to roughly one-eighth of the size with only a small loss in quality. This is how large AI models can run on the Pi's limited RAM. R Term Meaning RAM (Random Access Memory) Fast, temporary working memory that the CPU uses while programs are running. The Raspberry Pi 5 in your kit has 16 GB of RAM — enough to run multiple programs, a desktop, a browser, and even a small AI model at the same time. When you switch the Pi off, RAM is wiped clean. raspi-config The official Raspberry Pi configuration tool, launched from the terminal with sudo raspi-config . It gives you a text-based menu for changing settings such as enabling SSH , I2C , SPI , the camera, Wi-Fi country, display resolution, and the hostname — all without needing to edit config files by hand. Raspberry Pi Connect An official remote-access service from the Raspberry Pi Foundation. It lets you securely view and control your Pi's desktop from any web browser, anywhere in the world, without needing to configure port-forwarding on your router. Raspberry Pi Imager The official, free tool from the Raspberry Pi Foundation for writing (flashing) an operating system image to a microSD card. You run it on your Windows PC, choose an OS, choose your card, and it downloads, verifies, and writes everything for you. It also lets you pre-configure Wi-Fi, hostname, and SSH before writing. Repository (software) An online library of software packages that apt can download from. The official Raspberry Pi and Debian repositories are already configured on your Pi. Third-party software sometimes asks you to add an extra repository before installing. Resistor A small electronic component that limits the flow of current. On a breadboard, resistors protect LEDs from burning out. They are colour-coded bands on a tiny cylinder. A 330-ohm resistor is the standard choice when connecting an LED to a 3.3 V GPIO pin. Root (filesystem) The very top of the Linux directory tree, written as a single forward slash / . Every file and directory on the system lives somewhere beneath it. It is like the C: drive on Windows, except there is only one tree covering everything. root (superuser) The all-powerful system administrator account on Linux. The root user can read, change, or delete any file. You become root temporarily by using sudo . Logging in permanently as root is dangerous because a single mistyped command can destroy the entire system. RTC (Real-Time Clock) A small, battery-backed clock circuit that keeps track of the current time even when the main power is off. The Raspberry Pi 5 has an on-board RTC battery connector. Without a battery in that connector and an internet connection, the Pi's clock resets every time you unplug it. S Term Meaning Samba A software package that lets Linux computers (including your Pi) share files and printers with Windows computers on the same network. With Samba, your Pi can appear as a shared drive in Windows Explorer. scp / SFTP Two methods for transferring files securely over a network connection. scp (Secure Copy) is a command-line tool. SFTP (SSH File Transfer Protocol) is used by graphical apps like FileZilla. Both tunnel their traffic through SSH , so they are encrypted. Script A text file containing a sequence of commands or programming instructions that the computer runs in order. A Python script ends in .py ; a Bash shell script often ends in .sh . Scripts are how you automate repetitive tasks. Server A program (or a whole computer) that listens for requests over a network and responds to them. Your Pi can act as a web server, a file server, a media server, or a home-automation server — all at the same time. Shell A program that interprets the commands you type in a terminal and runs them. The most common shell on Linux is Bash . The shell is what sits between you and the operating system kernel. SoC (System on a Chip) A single integrated circuit that contains the CPU , GPU , memory controller, and other components all on one piece of silicon. The Raspberry Pi 5's SoC is the Broadcom BCM2712. Packing everything onto one chip makes the Pi small and power-efficient. SPI (Serial Peripheral Interface) A fast, four-wire communication protocol used to connect components such as display screens, SD card readers, and analogue-to-digital converters to the Pi's GPIO pins. You enable SPI in raspi-config under Interface Options. SSH (Secure Shell) A way of logging in to another computer over a network and controlling it via a text terminal — all encrypted so nobody can eavesdrop. You use SSH from your Windows PC to connect to your Pi remotely. Enable it in Raspberry Pi OS via sudo raspi-config under Interface Options, or tick the box in the Raspberry Pi Imager before writing your card. SSH key A pair of mathematically linked files — a private key (kept on your PC) and a public key (stored on the Pi) — that let you log in via SSH without typing a password. It is both more convenient and more secure than password login. You generate a key pair with ssh-keygen on your PC. SSD (Solid-State Drive) A storage device with no moving parts that uses flash memory — much faster and more durable than old-style spinning hard drives. An NVMe SSD attached to your Pi via a HAT is the fastest storage option available. Storage Non-volatile memory that keeps files even when the power is off. On the Pi, storage is usually a microSD card. You can upgrade to an SSD for much faster performance and longer lifespan. sudo A command prefix that temporarily grants root (superuser) powers to the current user for one command. You type sudo apt install vlc rather than apt install vlc because installing software requires administrator permission. The name stands for "superuser do". swap A portion of your storage (microSD or SSD) that the operating system uses as overflow when it runs out of RAM . Because storage is far slower than RAM, heavy swap usage makes the Pi feel sluggish. With 16 GB of RAM in your kit, swap is rarely needed, but it acts as a safety net. systemd / service systemd is the system manager that starts and stops everything on modern Linux, including Raspberry Pi OS. A "service" is a background program managed by systemd — for example, a web server or SSH. You control services with sudo systemctl start <name> , sudo systemctl stop <name> , and sudo systemctl enable <name> (to start automatically at boot). T Term Meaning Terminal A program that gives you a text window where you can type commands and see the output. On Raspberry Pi OS Desktop, you open it from the taskbar or by pressing Ctrl + Alt + T . "Terminal", "console", and "command prompt" are often used interchangeably. Throttling When the Pi automatically slows its CPU down to prevent overheating. If the chip temperature rises above a threshold (typically 85 °C on the Pi 5), the Pi reduces its speed to generate less heat. The Active Cooler in your kit prevents throttling under normal conditions. Thonny A beginner-friendly Python IDE that comes pre-installed on Raspberry Pi OS. It shows your code on top and the output at the bottom, highlights errors clearly, and includes a simple debugger. It is the recommended way to write Python on the Pi if you are new to programming. U Term Meaning UART (Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter) A simple two-wire serial communication interface (one wire for sending, one for receiving) used to connect the Pi to devices such as GPS modules, serial displays, and microcontrollers like the Arduino. Available on the GPIO header; enable it in raspi-config under Interface Options. ufw (Uncomplicated Firewall) A beginner-friendly command-line tool for managing the Linux firewall . With commands like sudo ufw allow ssh and sudo ufw enable , you can quickly set rules for which network connections are allowed. Undervoltage When the Pi does not receive enough electrical voltage from its power supply. The Pi needs a stable 5.1 V; if it drops below about 4.63 V, a yellow lightning bolt appears in the corner of the screen and performance suffers. Always use the official 27 W USB-C power supply, and avoid cheap or long cables. USB (Universal Serial Bus) The standard connector family used for keyboards, mice, USB drives, and many peripherals. The Pi 5 has two USB 3.0 ports (blue, fast — up to 5 Gb/s) and two USB 2.0 ports (black, standard speed — up to 480 Mb/s). Use the blue USB 3.0 ports for USB drives or SSDs to get the full speed benefit. User An account on the system with its own files, settings, and permissions. On a fresh Raspberry Pi OS installation, you create your own username during the first-run wizard. Users cannot change system-wide settings without using sudo . V Term Meaning Variable In programming, a named box that stores a value. In Python, name = "Alice" creates a variable called name holding the text "Alice". Variables let your program remember and work with information. venv (Virtual environment) An isolated copy of Python — with its own set of installed libraries — that is separate from the system Python. Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm marks the system Python as "externally managed", meaning you cannot install packages into it directly with pip. Create a virtual environment with python3 -m venv myenv , then activate it with source myenv/bin/activate before using pip . VNC (Virtual Network Computing) A protocol for sharing a graphical desktop over a network. With a VNC client on your Windows PC and VNC enabled on the Pi, you see the Pi's full desktop in a window on your PC and can control it with your mouse and keyboard. Useful when you cannot connect a monitor directly to the Pi. Voltage The "pressure" that pushes electrical current through a circuit, measured in volts (V). The Pi's GPIO pins output 3.3 V. The power supply provides 5.1 V. Connecting a 5 V signal directly to a 3.3 V GPIO pin can permanently damage the Pi. W Term Meaning Wayland The modern display system used by Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm to draw windows on screen. It replaces the older X11 system. Most applications work with it transparently. Very occasionally, an old application only supports X11 and you may need to switch or use a compatibility layer called XWayland. Wi-Fi Wireless network connectivity using radio waves. The Raspberry Pi 5 has dual-band Wi-Fi (2.4 GHz and 5 GHz) built in. The 5 GHz band is faster but has shorter range; 2.4 GHz has longer range but is often more congested. You configure Wi-Fi during first boot or via the desktop network icon. X Term Meaning X11 / X Windows The older display system for Linux desktops, now replaced by Wayland in Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm. You may still encounter it in documentation, and some software still relies on it — in that case XWayland provides backwards compatibility. xz / tar.xz A compression format used for disk images and other large files. Raspberry Pi OS downloads often end in .img.xz . The Raspberry Pi Imager tool decompresses these automatically when it writes to your card. Y Term Meaning YAML A human-readable text format used in configuration files, particularly by Docker (docker-compose.yml) and Home Assistant . The name is a recursive acronym standing for "YAML Ain't Markup Language". It uses indentation (spaces, not tabs) to show structure, like an outline. Getting the indentation wrong causes errors, so be careful when editing. Z Term Meaning Zeroconf A set of technologies (including mDNS ) that lets devices on a local network find and talk to each other automatically, without manual configuration. It is why you can type raspberrypi.local in a browser and reach your Pi without knowing its IP address. zip / unzip A very common compression format for bundling files together. You may download zip files of projects or code. On Raspberry Pi OS you can extract them with unzip filename.zip in the terminal, or by right-clicking in the file manager. Key terms apt - the command-line tool for installing and updating software on Raspberry Pi OS. Bookworm - the codename for Debian 12, the foundation of the current Raspberry Pi OS. CLI - Command-Line Interface; controlling the computer by typing commands. GPIO - the 40 programmable pins on the Pi used to connect electronic components. gpiozero - the beginner-friendly Python library for controlling GPIO pins. GUI - Graphical User Interface; using a computer through windows and icons. HAT - Hardware Attached on Top; a standard add-on board for the Pi's GPIO header. I2C / SPI / UART - common communication protocols for connecting sensors and modules to the GPIO pins. pip - Python's package installer; on Bookworm, use it inside a virtual environment. PWM - Pulse Width Modulation; technique for producing variable power levels on a digital pin. raspi-config - the official text-menu tool for configuring the Pi's interfaces and settings. Raspberry Pi Imager - the official tool for writing an OS image to a microSD card. RTC - Real-Time Clock; battery-backed clock circuit on the Pi 5 that keeps time when power is off. SSH - Secure Shell; encrypted remote terminal access to the Pi over a network. sudo - a prefix that grants temporary administrator (root) privileges for one command. swap - disk space used as overflow when RAM is full; slower than real RAM. systemd - the system manager that starts and controls background services on the Pi. venv - a Python virtual environment; an isolated Python installation with its own libraries. VNC - Virtual Network Computing; lets you see and control the Pi's desktop remotely. YAML - "YAML Ain't Markup Language"; a human-readable text format used in config files.
